Hindus revere the river as the goddess Ganga, and cities such as Varanasi have grown up as pilgrimage centres on its banks.

facts.title: Half of a Yellow Sun
facts.body: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's novel of 2006 is set during the Nigerian Civil War of 1967 to 1970, when the breakaway state of Biafra fought for independence. Told through characters of different backgrounds, it shows the war's human cost, including famine. It won the Orange Prize for Fiction and brought the war to a new generation of readers.

facts.title: Leafcutter ants are fungus farmers
facts.body: Leafcutter ants of the Americas do not eat the leaves they carry. They chew them into a pulp to grow a fungus garden in their nest, and the fungus feeds their larvae. Ants were farming fungus millions of years before humans farmed anything.

facts.title: Fela Kuti and Afrobeat
facts.body: In Lagos in the late 1960s and 1970s, Fela Kuti, with the drummer Tony Allen, created Afrobeat, mixing highlife, jazz, funk and Yoruba rhythms. His long songs attacked corruption and Nigeria's military governments, which repeatedly persecuted him. Afrobeat became a major influence on music in Africa and beyond.

facts.title: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex
facts.body: In The Second Sex (1949), Simone de Beauvoir argued that woman has been defined as the 'Other' in relation to man, and that 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman'. Applying existentialist ideas to women's situation, she showed how femininity is shaped by society rather than nature. The book became a founding text of modern feminism.

facts.title: The Marginal Revolution
facts.body: In the early 1870s William Stanley Jevons in England, Carl Menger in Austria and Léon Walras in Switzerland independently argued that value depends on marginal utility, the extra satisfaction from one more unit of a good. This resolved the old paradox of why water, essential to life, is cheap while diamonds are dear. Their work moved economics away from labour theories of value and laid the foundations of modern microeconomics.

facts.title: Fizzy drink bubbles start on tiny flaws
facts.body: Bubbles in a fizzy drink mostly form at scratches, dust or fibres in the glass, where gas can gather. That is why streams of bubbles rise from the same spots, and why sweets dropped in cola fizz wildly.

facts.title: Justinian's Code
facts.body: In the 520s and 530s the Byzantine emperor Justinian I had centuries of Roman law collected and systematised in what later became known as the Corpus Juris Civilis. Rediscovered in Western Europe around 1100 and studied at Bologna, it became the basis of the civil law tradition used across continental Europe, Latin America and beyond.

facts.title: Kanji and Kana
facts.body: Japanese is written with a mixture of scripts. Kanji, Chinese characters adopted by around the 5th century AD, write most nouns and the stems of verbs and adjectives, while two syllabaries, hiragana and katakana, developed from simplified characters by around the 9th century. Hiragana writes grammatical endings and particles, and katakana is used mainly for foreign loanwords and emphasis.

facts.title: The Mobile Phone
facts.body: In 1973 the Motorola engineer Martin Cooper made the first call from a handheld mobile phone, in New York. Commercial cellular networks, which divide an area into cells each served by its own transmitter, opened in Japan in 1979 and in Europe and the United States in the early 1980s. Mobile phones later reached billions of people, including in regions that never had extensive landline networks.

facts.title: Australia is wider than the Moon
facts.body: Mainland Australia stretches about 4,000 km from east to west. The Moon's diameter is only about 3,475 km, so it would fit across the continent.

facts.title: The Kingdom of Kush
facts.body: Kush, on the Nile in present-day Sudan, was one of Africa's earliest states and a long-time rival of Egypt. In the 8th century BC its kings conquered Egypt and ruled it as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty. Later, centred on Meroë, Kush flourished for centuries and its rulers built many pyramids.

facts.title: The Eruption of Krakatoa
facts.body: In August 1883 the volcanic island of Krakatoa, between Java and Sumatra, was destroyed in one of the most violent eruptions in recorded history, and the tsunamis it caused killed more than 30,000 people. Its explosions were heard thousands of kilometres away, and barometers around the world recorded its pressure wave. Ash and sulphur gases thrown into the upper atmosphere caused vivid sunsets worldwide and cooled the global climate for a time; in 1888 a Royal Society report gathered observations of its effects from around the world.

facts.title: Fjords
facts.body: A fjord is a long, narrow, steep-sided sea inlet carved by a glacier and later flooded by the sea when the ice melted. Fjords are often very deep inland but shallower at the mouth, where the glacier left a ridge of rock and debris. They are typical of formerly glaciated coasts such as Norway, Chile, New Zealand, Greenland and Alaska, and the word itself is Norwegian.

facts.title: The Olympics once gave medals for art
facts.body: From 1912 to 1948 the Olympic Games held competitions in painting, sculpture, music, literature and architecture. The founder of the modern Games, Pierre de Coubertin, won a gold for a poem under a pen name.

facts.title: Citizen Kane
facts.body: Orson Welles co-wrote, directed and starred in Citizen Kane, released in 1941 when he was in his mid-twenties. Tracing the life of a newspaper tycoon through the memories of different witnesses, it used deep-focus photography, low camera angles and inventive sound. It is widely regarded as one of the most innovative films ever made.

facts.title: Major and Minor Keys
facts.body: During the 17th century the medieval church modes gave way to the major-minor system, in which music is centred on a home note, the tonic. Harmony creates tension that is resolved by returning to it, typically through the dominant chord. This tonal system underpinned Western music from the Baroque era onwards and still shapes most popular music.

facts.title: Inca Religion
facts.body: Inca religion honoured Inti, the sun god, from whom the Sapa Inca, the emperor, claimed descent, alongside the creator god Viracocha and Pachamama, the earth mother. The Coricancha temple in Cusco, adorned with gold, was its centre. Sacred places and objects called huacas, from mountains to the mummies of ancestors, were venerated across the empire, and Andean beliefs survived the Spanish conquest blended with Catholicism.

facts.title: One jellyfish can turn back its life
facts.body: The tiny jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii can, when stressed or injured, transform back into its early polyp stage and grow up all over again. In principle this lets it escape death from old age, though it still gets eaten or falls ill.

facts.title: The Lewis Dual-Sector Model
facts.body: In 1954 the St Lucian economist Arthur Lewis described developing economies as having a traditional agricultural sector with surplus labour and a modern capitalist sector. As the modern sector grows, it can draw workers from agriculture without raising wages much, until the surplus is used up. Lewis shared the 1979 Nobel memorial prize in economics, becoming the first Black laureate in a category other than peace.

facts.title: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo
facts.body: From 1977 mothers whose children had been 'disappeared' by Argentina's military dictatorship marched each week in front of the presidential palace in Buenos Aires, wearing white headscarves. Their protest defied a regime that banned public gatherings and drew world attention to state terror. Related groups later worked to trace children taken from detained parents.

facts.title: The Austronesian Languages
facts.body: Most linguists trace the Austronesian family to Taiwan, from where it spread through the Philippines and Indonesia and then across the Pacific and Indian Oceans over several thousand years. It includes Malay, Javanese, Tagalog, Malagasy in Madagascar, and the Polynesian languages of Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island. Before the colonial era it was among the most geographically widespread language families, a testament to the seafaring skills of its speakers.

facts.title: A sugar cube of neutron star weighs billions
facts.body: A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 kilometres across. Its matter is so tightly crushed that a sugar-cube-sized piece would weigh around a billion tonnes on Earth.

facts.title: Babbage's Analytical Engine
facts.body: In the 1830s Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, a general-purpose mechanical computer with a memory, a processing unit and punched-card input. It was never completed. Ada Lovelace's notes on it, published in 1843, include what is often described as the first computer program and foresaw that such machines could handle more than numbers.

facts.title: Napoleon Bonaparte
facts.body: A general of the French Revolution, Napoleon seized power in 1799 and crowned himself emperor in 1804. His armies conquered much of Europe, and his Civil Code spread legal equality far beyond France. After a disastrous invasion of Russia in 1812 he fell, and defeat at Waterloo in 1815 ended in his exile to St Helena.

facts.title: Hutton and Deep Time
facts.body: The Scottish geologist James Hutton argued in the 1780s that the Earth was shaped by slow processes still at work, such as erosion, deposition and uplift, acting over immense periods. Rock formations such as the tilted layers at Siccar Point convinced him that the Earth is vastly older than a few thousand years. His idea of deep time, developed by Charles Lyell, influenced Darwin.

facts.title: Finland holds a wife-carrying championship
facts.body: Every summer in Sonkajärvi, couples race over an obstacle course with one partner carried by the other. It is inspired by local legends about a 19th-century bandit called Rosvo-Ronkainen.

facts.title: The Mekong
facts.body: The Mekong rises on the Tibetan Plateau and flows through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam to the South China Sea. In the rainy season its floodwaters force the Tonlé Sap river in Cambodia to reverse direction and fill a great lake. Its fisheries and its delta, a major rice-growing region, feed tens of millions of people.

facts.title: The Shahnameh
facts.body: The Persian poet Ferdowsi completed the Shahnameh, or Book of Kings, around 1010 after some three decades of work. In about 50,000 couplets it tells the history of Iran from mythical times to the Arab conquest, including the deeds of the hero Rostam. Written in a Persian with few Arabic words, it helped preserve the language and is Iran's national epic.

facts.title: Umm Kulthum
facts.body: Umm Kulthum (around 1904–1975) was one of the most celebrated singers of the Arab world. Her monthly concerts in Cairo were broadcast across the region, with single songs lasting an hour or more as she varied and repeated lines to build emotion. Her funeral drew vast crowds, a measure of her place in 20th-century Arab culture.

facts.title: The brass saxophone is a woodwind
facts.body: The saxophone, patented by the Belgian Adolphe Sax in the 1840s, has a brass body. It is classed as a woodwind because its sound is made by a single reed, just like a clarinet.

facts.title: Mencius and Human Goodness
facts.body: Mencius, a Confucian thinker of the 4th century BC, argued that human nature is fundamentally good. Everyone, he said, has 'sprouts' of virtue, such as the instinctive alarm at seeing a child about to fall into a well, which must be cultivated. His later rival Xunzi held the opposite view, but Chinese tradition came to rank Mencius second only to Confucius.

facts.title: Price Elasticity of Demand
facts.body: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly the quantity bought responds to a change in price. Demand for necessities with few substitutes, such as fuel in the short run, is inelastic, so higher prices barely reduce purchases, while demand for goods with close substitutes is elastic. The concept, formalised by Alfred Marshall, helps explain why governments tax goods such as tobacco and how firms set prices.

facts.title: The English Bill of Rights
facts.body: Passed in 1689 after the Glorious Revolution placed William III and Mary II on the throne, the Bill of Rights barred the Crown from suspending laws, levying taxes or keeping a standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent. It also protected free elections and freedom of speech in Parliament. It is a cornerstone of constitutional monarchy and influenced the American Bill of Rights.

facts.title: Your body faintly glows
facts.body: Humans give off visible light, about a thousand times too weak for our eyes to detect. Japanese researchers photographed it in 2009 with very sensitive cameras; it comes from chemical reactions in the skin and peaks in the afternoon.

facts.title: The King James Bible
facts.body: The English Bible commissioned by James I was published in 1611 after work by around fifty scholars. It drew heavily on William Tyndale's translation of the 1520s and 1530s, for which Tyndale had been executed as a heretic in 1536. Its phrasing, such as 'the salt of the earth' and 'a law unto themselves', passed into everyday English and shaped English prose for centuries.

facts.title: Mesoamerican Rubber
facts.body: By around 1600 BC people in Mesoamerica were processing latex from rubber trees, mixing it with juice from morning glory vines to make it stronger and more elastic. They used it for the balls of the ritual ballgame, as well as for sandals and bindings. This chemical processing of rubber came more than 3,000 years before Charles Goodyear's vulcanisation in the 19th century.

facts.title: The Early Islamic Conquests
facts.body: In the decades after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632, Arab Muslim armies conquered the Sasanian Persian Empire and took Syria, Egypt and North Africa from the Byzantines. By the early 8th century the caliphate stretched from Spain to Central Asia. The conquests spread Arabic and, more gradually, Islam across the region.

facts.title: A cracking whip breaks the sound barrier
facts.body: The crack of a whip is a small sonic boom. As the loop travels down the tapering whip, it speeds up until the tip moves faster than sound, about 343 metres per second in air.

facts.title: Carlos Finlay and Yellow Fever
facts.body: In 1881 the Cuban physician Carlos Finlay proposed that yellow fever is spread by a mosquito, now known as Aedes aegypti. His idea was largely ignored until 1900, when a US Army commission led by Walter Reed confirmed it in Cuba. Mosquito control then sharply reduced yellow fever, notably in Havana and during the building of the Panama Canal.

facts.title: The Tibetan Plateau
facts.body: The Tibetan Plateau is the highest and largest plateau on Earth, with an average height of more than 4,500 metres. It was lifted by the same collision of India with Asia that raised the Himalayas on its southern edge. Great Asian rivers including the Yangtze, Yellow, Mekong, Indus and Brahmaputra rise there, and its ice is sometimes called the Third Pole.

facts.title: Chingiz Aitmatov
facts.body: Chingiz Aitmatov, from Soviet Kyrgyzstan, was the best-known Central Asian writer of the 20th century. His novella Jamilia of 1958, a love story set in a wartime village, was translated into French by the poet Louis Aragon, who praised it highly. Novels such as The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years combined Kyrgyz legend with reflection on Soviet life.

facts.title: September was once the seventh month
facts.body: The names September to December come from the Latin for seven to ten. The early Roman year began in March, so these really were the seventh to tenth months.

facts.title: Vedic Chant
facts.body: The Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, have been passed on orally for around three thousand years through precise chanting. The Samaveda arranges hymns specifically for melodic singing, and elaborate memorisation techniques kept the texts and their pitch accents stable. Indian tradition regards the Samaveda as a root of Indian classical music.

facts.title: Mana and Tapu in Polynesia
facts.body: Mana and tapu are key concepts across Polynesian cultures. Mana is spiritual power, authority and prestige, which can be inherited, gained or lost; tapu marks people, places and things as sacred or set apart, and breaking it brought danger. The English word 'taboo' entered the language after Captain James Cook recorded it in Tonga in 1777.

facts.title: Cacao Beans as Currency
facts.body: In Mesoamerica, cacao beans served as a form of money alongside lengths of cotton cloth. In the Aztec world they were used for small purchases in great markets such as Tlatelolco and were also paid as tribute. Spanish accounts describe counterfeit beans made by filling empty husks with earth, and cacao continued to circulate as small change in parts of colonial Mexico.

facts.title: A novel without the letter e
facts.body: Georges Perec's 1969 French novel La Disparition contains no letter e at all. Even more remarkably, its English translation, A Void by Gilbert Adair, avoids the letter too.

facts.title: Nepal's Abolition of the Monarchy
facts.body: After a decade-long Maoist insurgency and mass protests in 2006, Nepal's newly elected Constituent Assembly abolished the centuries-old Shah monarchy in May 2008 and declared a federal democratic republic. After years of deadlock, a new constitution was adopted in 2015.

facts.title: The Navajo Code Talkers
facts.body: During the Second World War the US Marine Corps recruited Navajo speakers to send messages in the Pacific in a code based on their language. Navajo was unwritten at the time for most purposes, grammatically complex and almost unknown outside the Navajo Nation, and the code was never broken by the Japanese. Their role remained classified until 1968, although many of them had been punished at school for speaking Navajo.

facts.title: The Microprocessor
facts.body: In 1971 Intel released the 4004, the first commercial microprocessor, which put a computer's whole central processing unit on one chip. It was designed by Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff and Stanley Mazor, with Masatoshi Shima of the Japanese calculator firm Busicom, which had commissioned it. Microprocessors made personal computers and countless embedded devices possible.

facts.title: Honeybees give directions by dancing
facts.body: A forager honeybee that finds food performs a 'waggle dance' in the hive. The angle of the dance relative to vertical shows the direction of the food relative to the Sun, and the length of the waggle shows the distance. Karl von Frisch shared a Nobel Prize in 1973 for decoding it.

facts.title: The Scramble for Africa
facts.body: In the late 19th century European powers raced to colonise Africa; by 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent. The Berlin Conference of 1884–85 set rules for claiming territory. Borders drawn by the colonisers, often ignoring existing peoples and states, became those of most modern African countries.

facts.title: The Raman Effect
facts.body: In 1928 Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman and his colleague Kariamanikkam Srinivasa Krishnan, working in Calcutta, found that when light is scattered by molecules a tiny fraction changes wavelength, revealing the molecules' vibrations. Raman spectroscopy became a standard way to identify substances. Raman received the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics, and India marks the discovery each year on National Science Day.

facts.title: The Aral Sea
facts.body: The Aral Sea, between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was once one of the largest lakes in the world. From the 1960s Soviet irrigation schemes diverted the rivers feeding it to grow cotton, and the lake shrank dramatically and split into separate parts. Its collapse, which left fishing towns stranded far from water, is one of the worst human-caused environmental disasters.

facts.title: One Swedish village named four elements
facts.body: Yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium are all named after Ytterby, a village near Stockholm. Its quarry yielded unusual minerals in which chemists found several new elements.

facts.title: The Canterbury Tales
facts.body: Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in the late 14th century and left it unfinished at his death in 1400. A group of pilgrims travelling to Canterbury tell each other stories, from the courtly Knight to the bawdy Miller and the Wife of Bath. Written in English rather than French or Latin, it helped establish English as a literary language.

facts.title: Bebop
facts.body: Bebop developed in New York in the 1940s around Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie and Thelonious Monk. With fast tempos, complex harmonies and virtuoso improvisation in small groups, it turned jazz from dance music into art music for listening. It set the foundation for modern jazz.

facts.title: Abraham and the Abrahamic Religions
facts.body: Abraham is revered as a founding patriarch by Judaism, Christianity and Islam, which are therefore called the Abrahamic religions. In Genesis, God calls him to leave Mesopotamia for Canaan and makes a covenant promising him countless descendants. In Islam he is Ibrahim, a prophet who with his son Ismail built the Kaaba in Mecca. Historians cannot confirm that he existed.

facts.title: Harvard is older than calculus
facts.body: Harvard was founded in 1636, decades before Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz independently developed calculus in the 1660s to 1680s. Early students studied Latin, Greek and theology rather than modern maths.

facts.title: Gresham's Law
facts.body: Gresham's law states that 'bad money drives out good': when two coins have the same legal value but different metal content, people spend the debased coin and hoard the better one. It is named after the 16th-century English financier Sir Thomas Gresham, although Nicole Oresme and Nicolaus Copernicus had described the effect earlier. The name was given in the 19th century by the economist Henry Dunning Macleod.

facts.title: From the OAU to the African Union
facts.body: The Organisation of African Unity was founded in Addis Ababa in 1963 to support decolonisation and defend the sovereignty of new states, but its principle of non-interference kept it largely silent on abuses within them. It was replaced in 2002 by the African Union, whose founding act allows intervention in a member state in cases of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

facts.title: Brazil's Língua Geral
facts.body: In colonial Brazil, Jesuit missionaries and settlers used a lingua franca based on Tupi, the língua geral, which in some regions was more widely spoken than Portuguese. In the 1750s the reforms of the Marquis of Pombal imposed Portuguese and restricted its use. A descendant, Nheengatu, is still spoken in the Amazon, and Tupi gave Portuguese and English words such as jaguar, piranha, tapioca and cashew.

facts.title: Dimples make golf balls fly further
facts.body: The dimples on a golf ball create a thin layer of turbulent air around it, which reduces drag. A dimpled ball flies much further than a perfectly smooth one.

facts.title: Gunpowder
facts.body: Gunpowder, a mixture of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal, was discovered by Chinese alchemists, probably in the 9th century. A military treatise of 1044 gives the earliest known written formulas. It was used in fire arrows, bombs and early guns, and by the 14th century cannon had spread to the Islamic world and Europe, transforming warfare.

facts.title: The Outbreak of the First World War
facts.body: On 28 June 1914 a Bosnian Serb nationalist assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, in Sarajevo. Through alliances and mobilisations, the crisis drew in Russia, Germany, France and Britain within weeks. The war brought down four empires: the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman.

facts.title: Catalysts and Enzymes
facts.body: A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up, by offering a pathway that needs less energy. Jöns Jacob Berzelius coined the term catalysis in 1835. Enzymes, mostly proteins, are the catalysts of living things, making possible the reactions of digestion, metabolism and DNA copying at body temperature.

facts.title: Venus flytraps can count
facts.body: A Venus flytrap only snaps shut when a trigger hair is touched twice within about 20 seconds, avoiding false alarms from raindrops. Research in 2016 showed it starts producing digestive enzymes only after about five touches.

facts.title: The Savanna
facts.body: A savanna is tropical grassland with scattered trees, shaped by a long dry season and frequent fires. The largest savannas are in Africa, home to great herds of grazing animals and the predators that follow them, as in the Serengeti. Similar landscapes cover large parts of Brazil, northern Australia and India.

facts.title: The Ramayana
facts.body: The Ramayana, attributed to the sage Valmiki, is a Sanskrit epic about Prince Rama, whose wife Sita is abducted by Ravana, the demon king of Lanka. With the help of the monkey hero Hanuman, Rama rescues her. Retold in many languages and art forms, from Tulsidas's Hindi version to Thai and Javanese dance, it is one of the most influential stories in Asia.

facts.title: The Sitar
facts.body: The sitar is a long-necked lute of Hindustani classical music, with a gourd resonator, movable curved frets and sympathetic strings that ring when the main strings are played. It took its form in northern India in the Mughal period, though its exact origins are debated. Its frets allow the player to pull strings to bend notes and shape the ornaments of a raga.

facts.title: Folding paper 42 times would reach the Moon
facts.body: Each fold doubles the thickness, so a sheet 0.1 millimetres thick folded 42 times would be about 440,000 kilometres thick, beyond the Moon. In practice, paper becomes impossible to fold after only a handful of folds.

facts.title: Erasmus and Christian Humanism
facts.body: Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam (died 1536) was the leading figure of northern Renaissance humanism, which sought to renew learning and Christian life by returning to classical and biblical sources. He published an edition of the Greek New Testament in 1516 and mocked the abuses of the clergy in The Praise of Folly. Though he criticised the Church, he refused to join Luther's break with Rome.

facts.title: Prospect Theory
facts.body: The psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky proposed prospect theory in 1979 to describe how people actually make decisions under risk. People judge outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, and losses loom larger than equivalent gains. Their work helped found behavioural economics, and Kahneman received the Nobel memorial prize in economics in 2002, after Tversky's death.

facts.title: The Mandate of Heaven
facts.body: The Zhou dynasty, which overthrew the Shang in the 11th century BC, justified its rule by claiming that Heaven grants the right to rule to a virtuous ruler and withdraws it from a corrupt one. Natural disasters and revolts could be read as signs that the mandate had been lost. The idea legitimised both imperial rule and successful rebellion throughout Chinese history.

facts.title: Alaska is the USA's farthest west and east
facts.body: Alaska's Aleutian Islands cross the 180° line of longitude. Some lie in the Eastern Hemisphere, making Alaska both the westernmost and easternmost US state, as well as the northernmost.

facts.title: Boycott
facts.body: In 1880 Irish tenants, organised by the Land League in a campaign against high rents and evictions, refused all dealings with Captain Charles Boycott, a land agent in County Mayo. Labourers would not work his fields and shops would not serve him. His name quickly became a word for collective refusal to deal with a person, firm or country, a tactic later used from the Indian independence movement to the campaign against apartheid.

facts.title: Radar
facts.body: Radar detects distant objects by sending out radio waves and timing their echoes. Several countries developed it in the 1930s, and Britain's Chain Home network, based on work by Robert Watson-Watt, gave early warning of German air raids in 1940. The cavity magnetron, invented in Britain in 1940, made compact, powerful radar possible, and radar later became essential for air traffic control and weather forecasting.

facts.title: Túpac Amaru II's Rebellion
facts.body: In 1780 José Gabriel Condorcanqui, a local chief of Inca descent who took the name Túpac Amaru II, led a great Andean rebellion against Spanish colonial abuses such as forced labour. He was captured and executed in Cusco in 1781, but became a lasting symbol of indigenous resistance.

facts.title: A clue was once a ball of thread
facts.body: "Clue" comes from clew, a ball of yarn. In the Greek myth, Theseus unwound a clew to find his way out of the Minotaur's labyrinth, so following a clue came to mean solving a puzzle.

facts.title: Leeuwenhoek's Animalcules
facts.body: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a draper in Delft, made tiny single-lens microscopes of remarkable power. From the 1670s he reported to the Royal Society in London that drops of water and scrapings from teeth teemed with minute creatures he called animalcules. He was the first to observe bacteria and single-celled organisms, revealing a world of life invisible to the naked eye.

facts.title: The Andes
facts.body: The Andes run some 7,000 kilometres down the western edge of South America, making them the longest continental mountain range. They were raised by the oceanic Nazca plate sliding beneath the South American plate, which also causes frequent earthquakes and volcanoes. Aconcagua in Argentina is the highest mountain outside Asia, and the range was the heartland of the Inca state.

facts.title: Madame Bovary
facts.body: Gustave Flaubert's novel, serialised in 1856 and published as a book in 1857, tells of Emma Bovary, a doctor's wife in provincial Normandy whose romantic dreams lead to adultery, debt and suicide. Flaubert was prosecuted for offending public morals and acquitted. His precise, impersonal style made the book a model of literary realism.

facts.title: A fungus turns ants into puppets
facts.body: In tropical forests a fungus infects carpenter ants and makes them climb a plant and clamp their jaws on a leaf vein. The fungus then grows out of the ant and showers spores on the ants below.

facts.title: Arabic Maqam
facts.body: A maqam is a melodic mode of Arabic music, defined by its scale, typical phrases and character. Some maqams use intervals between a semitone and a whole tone, often described as quarter tones. Musicians move between maqams within a piece, and improvise on them in solo preludes called taqsim.

facts.title: Ma'at in Ancient Egypt
facts.body: In ancient Egyptian religion, Ma'at was both a goddess and the principle of truth, justice and cosmic order. The pharaoh's central duty was to uphold ma'at against chaos. In the judgement of the dead, as depicted in the Book of the Dead, a person's heart was weighed against the feather of Ma'at, and only a heart in balance could pass into the afterlife.

facts.title: Debasement of the Roman Coinage
facts.body: Roman emperors repeatedly reduced the silver content of the denarius and its successor coins to stretch limited bullion and pay their armies. During the crisis of the 3rd century AD the silver coinage was debased until it was little more than bronze with a thin silver wash. Prices rose sharply and trust in the currency collapsed, a classic case of inflation caused by debasing money.

facts.title: Ancient corals recorded shorter days
facts.body: Growth bands in fossil corals about 400 million years old suggest a year then had roughly 400 days. Earth spun faster, so each day lasted about 22 hours; tidal friction has been slowing it ever since.

facts.title: UN Peacekeeping
facts.body: The first UN military observer mission was sent to the Middle East in 1948, and the first armed peacekeeping force was deployed in 1956 during the Suez Crisis. Blue-helmeted peacekeepers, contributed by member states and lightly armed, monitor ceasefires and help carry out peace agreements, normally with the consent of the parties. UN peacekeeping forces received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988.

facts.title: The Bantu Expansion
facts.body: The Bantu languages, a branch of the Niger–Congo family, are spoken across most of Africa south of the equator, from Kikongo and Swahili to Zulu and Shona. Their close similarities reflect a spread of farming peoples from the region of today's Nigeria and Cameroon that began several thousand years ago. Bantu languages typically sort nouns into many classes marked by prefixes, as in Swahili mtu (person) and watu (people).

facts.title: Stepwells of India
facts.body: Stepwells are deep wells reached by long flights of steps, built especially in western India to give access to groundwater that rose and fell with the monsoon. They also offered a cool place to gather and worship, and many were richly carved. Rani ki Vav in Gujarat, built in the 11th century, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

facts.title: People chase a cheese down an English hill
facts.body: At Cooper's Hill in Gloucestershire, competitors race a round of Double Gloucester cheese down a very steep slope. The first to the bottom wins the cheese.

facts.title: Cahokia
facts.body: Cahokia, near present-day St Louis, was the largest settlement of the Mississippian culture and of pre-Columbian North America north of Mexico. At its height, around 1050–1200, it was dominated by Monks Mound, a huge earthen platform, and probably housed ten thousand or more people, though estimates vary widely. It was largely abandoned by the late 14th century.

facts.title: Babylonian Astronomy
facts.body: For centuries Babylonian scribes recorded the movements of the Moon and planets on clay tablets. In the 1st millennium BC they developed arithmetical methods to predict lunar phenomena, including eclipses, among the first mathematical astronomy anywhere. Their base-60 number system survives in the 60 minutes of an hour and the 360 degrees of a circle.

facts.title: The Mercator Projection
facts.body: In 1569 the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator published a world map on which lines of constant compass bearing appear as straight lines, a great help to navigators. The price is distortion of size, which grows towards the poles. Greenland looks about as large as Africa, though Africa is many times bigger.

facts.title: Birds cannot feel the heat of chillies
facts.body: Birds lack the receptor that makes capsaicin feel hot, so they happily eat chillies. That suits the plant: birds swallow the seeds whole and spread them, while mammals would chew and destroy them.

facts.title: Satyajit Ray's Apu Trilogy
facts.body: The Bengali director Satyajit Ray released Pather Panchali in 1955, the first film of a trilogy following Apu from a village childhood to adulthood in Calcutta. Shot on a tiny budget with largely non-professional actors, it brought Indian cinema to international attention. Ray received an honorary Academy Award shortly before his death in 1992.

facts.title: Claude Debussy
facts.body: Debussy (1862–1918) broke with traditional harmony in works such as Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune and La Mer, using whole-tone and pentatonic scales and chords valued for their colour. Hearing a Javanese gamelan in Paris in 1889 influenced him. He is often called an Impressionist, a label he disliked, and his work opened the way to 20th-century music.

facts.title: Aquinas's Five Ways
facts.body: Thomas Aquinas (around 1225–1274), a Dominican friar, combined Aristotle's philosophy with Christian theology in his unfinished Summa Theologiae. In it he offered five ways of showing that God exists, arguing from motion, causation, contingency, degrees of perfection and the order of nature. He held that reason and faith cannot truly conflict, and his synthesis became central to Catholic teaching.

facts.title: Male seahorses give birth
facts.body: In seahorses the female places her eggs in a pouch on the male's belly. He fertilises them, supplies oxygen and nutrients, then after a few weeks pushes out dozens or hundreds of fully formed babies.

facts.title: Diminishing Returns
facts.body: The law of diminishing returns states that adding more of one input, such as labour, to a fixed amount of another, such as land, eventually yields smaller and smaller increases in output. Classical economists including David Ricardo and Thomas Malthus used it to explain rising rents and the limits to food production. It underlies much economic reasoning about costs and production.

facts.title: Ibn Khaldun's Asabiyyah
facts.body: In the Muqaddimah (1377), the North African scholar Ibn Khaldun argued that dynasties rise on asabiyyah, the group solidarity of hardy, often nomadic peoples, and decline as luxury erodes it, typically within a few generations. His cyclical theory of how states form and fall has earned him a place among the forerunners of sociology and political science.

facts.title: Dhvani: Suggestion in Sanskrit Poetics
facts.body: The Kashmiri critic Anandavardhana argued in the 9th century that the soul of poetry is dhvani, 'suggestion': meaning that is neither stated nor logically implied but evoked. A poem may describe only a scene, for example, yet convey longing. His theory, developed by Abhinavagupta, became central to Sanskrit poetics and anticipates modern ideas about implied meaning and connotation.

facts.title: Popcorn pops because of steam
facts.body: Each popcorn kernel holds a little water inside a tough hull. Heated to about 180 degrees Celsius, the water turns to high-pressure steam until the hull bursts and the starch puffs into foam.

facts.title: The Cotton Gin
facts.body: In 1793 Eli Whitney invented the cotton gin, a machine that quickly separated cotton fibres from their sticky seeds. It made short-staple cotton profitable to grow across the American South. The result was a huge expansion of cotton plantations and of slavery, which grew sharply in the decades that followed.

facts.title: The Rwandan Genocide
facts.body: Over about a hundred days from April 1994, Hutu extremists in Rwanda killed hundreds of thousands of people, with estimates ranging from about 500,000 to over 800,000, mostly from the Tutsi minority, along with moderate Hutu. The international community, including UN peacekeepers on the ground, failed to stop it. It ended when the Tutsi-led Rwandan Patriotic Front took control of most of the country.

facts.title: The Genetic Code
facts.body: In 1961 Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei took the first step in cracking the genetic code, showing that RNA made only of the base U produces a chain of the amino acid phenylalanine. By the mid-1960s it was known that each sequence of three bases, a codon, specifies one of 20 amino acids or a stop signal. The code is almost the same in all living things, strong evidence of their common ancestry.

facts.title: Ethiopia's calendar has thirteen months
facts.body: The Ethiopian calendar has twelve months of 30 days plus a short thirteenth month of five or six days. It also counts years differently, running about seven to eight years behind the Gregorian calendar.

facts.title: The Rocky Mountains
facts.body: The Rockies stretch roughly 4,800 kilometres from western Canada to New Mexico in the United States. Along them runs the Continental Divide, which separates rivers draining to the Pacific from those draining to the Atlantic, the Gulf of Mexico and the Arctic. The range was a formidable barrier to westward travel in the 19th century.

facts.title: The Bust of Nefertiti
facts.body: This painted limestone bust of Queen Nefertiti, wife of the pharaoh Akhenaten, was made in the 14th century BC and found in 1912 in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose at Amarna. With its elegant long neck and tall crown, it is one of the most famous images from ancient Egypt. It is kept in Berlin, and Egypt has long called for its return.

facts.title: K-pop
facts.body: K-pop is South Korean pop music produced by agencies that train singers and dancers for years before their debut. Its modern form is often traced to Seo Taiji and Boys in 1992. In the 21st century, through the internet and acts such as BTS, it became a global phenomenon and a pillar of South Korea's cultural influence.

facts.title: A melted sweet led to the microwave oven
facts.body: In the 1940s engineer Percy Spencer was working near a radar magnetron when a sweet in his pocket melted. He realised microwaves could heat food, and his company Raytheon built the first microwave ovens.

facts.title: Nagarjuna and Emptiness
facts.body: Nagarjuna, an Indian monk who probably lived in the 2nd century AD, founded the Madhyamaka, or 'Middle Way', school of Mahayana Buddhism. He argued that all things are empty (shunyata) of independent, inherent existence, because everything arises in dependence on other things. He is often considered the most important Buddhist philosopher after the Buddha himself.

facts.title: The Islamic Gold Dinar
facts.body: In the 690s the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik replaced Byzantine- and Persian-style coins with a new gold dinar and silver dirham bearing Arabic religious inscriptions instead of images. The standardised coinage helped unify the economy of an empire stretching from North Africa to Central Asia. The dinar became one of the leading trade currencies of the medieval Mediterranean and Middle East.

facts.title: The American Civil Rights Movement
facts.body: Through boycotts, sit-ins and marches, including the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955–56 sparked by Rosa Parks and the 1963 March on Washington, African Americans challenged segregation and disenfranchisement in the South. Led by figures such as Martin Luther King Jr., the movement won the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

facts.title: Goosebumps are left over from furry ancestors
facts.body: When you feel cold or thrilled, tiny muscles pull each body hair upright, making goosebumps. In furrier mammals this fluffs up the coat to trap warm air or to look bigger, but on our thin hair it does almost nothing.

facts.title: The Turkic Languages
facts.body: The Turkic languages, including Turkish, Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Kazakh, Uyghur, Tatar and Yakut, stretch from the Balkans to north-eastern Siberia. Their earliest substantial texts are the 8th-century Orkhon inscriptions in Mongolia, carved in an Old Turkic script that resembles runes. Some scholars group Turkic with Mongolic and Tungusic in an 'Altaic' family, but most linguists now attribute their similarities to long contact rather than common descent.

facts.title: Zhang Heng's Seismoscope
facts.body: In AD 132 the Chinese scholar Zhang Heng built an instrument to detect earthquakes. According to historical accounts, a bronze vessel with dragon heads dropped a ball into the mouth of a bronze toad to indicate the direction of a distant tremor. It is the earliest known seismoscope, though its inner mechanism is not known for certain.

facts.title: The Maurya Empire and Ashoka
facts.body: Founded by Chandragupta Maurya around 320 BC, the Maurya Empire was the first to unite most of the Indian subcontinent. His grandson Ashoka, appalled by the bloodshed of his conquest of Kalinga, embraced Buddhism and promoted non-violence. His edicts, carved on rocks and pillars, are among India's oldest written records.

facts.title: Moon footprints could last for ages
facts.body: The bootprints left by Apollo astronauts may survive for millions of years. The Moon has no wind, rain or flowing water to wipe them away, only a very slow rain of tiny meteorites.

facts.title: John Snow and Cholera
facts.body: During a cholera outbreak in London's Soho in 1854, the physician John Snow mapped the deaths and found them clustered around a water pump on Broad Street. He persuaded the authorities to remove the pump's handle, arguing that cholera spread through contaminated water rather than bad air. His work is a founding example of epidemiology.

facts.title: The Southern Alps
facts.body: The Southern Alps run along most of the length of New Zealand's South Island. They are being pushed up along the Alpine Fault, where the Pacific and Australian plates meet, and Aoraki/Mount Cook is their highest peak. Westerly winds drop heavy rain and snow on the western side, feeding glaciers and rainforest, while the plains to the east lie in a much drier rain shadow.

facts.title: Bernini
facts.body: Gian Lorenzo Bernini was the leading sculptor and architect of Baroque Rome in the 17th century. Marble works such as Apollo and Daphne and The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa capture moments of intense movement and emotion. He also designed the colonnade of St Peter's Square, which embraces visitors like a pair of arms.

facts.title: The Byzantines never called themselves Byzantine
facts.body: People of the eastern empire ruled from Constantinople called themselves Romans until its fall in 1453. The label 'Byzantine' was popularised by Western scholars, notably Hieronymus Wolf in the 16th century.

facts.title: John Cage's 4′33″
facts.body: In 1952 the pianist David Tudor premiered John Cage's 4′33″, in which the performer plays nothing for three movements. The piece consists of whatever sounds occur in the room. It challenged the boundary between music and noise and remains a central reference in debates about what music is.

facts.title: The Aztec Fifth Sun
facts.body: The Aztecs believed the world had been created and destroyed four times and that they lived in the age of the Fifth Sun, which would also end in catastrophe. The gods had sacrificed themselves to set the sun in motion, so humans owed them a debt to be repaid in blood. This belief underpinned the human sacrifices at the Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan, dedicated to the war god Huitzilopochtli and the rain god Tlaloc.

facts.title: The Malthusian Trap
facts.body: In 1798 Thomas Malthus argued that population tends to grow geometrically while food supply grows only arithmetically. Any rise in living standards would therefore be absorbed by population growth until famine, disease or restraint brought it back down. His model fits much of pre-industrial history, but the sustained growth of productivity since the Industrial Revolution allowed much of the world to escape the trap.

facts.title: Rodin's Thinker was first called The Poet
facts.body: The famous figure began as part of Rodin's Gates of Hell, a doorway inspired by Dante's Divine Comedy, where it sat above the door and was called The Poet. Many think it was meant to show Dante pondering his great work.

facts.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
facts.body: This clay cylinder, inscribed in Akkadian after Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC, describes how he restored temples and allowed displaced peoples to return home. It is sometimes called the first charter of human rights, but most historians regard that label as anachronistic, since the text follows a traditional Mesopotamian genre of royal propaganda.

facts.title: The Indo-European Homeland Debate
facts.body: Where Proto-Indo-European was spoken has long been debated. The steppe (or Kurgan) hypothesis places it north of the Black and Caspian Seas around 4000–3000 BC, while the Anatolian hypothesis links its spread to early farmers moving out of Anatolia. Ancient DNA studies published from 2015 onwards found large population movements from the steppe into Europe around 3000 BC, which many scholars see as strong support for the steppe view.

facts.title: Breaking Enigma
facts.body: The German military encrypted messages with the Enigma machine, whose rotors changed the cipher with every key pressed. Polish mathematicians led by Marian Rejewski first broke it in the 1930s and shared their methods with Britain and France in 1939. At Bletchley Park, Alan Turing and others built electromechanical machines called bombes to break Enigma traffic, producing intelligence that influenced the course of the Second World War.

facts.title: Giraffes have as many neck bones as you
facts.body: Despite its enormous neck, a giraffe has seven neck vertebrae, the same number as a human and almost every other mammal. Each giraffe vertebra is simply much longer, some over 25 centimetres.

facts.title: The Unification of Germany
facts.body: Guided by Otto von Bismarck, Prussia won wars against Denmark in 1864, Austria in 1866 and France in 1870–71. In January 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles, with the Prussian king as emperor. The new state, which excluded Austria, quickly became a leading industrial and military power.

facts.title: The Discovery of Insulin
facts.body: In 1921 and 1922 Frederick Banting and Charles Best, in John Macleod's laboratory in Toronto and with the chemist James Collip, isolated insulin from the pancreas. Injected into a diabetic boy in January 1922, it brought his blood sugar under control. Insulin turned type 1 diabetes from a fatal disease into a manageable one, and Banting and Macleod received the 1923 Nobel Prize.

facts.title: The Anthropocene
facts.body: The Anthropocene is a proposed new epoch of Earth's history in which human activity has become a dominant influence on climate, landscapes and ecosystems. The term was popularised around 2000 by the atmospheric chemist Paul Crutzen. In 2024 the relevant geological body voted not to adopt it as a formal unit of the geological time scale, but it remains widely used informally.

facts.title: Sunlight is ancient by the time it leaves
facts.body: Energy made in the Sun's core takes tens of thousands of years or more to reach the surface, as light is absorbed and re-emitted countless times. Once out, it reaches Earth in about eight minutes.

facts.title: The Epic of Sundiata
facts.body: The Epic of Sundiata tells of the founder of the Mali Empire in the 13th century, a boy unable to walk who grows into a hero and defeats the sorcerer-king Sumanguru. It has been passed down orally for centuries by griots, the hereditary bards of West Africa who are also historians and genealogists. It is one of the great epics of African oral literature.

facts.title: Gagaku
facts.body: Gagaku is the court music of Japan, built largely on music imported from China and Korea from about the 6th century and established at court by the 8th. Played by instruments such as the shō mouth organ, the hichiriki oboe, flutes, lutes, zithers and drums, it has been maintained at the imperial court for more than a thousand years. It is often described as one of the oldest orchestral traditions still performed.

facts.title: Heraclitus and Flux
facts.body: Heraclitus of Ephesus, active around 500 BC, taught that everything is in flux, an idea summed up in the saying attributed to him that you cannot step into the same river twice. He held that the world is a unity of opposites in constant tension, ordered by the logos, a rational principle. His near-contemporary Parmenides argued that change is an illusion, and their clash shaped Greek metaphysics.

facts.title: Reno lies west of Los Angeles
facts.body: Although Nevada is east of California, Reno is farther west than Los Angeles. California's coast curves south-east, so LA sits well to the east of much of the state.

facts.title: The China Shock
facts.body: After China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, its exports of manufactured goods surged. The economists David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson found that the parts of the United States most exposed to Chinese import competition suffered lasting losses of manufacturing jobs and lower wages. Their research on this 'China shock' challenged the assumption that workers displaced by trade easily find other work.

facts.title: The May Fourth Movement
facts.body: On 4 May 1919 students in Beijing protested against the Paris Peace Conference's decision to transfer Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan rather than return them to China. The protests grew into a broad cultural and political movement championing science, democracy and writing in vernacular Chinese. Its activists included several founders of the Chinese Communist Party, established in 1921.

facts.title: Arabic Words in European Languages
facts.body: Medieval contact through Spain, Sicily and the Mediterranean brought many Arabic words into European languages. Algebra comes from al-jabr in the title of a book by al-Khwarizmi, whose own name gave algorithm; zero and cipher come from Arabic sifr, itself a translation of Sanskrit śūnya, 'empty'. Admiral, alchemy, alcohol, sugar and tariff also reached English through Arabic.

facts.title: A one-page piano piece lasting 18 hours
facts.body: Erik Satie's Vexations is only a page long, but a note on it is often read as asking for 840 repetitions. When John Cage organised a full performance in 1963, a team of pianists took about 18 hours.

facts.title: Papyrus
facts.body: The ancient Egyptians made a writing material from the papyrus reed of the Nile by laying strips of its pith crosswise and pressing them together. It was in use by around 3000 BC and became the main writing surface of the Mediterranean world for thousands of years. The word paper comes from papyrus, though true paper is made differently, from pulped fibres.

facts.title: The Code of Hammurabi
facts.body: Hammurabi, king of Babylon in the 18th century BC, had nearly 300 laws inscribed on stone stelae; the best-preserved is in the Louvre. It is one of the most complete early legal texts. Its punishments often followed 'an eye for an eye' and varied with social rank.

facts.title: Archimedes' Principle
facts.body: In the 3rd century BC Archimedes of Syracuse showed that a body immersed in a fluid is pushed upwards by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. The principle explains why ships float and balloons rise. The famous story of his discovery in the bath comes from a later Roman writer and may be legend.

facts.title: Young sunflowers follow the Sun
facts.body: Growing sunflowers turn east to west during the day and swing back at night, guided by an internal clock. Once they bloom they stop and face east, which warms the flowers in the morning and attracts more bees.

facts.title: The Congo River
facts.body: The Congo carries more water to the sea than any other river except the Amazon. It flows in a great arc through central Africa, crossing the equator twice, and parts of it are among the deepest river channels known. Its basin holds the world's second-largest tropical rainforest.

facts.title: The Parthenon
facts.body: The Parthenon was built on the Acropolis of Athens between 447 and 432 BC as a temple to the goddess Athena. Designed by Ictinus and Callicrates, with sculpture overseen by Phidias, it is the supreme example of the Doric order. Many of its surviving sculptures, the Elgin Marbles, are in the British Museum, and Greece has long sought their return.

facts.title: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina
facts.body: Palestrina (around 1525–1594) spent his career in Rome writing polyphonic sacred music, including the Missa Papae Marcelli. A popular legend that this mass persuaded the Council of Trent not to ban polyphony is unfounded. His smooth, clear voice-leading became the model for teaching counterpoint for centuries.

facts.title: Diamonds can burn
facts.body: Diamond is pure carbon, so heated strongly in oxygen it burns to carbon dioxide like coal. In the 1770s Antoine Lavoisier burned diamonds with a giant magnifying lens to show this.

facts.title: The Four Aims of Hindu Life
facts.body: Classical Hindu thought names four legitimate goals of human life, the purusharthas: dharma (duty and righteousness), artha (wealth and power), kama (pleasure and love) and moksha (liberation from rebirth). The first three are to be pursued in balance, with dharma guiding the others, while moksha is the highest goal. The scheme frames classical Indian works from the Arthashastra on statecraft to the Kamasutra.

facts.title: The Drain of Wealth Theory
facts.body: Dadabhai Naoroji, an Indian economist and politician, argued in the late 19th century that British rule was draining India's wealth. Through payments such as pensions and salaries of British officials and interest on debt, a large share of India's revenue flowed to Britain without return. His book Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901) shaped Indian nationalist economic thought.

facts.title: Tocqueville's Democracy in America
facts.body: After travelling through the United States in 1831–32, the French aristocrat Alexis de Tocqueville published Democracy in America in two volumes, in 1835 and 1840. He admired Americans' local self-government and voluntary associations, but warned of the 'tyranny of the majority' and of a soft despotism of conformity. It is a classic analysis of democratic society.

facts.title: Iceland celebrates Christmas with a book flood
facts.body: In Iceland it is a tradition to give books on Christmas Eve and spend the night reading. The pre-Christmas rush of new titles is called Jólabókaflóð, the 'Christmas book flood'.

facts.title: The Māori Language Revival
facts.body: By the 1970s te reo Māori was spoken by a shrinking and ageing population after decades in which schools had discouraged it. Activists responded: a petition in 1972 led to an annual Māori Language Day, and from 1982 kōhanga reo, 'language nests', immersed preschool children in Māori. The Māori Language Act 1987 made it an official language of New Zealand, and the revival has inspired indigenous language movements elsewhere.

facts.title: The Shinkansen
facts.body: Japan's Shinkansen, the first high-speed railway, opened between Tokyo and Osaka in 1964, just before the Tokyo Olympics. Running on dedicated, purpose-built tracks, its bullet trains cut the journey time dramatically. It inspired high-speed rail in Europe and elsewhere, and is known for its punctuality and safety.

facts.title: The Aztec Empire
facts.body: The Mexica, or Aztecs, founded their capital Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, traditionally in 1325, and through a triple alliance came to dominate central Mexico. In 1519–1521 Hernán Cortés, aided by many thousands of indigenous allies and by smallpox, destroyed the empire, and Mexico City was built on its ruins.

facts.title: Green Eggs and Ham uses just 50 words
facts.body: Dr Seuss wrote Green Eggs and Ham after his publisher bet him he could not write a book using only 50 different words. He managed it and won the bet.

facts.title: Yukawa and the Strong Force
facts.body: In 1935 the Japanese physicist Hideki Yukawa proposed that protons and neutrons are held together in the nucleus by a force carried by a new particle, later called the meson. He predicted its mass from the short range of the force. A particle matching his prediction, the pion, was found in 1947, and in 1949 Yukawa became the first Japanese Nobel laureate.

facts.title: Yellowstone
facts.body: Yellowstone, mostly in Wyoming, was established in 1872 and is widely regarded as the world's first national park. It sits on a volcanic hotspot that has produced enormous eruptions in the distant past, and its heat drives famous geysers such as Old Faithful and hot springs. The park's creation set a model for protected areas around the world.

facts.title: Wole Soyinka
facts.body: The Nigerian playwright and poet Wole Soyinka became the first Black African to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1986. Plays such as Death and the King's Horseman blend Yoruba myth and ritual with European dramatic forms. He was imprisoned during the Nigerian Civil War and became an outspoken critic of military dictatorship.

facts.title: Some mushrooms glow in the dark
facts.body: Over a hundred kinds of fungi give off a soft green light, once called 'foxfire'. In Japan, Mycena chlorophos lights up damp forests at night. The glow may attract insects that help spread spores.

facts.title: Consonance and Dissonance
facts.body: Consonant intervals sound stable and at rest, while dissonant ones sound tense and seem to require resolution. Intervals with simple frequency ratios tend to be heard as consonant, but the boundary is partly cultural. Medieval theorists treated thirds as imperfect, while later Western harmony was built on them.

facts.title: The Trolley Problem
facts.body: In 1967 the British philosopher Philippa Foot posed a dilemma: a runaway tram will kill five people unless it is diverted onto a track where it will kill one. Most people think diverting it is permissible, yet few approve of pushing someone into its path to save five, though the numbers are the same. Developed further by Judith Jarvis Thomson, the 'trolley problem' probes the moral difference between killing and letting die, or intending and foreseeing harm.

facts.title: The 1997 Asian Financial Crisis
facts.body: In July 1997 Thailand was forced to abandon the peg of the baht to the US dollar after speculative attacks. Panic spread to Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia and other economies that had borrowed heavily in foreign currencies, and their currencies and stock markets collapsed. The IMF's rescue packages, with conditions of austerity and reform, were highly controversial, and Indonesia's crisis contributed to the fall of Suharto in 1998.

facts.title: Multiplying ones makes a perfect palindrome
facts.body: Multiply 111,111,111 by itself and you get 12,345,678,987,654,321. The digits climb from 1 to 9 and back down because of the way the carries line up when long multiplication adds the columns.

facts.title: The Law of the Sea Convention
facts.body: Concluded in 1982 after nearly a decade of negotiation, the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea sets the legal framework for the world's oceans. It fixes territorial waters at up to 12 nautical miles and gives coastal states exclusive economic zones of up to 200 nautical miles, while treating the deep seabed beyond national jurisdiction as the common heritage of mankind.

facts.title: Yan Fu's Three Principles of Translation
facts.body: Yan Fu introduced Western ideas to China through translations of works such as Thomas Huxley's Evolution and Ethics, published in the late 1890s, and Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations. In his preface to the Huxley translation he set out three criteria for a good translation: faithfulness (xin), expressiveness (da) and elegance (ya). The formula became a touchstone of translation theory in China.

facts.title: Roman Aqueducts
facts.body: The Romans built aqueducts that carried water over long distances to cities using only a slight, steady downhill gradient. Most of each channel ran underground or at ground level, with arched bridges such as the Pont du Gard in France used to cross valleys. By the 3rd century AD eleven aqueducts supplied the city of Rome with water for fountains, baths and public latrines.

facts.title: Revolutionary France tried ten-hour days
facts.body: After the Revolution, France introduced a calendar with ten-day weeks and days named after plants, animals and tools. For a while it even promoted decimal clocks with ten hours a day, but they never caught on.

facts.title: The Qing Conquest of China
facts.body: In 1644 rebels took Beijing and the last Ming emperor killed himself; Manchu forces from the north-east then seized the city and founded the Qing dynasty. Over the following decades the Qing conquered all of China, and under emperors such as Kangxi and Qianlong greatly expanded it, adding Taiwan, Mongolia, Xinjiang and Tibet.

facts.title: Hippocratic Medicine
facts.body: Hippocrates of Kos, who lived in the 5th and 4th centuries BC, is regarded as the father of Western medicine. The writings attributed to him, in fact by many authors, treat illness as having natural rather than divine causes and stress careful observation of patients. The Hippocratic Oath, a pledge of medical ethics, is named after him.

facts.title: The Tundra
facts.body: Tundra is a treeless landscape of mosses, lichens, grasses and low shrubs, found around the Arctic and above the tree line on high mountains. The growing season is short, and in the Arctic the subsoil stays permanently frozen as permafrost. Thawing permafrost releases stored carbon, which is why the tundra matters for climate change.

facts.title: The chess queen was once very weak
facts.body: In early chess the queen's place was held by a counsellor that moved only one square diagonally. Around the late 15th century, probably in Spain, the queen gained her powerful sweeping moves.

facts.title: The Moai of Rapa Nui
facts.body: The people of Rapa Nui, or Easter Island, carved nearly a thousand monumental stone figures known as moai, most of them between roughly the 13th and 16th centuries. Thought to represent deified ancestors, many stood on stone platforms facing inland, watching over the communities. How they were moved is debated, though many researchers think they were 'walked' upright with ropes.

facts.title: The Notre-Dame School
facts.body: Around 1200, composers linked to Notre-Dame cathedral in Paris, notably Léonin and Pérotin, elaborated plainchant into organum by adding new voices above it. Pérotin wrote pieces for up to four voices. Their use of rhythmic patterns in notation was a decisive step towards the measured polyphony at the heart of later Western music.

facts.title: Shinto
facts.body: Shinto is the indigenous religion of Japan, centred on the worship of kami, spirits present in nature, places, ancestors and outstanding people. It has no founder or single scripture and focuses on ritual purity, shrines and festivals. For centuries it coexisted and blended with Buddhism, and from the Meiji period until 1945 a state form of Shinto was promoted to support the cult of the emperor.

facts.title: Mantis shrimp see colour unusually
facts.body: Mantis shrimp have more than ten types of colour receptor, compared with our three. Yet tests show they are poor at telling similar colours apart; they seem to recognise colours instantly instead of comparing signals as our brains do.

facts.title: The Arthashastra
facts.body: The Arthashastra is an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, economic policy and military strategy, traditionally attributed to Kautilya, adviser to the emperor Chandragupta Maurya. It discusses taxation, state control of mines and trade, market regulation and the management of the treasury. Many scholars think the surviving text was compiled and revised over several centuries, so its date and authorship are debated.

facts.title: The Meiji Constitution
facts.body: Promulgated in 1889, the Constitution of the Empire of Japan was the first modern constitution in East Asia. Modelled largely on Prussia's, it created an elected lower house in a parliament called the Diet but kept sovereignty with the emperor and gave the armed forces direct access to him. That weak civilian control is often seen as helping militarists dominate government in the 1930s.

facts.title: Coptic
facts.body: Coptic is the last stage of the ancient Egyptian language, written from the early centuries AD in the Greek alphabet with several extra letters taken from Demotic. It was the language of Christian Egypt until Arabic gradually replaced it after the Arab conquest, and it survives as the liturgical language of the Coptic Church. Champollion's knowledge of Coptic was crucial to his decipherment of hieroglyphs.

facts.title: A fluffy cloud weighs hundreds of tonnes
facts.body: A typical small cumulus cloud holds hundreds of tonnes of water in tiny droplets. It floats because the droplets are spread through a huge volume of air and rising air currents keep them aloft.

facts.title: The Lithium-Ion Battery
facts.body: The lithium-ion battery was developed in the 1970s and 1980s through work by Stanley Whittingham, John Goodenough and Akira Yoshino, who shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Sony began selling it commercially in 1991. Light and rechargeable, it powers mobile phones, laptops and electric cars.

facts.title: The Persian Wars
facts.body: In 490 and 480–479 BC the Persian Empire invaded Greece. The Athenians defeated the first invasion at Marathon; the second was halted after Thermopylae by Greek victories at Salamis and Plataea. The victory, recorded by Herodotus, opened the way for Athens' golden age.

facts.title: Bose–Einstein Statistics
facts.body: In 1924 the Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose derived Planck's law of radiation by a new way of counting identical particles of light. He sent his paper to Einstein, who had it published and extended the method to atoms. Particles that follow these statistics are called bosons in his honour, and the theory predicted the Bose–Einstein condensate, first created in a laboratory in 1995.

facts.title: Not holy, not Roman, not an empire
facts.body: Voltaire joked that the Holy Roman Empire was 'neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire'. By his day it was a loose patchwork of German-speaking states with an elected emperor and little central power.

facts.title: The Great Trigonometrical Survey
facts.body: Begun in 1802, the Great Trigonometrical Survey measured the Indian subcontinent with great precision using chains of triangles across the land. It took decades and was one of the most ambitious scientific projects of its time. In the 1850s its calculations showed that Peak XV in the Himalayas was the highest in the world, and it was named after the former Surveyor General, George Everest.

facts.title: Han Kang
facts.body: The South Korean writer Han Kang won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2024, the first Korean author to do so. Her novel The Vegetarian, about a woman whose refusal to eat meat provokes her family's violence, won the International Booker Prize in English translation in 2016. Works such as Human Acts confront historical trauma, including the Gwangju massacre of 1980.

facts.title: Ravi Shankar
facts.body: Ravi Shankar (1920–2012) was a sitar virtuoso who brought Indian classical music to Western audiences. He collaborated with the violinist Yehudi Menuhin, taught George Harrison of the Beatles and played at the Monterey and Woodstock festivals. With Harrison he organised the Concert for Bangladesh in 1971.

facts.title: There is no horse in a nightmare
facts.body: The "mare" in nightmare has nothing to do with horses. It comes from Old English mære, an evil spirit believed to sit on people's chests while they slept and give them bad dreams.

facts.title: Popper and Falsifiability
facts.body: Karl Popper (1902–1994) argued that what distinguishes science from non-science is not that its theories can be proved but that they can be falsified: a scientific theory makes predictions that could turn out wrong. No number of white swans proves that all swans are white, but one black swan disproves it. On this basis he criticised Marxism and psychoanalysis as unfalsifiable.

facts.title: Inflation Targeting
facts.body: In 1990 New Zealand became the first country to give its central bank an explicit inflation target, under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act of 1989. The bank was made independent in pursuing a low inflation range agreed with the government, and its governor was held accountable for meeting it. The approach spread to many central banks around the world, which commonly aim for inflation of about 2 per cent.

facts.title: The Constitution of Carthage
facts.body: The Phoenician city of Carthage in North Africa was governed by two annually elected chief magistrates called suffetes, a council of elders, a court of 104 judges that held generals to account, and a popular assembly. Aristotle discussed it in his Politics alongside Sparta and Crete and praised it as a well-balanced constitution. It is one of the few non-Greek constitutions described in classical political thought.

facts.title: Your smallest bone is in your ear
facts.body: The stapes, or stirrup, in the middle ear is the smallest bone in the body at roughly three millimetres long. It passes sound vibrations from the eardrum to the fluid-filled inner ear.

facts.title: Tocharian
facts.body: In the early 20th century, expeditions to the Tarim Basin in what is now western China found manuscripts from roughly the 6th to 8th centuries AD in two previously unknown languages, now called Tocharian A and B. Written in a Brahmi-derived script and largely containing Buddhist texts, they proved to be Indo-European. Their location, far to the east of any other ancient Indo-European language, changed ideas about the family's early spread.

facts.title: The Antikythera Mechanism
facts.body: Recovered in the early 1900s from an ancient shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, this corroded bronze device dates from around the 2nd or 1st century BC. Modern imaging has shown that it contained dozens of precisely cut gears that modelled the movements of the Sun and Moon, predicted eclipses and tracked the cycle of games such as the Olympics. Nothing of comparable mechanical complexity is known again for well over a thousand years.

facts.title: The Atlantic Slave Trade
facts.body: From the 16th to the 19th century around 12 million enslaved Africans were shipped across the Atlantic, many dying on the voyage known as the Middle Passage. Most were forced to work on plantations growing sugar, tobacco and cotton. The trade transformed the Americas and devastated parts of West and Central Africa.

facts.title: Venus is hotter than Mercury
facts.body: Mercury is closer to the Sun, but Venus has the hottest surface of any planet, about 464 degrees Celsius. Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, while airless Mercury swings from about 420 degrees by day to minus 170 at night.

facts.title: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine
facts.body: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born near Bukhara in 980 and completed the Canon of Medicine in the early 11th century. It combined Greek medicine, especially Galen's, with the knowledge of physicians of the Islamic world in one systematic encyclopaedia. Translated into Latin in the 12th century, it served as a standard textbook in European universities for centuries.

facts.title: The Niger River
facts.body: The Niger rises in the highlands of Guinea, not far from the Atlantic, but flows inland, north-east towards the Sahara. After forming a vast inland delta in Mali and bending past Timbuktu, it turns south-east through Niger and Nigeria to the Gulf of Guinea. Its unusual course puzzled European geographers until the early 19th century, and its waters have long supported trade and farming in West Africa.

facts.title: The Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela
facts.body: In the highlands of Ethiopia, eleven churches were carved directly out of solid rock, traditionally under King Lalibela around 1200. Hewn downwards from the surface and linked by trenches and tunnels, they were conceived, according to tradition, as a New Jerusalem. They remain a major place of Ethiopian Orthodox pilgrimage.

facts.title: Land that no country wants
facts.body: Bir Tawil, a desert area between Egypt and Sudan, is claimed by neither. Two different border lines exist, and each country prefers the one that gives it the more valuable Halaib Triangle instead.

facts.title: Reggaeton
facts.body: Reggaeton grew out of Puerto Rico in the 1990s, drawing on Spanish-language reggae from Panama, Jamaican dancehall and hip hop. Its signature is the dembow rhythm. Daddy Yankee's 'Gasolina' (2004) took it to a global audience, making Spanish-language pop a major force in world music in the 21st century.

facts.title: The Prophet Muhammad and the Hijra
facts.body: Muhammad (around 570–632), born in Mecca, is regarded by Muslims as the final prophet of God. From around 610 he reported revelations that were later collected as the Quran. Facing hostility in Mecca, he and his followers migrated to Medina in 622, the Hijra, which marks year one of the Islamic calendar. By his death he had united much of Arabia under Islam.

facts.title: Indian Calicoes and the Calico Acts
facts.body: In the 17th century, cheap and colourful cotton textiles from India, called calicoes after the port of Calicut, became highly fashionable in Europe. English wool and silk producers lobbied against them, and Parliament restricted them and then, in 1721, banned the use of most printed cotton cloth. Historians have argued that this protection, and the challenge of imitating Indian cloth, helped spur the mechanised British cotton industry.

facts.title: Most wasabi is really horseradish
facts.body: Real wasabi is hard to grow and expensive, so most of the green paste served with sushi outside Japan is horseradish mixed with mustard and green colouring.

facts.title: The Nuremberg Trials
facts.body: In 1945–46 an International Military Tribunal set up by the four main Allied powers tried leading Nazis for crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. It established that individuals, including heads of state and officials acting on orders, can be held criminally responsible under international law. Its principles laid the foundation for later international criminal courts.

facts.title: Orwell's Politics and the English Language
facts.body: In his 1946 essay 'Politics and the English Language', George Orwell argued that vague, inflated prose helps to hide ugly realities, as when bombing defenceless villages is called 'pacification'. He offered six rules, including never using a long word where a short one will do. The essay is widely cited on clear writing and political euphemism, themes he developed in Nineteen Eighty-Four.

facts.title: The Voyager Probes
facts.body: NASA launched the twin Voyager probes in 1977 to take advantage of a rare alignment of the outer planets. Between them they flew past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, Voyager 2 being the first spacecraft to visit the last two. In 2012 Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. Each carries a gold-plated record of sounds and images from Earth.

facts.title: The platypus hunts with electricity
facts.body: A platypus closes its eyes, ears and nose when it dives, yet still finds prey. Its bill carries tens of thousands of electroreceptors that sense the tiny electric fields made by the muscles of shrimps and worms in the riverbed.

facts.title: The Revolutions of 1848
facts.body: In 1848 revolutions broke out across Europe, in France, the German and Italian states, the Austrian Empire and elsewhere, demanding constitutions, national unity and political rights. In France the monarchy fell. Most revolts were crushed within a year or two, but they spread liberal and nationalist ideas.

facts.title: The First Image of a Black Hole
facts.body: Black holes, regions where gravity is so strong that not even light escapes, follow from Einstein's general relativity. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope, a network of radio observatories around the world acting as one Earth-sized dish, released the first image of one: a dark shadow ringed by glowing gas at the centre of the galaxy M87. In 2022 it imaged Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the heart of the Milky Way.

facts.title: The Great Lakes
facts.body: Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario together hold roughly a fifth of the fresh surface water on Earth.
