They were carved out by ice sheets and filled as the ice melted at the end of the last ice age. Linked to the Atlantic by the St Lawrence River, they made cities such as Chicago, Detroit and Toronto major industrial ports.

facts.title: A Martian volcano 2.5 Everests tall
facts.body: Olympus Mons rises about 21 kilometres, roughly two and a half times the height of Everest above sea level. Mars has no moving tectonic plates, so lava kept piling up over the same hotspot for an immensely long time.

facts.title: Caravaggio
facts.body: Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio, working in Rome around 1600, painted religious scenes using ordinary people as models and dramatic contrasts of light and darkness. Works such as The Calling of Saint Matthew struck contemporaries with their raw realism. His style, known as tenebrism, spread across Europe and shaped Baroque painting.

facts.title: Peking Opera
facts.body: Peking opera took shape in Beijing in the 19th century, after regional troupes from Anhui arrived in the capital in 1790. It combines singing, speech, mime, acrobatics and stylised movement, with fixed role types and painted faces that signal character. The performer Mei Lanfang made it known abroad in the 20th century.

facts.title: Augustine of Hippo
facts.body: Augustine (354–430), born in Roman North Africa, became bishop of Hippo, in present-day Algeria, and the most influential theologian of the Latin West. His Confessions, an account of his restless path to Christianity, is often called the first Western autobiography. In The City of God, written after the sack of Rome in 410, he contrasted the earthly city with the heavenly one, and his teaching on original sin and grace shaped both Catholic and Protestant thought.

facts.title: In Italy a kindly witch brings presents
facts.body: On the night before Epiphany, 6 January, Italian children await La Befana. The old woman on a broomstick fills stockings with sweets, or coal for naughty children.

facts.title: The Resource Curse
facts.body: Many studies have found that countries rich in oil or minerals often grow more slowly and are governed worse than resource-poor ones, a pattern called the resource curse. One mechanism is 'Dutch disease', named in 1977 after the Netherlands' experience following its natural gas discoveries: resource exports push up the currency and hurt other exports such as manufacturing. Volatile prices and corruption add to the problem, though countries such as Norway and Botswana show it can be avoided.

facts.title: Rwanda's Gacaca Courts
facts.body: After the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi, Rwanda's ordinary courts could not cope with more than 100,000 detained suspects. From the early 2000s until 2012 the country revived gacaca, a traditional form of community justice, with locally elected lay judges hearing well over a million cases. The courts were praised for speed and local participation but criticised for lacking fair-trial guarantees.

facts.title: Haitian Creole
facts.body: Haitian Creole emerged among enslaved Africans on the plantations of French Saint-Domingue, with a vocabulary mostly from French but a grammar very different from it; creolists debate how much it owes to West African languages. It is the first language of nearly all Haitians, while French long remained the language of the elite and the state. The 1987 constitution made Creole an official language alongside French.

facts.title: Pencil "lead" has never been lead
facts.body: Pencils are filled with graphite mixed with clay. When a large graphite deposit was found in England's Lake District in the 16th century, people mistook the shiny grey mineral for lead, and the name stuck.

facts.title: Champa Rice
facts.body: Champa rice was a fast-ripening, drought-tolerant variety from the kingdom of Champa, in what is now central Vietnam. In 1012 the Song emperor Zhenzong had its seed distributed to farmers in the Yangtze and Huai river regions. Because it matured quickly, farmers could often grow two crops a year, and it helped support strong population growth in Song China.

facts.title: The Tang Dynasty
facts.body: The Tang dynasty, which ruled China from 618 to 907, is often seen as a high point of Chinese civilisation. Its capital, Chang'an, was a cosmopolitan city at the end of the trade routes from Central Asia, and the era was a golden age of poetry. The An Lushan rebellion of the 750s weakened it badly.

facts.title: Air Pressure and the Vacuum
facts.body: In the 1640s Evangelista Torricelli filled a glass tube with mercury and upended it in a dish: the column fell to a fixed height, leaving an empty space above. He concluded that the weight of the air holds the column up, and Blaise Pascal confirmed this by having the experiment repeated on a mountain, where the column was shorter. The experiments gave rise to the barometer and showed, against Aristotle, that a vacuum can exist.

facts.title: Rafflesia has no leaves, stem or roots
facts.body: Rafflesia, of the rainforests of South-East Asia, makes one of the largest flowers in the world, yet has no leaves, stem or roots. It lives hidden inside a vine as a parasite and only appears when its huge flower bursts through the bark.

facts.title: The Strait of Malacca
facts.body: The Strait of Malacca runs between the Malay Peninsula and the Indonesian island of Sumatra. It is the shortest sea route between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific, and has been one of the world's great shipping lanes for centuries. Control of it made the fortunes of Malacca in the 15th century and of Singapore, at its southern end, in modern times.

facts.title: The Terracotta Army
facts.body: Thousands of life-size terracotta soldiers were buried near the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a unified China, who died in 210 BC. Farmers digging a well discovered them in 1974. The figures were assembled from moulded parts but finished individually, with varied faces, and were originally brightly painted.

facts.title: The Persian Dastgah
facts.body: Persian classical music is organised into a system of modal groups called dastgahs. Their melodies are preserved in the radif, a large repertoire of short pieces passed from master to pupil and memorised over many years. Performers improvise on this material on instruments such as the tar, setar, santur and kamancheh.

facts.title: Stretching a rubber band warms it up
facts.body: Stretch a rubber band quickly and touch it to your lips: it feels warm, and it cools as it relaxes. Stretching lines up its tangled molecular chains, and that ordering releases heat.

facts.title: The Golden Rule
facts.body: The Golden Rule, treating others as one would wish to be treated, appears in many traditions. Confucius stated it in negative form ('Do not impose on others what you do not wish for yourself'), as did the Jewish sage Hillel, while Jesus put it positively in the Sermon on the Mount. Its recurrence across cultures makes it a common reference point in ethics, though philosophers note that people's wishes differ.

facts.title: The Rochdale Pioneers
facts.body: In 1844 a group of weavers and other workers in Rochdale, England, opened a cooperative shop selling flour, butter, sugar and oatmeal. Their Rochdale Principles, including open membership, one member one vote and the sharing of surplus among members according to their purchases, became the basis of the modern cooperative movement. Cooperatives built on these ideas spread worldwide in retail, farming, banking and housing.

facts.title: Kemalism
facts.body: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, who founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923, pursued a programme later summed up in six principles: republicanism, nationalism, populism, statism, secularism and reformism. His government abolished the caliphate in 1924, replaced Islamic law with codes based on European models and introduced the Latin alphabet in 1928.

facts.title: Big Ben is kept on time with coins
facts.body: The Great Clock at Westminster is fine-tuned by placing old penny coins on its pendulum. Adding one penny shifts the weight slightly and changes the clock's rate by about two-fifths of a second a day.

facts.title: The Revival of Hebrew
facts.body: For about two thousand years Hebrew was used mainly for prayer and scholarship rather than everyday speech. From the 1880s Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, who settled in Jerusalem, championed it as a spoken language, raised his son in Hebrew and compiled a dictionary of modern Hebrew. Schools in the Jewish settlements adopted it, and it became an official language of Israel; it is the best-known case of a language revived for daily use.

facts.title: The Mouse and the Graphical Interface
facts.body: In 1968 Douglas Engelbart demonstrated the computer mouse, hypertext links and on-screen windows in a famous presentation in San Francisco. In the 1970s Xerox PARC developed a graphical interface with icons and overlapping windows on its Alto computer. Apple's Macintosh of 1984 brought the graphical interface to a mass market, followed by Microsoft Windows.

facts.title: The Partition of India
facts.body: In August 1947 British India became independent and was divided into India and Pakistan, whose eastern wing later became Bangladesh. The division along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and communal violence killed hundreds of thousands, possibly far more. The Kashmir dispute dates from Partition.

facts.title: In Japan broken pots are mended with gold
facts.body: Kintsugi is the Japanese art of repairing broken pottery with lacquer dusted with gold. Rather than hiding the cracks, it makes them shine, treating the damage as part of the object's history.

facts.title: The Asteroid That Ended the Dinosaurs
facts.body: In 1980 a team led by Luis and Walter Alvarez reported a worldwide clay layer rich in iridium, rare on Earth but common in asteroids, at the boundary marking the dinosaurs' extinction about 66 million years ago. They proposed that a large asteroid had struck the Earth. The Chicxulub crater beneath Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula was identified as the impact site around 1990, though the role of huge volcanic eruptions is still debated.

facts.title: The Indian Ocean
facts.body: The Indian Ocean is bounded by Africa, Asia and Australia, and is the third-largest of the oceans. Its regular monsoon winds, blowing one way in summer and the other in winter, allowed sailors to cross it long before the age of European exploration. Arab, Persian, Indian, Swahili and Chinese traders built a network across it that carried spices, textiles, ideas and religions.

facts.title: Rabindranath Tagore
facts.body: The Bengali poet, novelist and painter Rabindranath Tagore became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1913, largely for his collection Gitanjali. He reshaped Bengali literature and founded a university at Santiniketan. He also wrote the songs that became the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

facts.title: Baker's yeast was a genome pioneer
facts.body: In 1996 baker's yeast became the first organism with a nucleus to have its entire genome sequenced. Many of its genes have close human equivalents, so the fungus that raises bread has taught us a great deal about our own cells.

facts.title: The Troubadours
facts.body: The troubadours were poet-musicians of the 12th and 13th centuries in Occitania, in what is now southern France. Singing in Occitan, they developed the ideal of courtly love, and William IX, Duke of Aquitaine, is the earliest known of them. Their art inspired the trouvères of northern France and the Minnesänger of Germany.

facts.title: Kuhn's Paradigm Shifts
facts.body: In The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), Thomas Kuhn argued that science does not progress by steady accumulation. Periods of 'normal science' work within a paradigm, a shared framework of theories and methods, until anomalies pile up and a revolution replaces it, as when Copernican astronomy displaced the Ptolemaic system. The term 'paradigm shift' passed into everyday language.

facts.title: Microfinance and the Grameen Bank
facts.body: In 1976 the Bangladeshi economist Muhammad Yunus began lending small sums to poor villagers, mostly women, who had no access to banks. His Grameen Bank relied on groups of borrowers who supported one another, instead of on collateral. Yunus and the bank shared the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize, though later studies found microcredit's effect on poverty more modest than early supporters had hoped.

facts.title: Liquid oxygen is blue and magnetic
facts.body: Cooled below minus 183 degrees Celsius, oxygen becomes a pale blue liquid that clings to the poles of a strong magnet. Oxygen molecules have unpaired electrons, which make them attracted to magnetic fields.

facts.title: The Paris Agreement
facts.body: Adopted in December 2015 by nearly every country in the world, the agreement aims to keep global warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C. Instead of imposing binding emission quotas, it asks each country to set its own nationally determined contributions, to be updated and strengthened every five years.

facts.title: Isolating, Agglutinative and Fusional Languages
facts.body: Linguists classify languages by how they build words. Isolating languages such as Vietnamese use mostly invariable words; agglutinative languages such as Turkish and Finnish string together suffixes that each carry one meaning; fusional languages such as Latin pack several meanings, like case and number, into a single ending. Polysynthetic languages, found especially in the Arctic and the Americas, can express a whole sentence in one long word.

facts.title: Wikipedia
facts.body: Wikipedia was launched in January 2001 by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger as a free online encyclopedia that anyone can edit. Run by the non-profit Wikimedia Foundation and written by volunteers, it grew to millions of articles in hundreds of languages. It showed that large-scale voluntary collaboration over the internet could produce a widely used reference work.

facts.title: An ancient customer complaint survives in clay
facts.body: Around 1750 BC a Babylonian named Nanni wrote an angry tablet to the merchant Ea-nasir about poor-quality copper and rude service. It is now in the British Museum and is often called the oldest known written complaint.

facts.title: The Mongol Empire
facts.body: Temüjin united the Mongol tribes and in 1206 took the title Genghis Khan. He and his successors built the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from Korea to eastern Europe. It later split into separate khanates, but Mongol rule made overland travel and trade across Eurasia unusually secure.

facts.title: The Edwin Smith Papyrus
facts.body: This Egyptian medical text, written around 1600 BC and probably copied from older material, describes how to examine, diagnose and treat injuries such as wounds and fractures. Unlike most ancient medical writing, it relies mainly on practical treatment rather than magic. It contains some of the earliest known written descriptions of the brain.

facts.title: Central Place Theory
facts.body: In 1933 the German geographer Walter Christaller proposed that towns and cities form a hierarchy according to the goods and services they provide to the surrounding area. Many small places offer everyday services, while fewer large cities offer specialised ones, and in an ideal flat landscape their market areas form hexagons. The theory has shaped regional planning and the study of settlement patterns.

facts.title: Orchestras agreed to tune to 440 Hz
facts.body: For centuries the note A could vary widely from city to city. In 1939 an international conference in London recommended 440 vibrations a second, which became the usual standard.

facts.title: Greek Tragedy
facts.body: Tragedy developed in Athens in the 5th century BC, performed at festivals in honour of the god Dionysus. Its three great masters were Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, whose surviving plays include the Oresteia, Oedipus the King and Medea. Aristotle later analysed the form in his Poetics, and it remains a root of Western drama.

facts.title: The Natya Shastra
facts.body: This Sanskrit treatise on the performing arts, attributed to the sage Bharata, is most often dated to between about 200 BC and 200 AD, though estimates vary widely. It covers drama, dance and music, describing scales, the 22 microtonal shrutis of the octave and families of instruments. Its theory of rasa, the emotional flavour a performance evokes, still underpins Indian classical music and dance.

facts.title: Paul the Apostle
facts.body: Paul of Tarsus, a Jewish Pharisee who had persecuted Jesus's followers, became Christianity's most influential missionary after a vision of the risen Christ. In the AD 40s and 50s he travelled through Asia Minor and Greece, founding communities that welcomed non-Jews without requiring them to follow Jewish law. His letters are the earliest surviving Christian writings and form a large part of the New Testament.

facts.title: Axolotls can regrow lost limbs
facts.body: The axolotl, a salamander from the lakes around Mexico City, can regrow whole legs, parts of its heart and even its spinal cord. Cells at the wound turn back into a flexible state and rebuild the missing tissue without scarring.

facts.title: Public Goods
facts.body: A public good is non-excludable, meaning no one can be prevented from using it, and non-rival, meaning one person's use does not reduce what is available to others. National defence, street lighting and basic research are standard examples. Because people can benefit without paying, markets tend to under-provide such goods, a free-rider problem that Paul Samuelson formalised in 1954 and that justifies much government spending.

facts.title: The Bandung Conference
facts.body: In April 1955 leaders of 29 Asian and African countries, many newly independent, met in Bandung, Indonesia. Hosted by Sukarno and attended by figures such as Nehru, Zhou Enlai and Nasser, the conference condemned colonialism and called for cooperation among developing nations. It paved the way for the Non-Aligned Movement, founded in Belgrade in 1961.

facts.title: The Indus Script
facts.body: The Indus or Harappan civilisation of around 2600–1900 BC left thousands of short inscriptions, mostly on stamp seals, using several hundred signs. The script remains undeciphered: the inscriptions are very short, no bilingual text has been found, and the language behind them is unknown. Scholars even debate whether the signs fully encoded language.

facts.title: Bees picked the most efficient shape
facts.body: In 1999 mathematician Thomas Hales proved the honeycomb conjecture: hexagons divide a surface into equal cells using the least total wall length. Bees save wax by building hexagonal cells.

facts.title: The Blue LED
facts.body: Red light-emitting diodes existed from the 1960s, but an efficient blue LED proved very hard to make. In the early 1990s Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura succeeded using gallium nitride, and shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics. Blue LEDs made bright white LED lighting possible, which uses far less energy than incandescent bulbs.

facts.title: The Founding of the People's Republic of China
facts.body: After a long civil war against Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists, interrupted by the war against Japan, the Communist Party under Mao Zedong won mainland China. On 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People's Republic in Beijing, and the Nationalist government retreated to Taiwan.

facts.title: The Neanderthal Genome
facts.body: In 2010 a team led by Svante Pääbo in Leipzig published a draft genome of Neanderthals, sequenced from ancient bones. It showed that people whose ancestry lies outside Africa carry a small share, around 1 to 2%, of Neanderthal DNA, proof of interbreeding. The same year DNA from a finger bone in Siberia revealed another extinct group, the Denisovans, and Pääbo received the 2022 Nobel Prize.

facts.title: The busiest map spot is empty sea
facts.body: Null Island is the nickname for 0° latitude, 0° longitude in the Gulf of Guinea. Faulty location data often defaults to those coordinates, so many mapping errors pile up on this imaginary island.

facts.title: The Deccan Plateau
facts.body: The Deccan is the great plateau that covers most of southern India, between the Western and Eastern Ghats. Its north-western part is built of thick layers of lava, the Deccan Traps, from huge eruptions around the time the dinosaurs died out. The plateau tilts eastward, so its major rivers, such as the Godavari and Krishna, flow to the Bay of Bengal.

facts.title: Duchamp's Fountain
facts.body: In 1917 Marcel Duchamp submitted a mass-produced porcelain urinal, signed with a false name, to an exhibition in New York, where it was not displayed. By presenting an everyday object, or readymade, as art, he suggested that art is defined by the artist's choice and ideas rather than by craft. The original is lost, but Fountain became one of the most influential works of 20th-century art.

facts.title: Miriam Makeba
facts.body: Miriam Makeba (1932–2008), known as 'Mama Africa', was a South African singer who brought African music to a world audience with songs such as 'Pata Pata'. Exiled from 1960 after appearing in an anti-apartheid film, she spoke against apartheid before the United Nations. She returned home in 1990.

facts.title: Winnie-the-Pooh was named after a real bear
facts.body: Winnie was a black bear from Canada living at London Zoo, named after the city of Winnipeg. A. A. Milne's son Christopher Robin loved her and gave her name to his teddy bear.

facts.title: Guru Nanak and Sikhism
facts.body: Sikhism was founded in the Punjab by Guru Nanak (1469–1539), who taught devotion to one formless God, the equality of all people regardless of caste, and honest work and service to others. He was followed by nine human gurus; the tenth, Gobind Singh, declared that the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, would be the eternal Guru. The Golden Temple at Amritsar is the faith's holiest shrine.

facts.title: The Solow Growth Model
facts.body: In 1956 Robert Solow, and independently Trevor Swan in Australia, showed that adding capital alone cannot sustain growth, because each extra machine adds less output than the last. In their model, long-run growth in income per person comes from technological progress. Solow found that much of the growth in US output per worker could not be explained by more capital, a remainder known as the Solow residual.

facts.title: The Secret Ballot
facts.body: In 1856 the Australian colonies of Victoria and South Australia introduced government-printed ballot papers marked in private, which is why the secret ballot was long known as the 'Australian ballot'. Before it, voting was often public, leaving voters open to bribery and intimidation. Britain adopted it in 1872 and the method spread across the democratic world.

facts.title: The ocean's most common plant-like life
facts.body: Prochlorococcus, a microbe too small to see even with many ordinary microscopes, was only discovered in 1988. Yet it is the most abundant photosynthetic organism on Earth and produces a large share of the oxygen made in the sea.

facts.title: Webster's American Dictionary
facts.body: Noah Webster published his American Dictionary of the English Language in 1828, aiming to give the United States a linguistic identity of its own. He promoted spellings such as color, center and defense, which became the American standard. Earlier, his 'blue-backed speller', first published in 1783, had taught generations of American children to read.

facts.title: Bazalgette's London Sewers
facts.body: After the Great Stink of 1858, when the smell of the sewage-filled Thames overwhelmed Parliament, the engineer Joseph Bazalgette built a network of intercepting sewers for London. Constructed mainly in the 1860s and 1870s, it carried waste away from the city to outfalls downstream. It greatly reduced cholera outbreaks and became a model for urban sanitation.

facts.title: Peter the Great
facts.body: Peter I, tsar of Russia from 1682 until 1725, forcefully modernised his country on Western European lines, reforming the army and state and creating a navy. In 1703 he founded St Petersburg on the Baltic, later his capital. Victory over Sweden in the Great Northern War made Russia a major European power.

facts.title: Scotland's national animal is the unicorn
facts.body: The unicorn has long been a symbol of Scotland's kings and still supports the royal coat of arms used in Scotland, wearing a chain. It is widely regarded as the country's national animal.

facts.title: Absolute Zero
facts.body: Absolute zero, 0 kelvin or −273.15 °C, is the lowest possible temperature, at which a system has the least energy it can have. In 1848 William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, proposed a temperature scale starting from this point. The laws of thermodynamics imply that it can be approached ever more closely but never actually reached.

facts.title: The Atacama Desert
facts.body: The Atacama, in northern Chile between the Andes and the Pacific, is the driest non-polar desert on Earth, and some places in it have gone years without measurable rain. It is dry because it lies in the rain shadow of the Andes and beside a cold ocean current. Its clear skies have made it a centre for astronomical observatories, and its nitrate and copper deposits shaped Chile's economy.

facts.title: Virgil's Aeneid
facts.body: Virgil wrote the Aeneid in the last decade before his death in 19 BC, under the emperor Augustus. The Latin epic follows the Trojan prince Aeneas, who escapes the fall of Troy and travels to Italy, where his descendants will found Rome. Consciously modelled on Homer, it became the national epic of Rome and a central school text in Europe for centuries.

facts.title: Sinterklaas arrives in the Netherlands by boat
facts.body: Each November the Dutch Saint Nicholas is welcomed as he 'arrives from Spain' on a steamboat. His feast is celebrated with gifts on 5 December, the evening before St Nicholas's Day.

facts.title: Tchaikovsky's Ballets
facts.body: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky wrote Swan Lake (1877), The Sleeping Beauty (1890) and The Nutcracker (1892). Before him, ballet music was often seen as mere accompaniment, but he gave it symphonic depth and memorable melody. The three works remain at the core of the classical ballet repertoire.

facts.title: Pyrrho and Ancient Scepticism
facts.body: Pyrrho of Elis, who travelled with Alexander the Great as far as India, is regarded as the founder of Greek scepticism. Pyrrhonists argued that for every claim an equally strong counter-argument can be found, so one should suspend judgement, which they believed brings tranquillity. Preserved in the writings of Sextus Empiricus, these arguments were rediscovered in the Renaissance and influenced Montaigne and Descartes.

facts.title: The Discourses on Salt and Iron
facts.body: In 81 BC the Han court of China held a debate over the state monopolies on salt and iron set up under Emperor Wu. Officials defended them as a source of revenue for defence, while Confucian scholars argued that the state should not compete with the people for profit. The record of the debate, the Discourses on Salt and Iron, is a classic early statement of the argument between state intervention and free enterprise.

facts.title: Olympic gold medals are mostly silver
facts.body: Olympic gold medals are made mostly of silver and coated with gold. The last solid gold medals were awarded in 1912.

facts.title: Simon de Montfort's Parliament
facts.body: In 1265, while ruling England after capturing Henry III, the baron Simon de Montfort summoned a parliament that included not only nobles and clergy but also knights from each county and burgesses from the towns. It is seen as a milestone in the development of the House of Commons. Edward I's 'Model Parliament' of 1295 made such representation more regular.

facts.title: Metaphor and Metonymy
facts.body: A metaphor describes one thing in terms of another ('time is money'), while metonymy refers to something by an associated thing, as when 'the Crown' stands for the monarchy. Both were classified as figures of speech by ancient rhetoricians. Since George Lakoff and Mark Johnson's Metaphors We Live By (1980), many linguists have argued that metaphor structures everyday thought, not just poetry.

facts.title: Wootz Steel
facts.body: Wootz was a high-carbon steel made in southern India and Sri Lanka by melting iron with carbon-rich material in sealed clay crucibles. Production goes back at least 2,000 years. Traded to the Middle East, it was forged into the famous Damascus blades, prized for their toughness and watery surface pattern.

facts.title: Your corneas breathe straight from the air
facts.body: The cornea, the clear front of the eye, has no blood vessels, since they would cloud vision. Instead it takes most of its oxygen directly from the air, dissolved in the film of tears.

facts.title: The Bronze Age Collapse
facts.body: In the decades around 1200 BC many societies of the eastern Mediterranean collapsed, including the Hittite Empire and the Mycenaean palaces of Greece. Cities were destroyed and trade networks broke down. Historians still debate the causes, which may include drought, invasions such as those of the 'Sea Peoples', and systemic failure.

facts.title: Maxwell's Equations
facts.body: In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell united electricity and magnetism in a single set of equations. They predicted electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light, leading Maxwell to conclude that light itself is such a wave. Heinrich Hertz produced radio waves in the late 1880s, confirming the theory that underlies radio, radar and much of modern physics.

facts.title: El Niño
facts.body: El Niño is an irregular warming of the surface waters of the central and eastern tropical Pacific, occurring every few years. Peruvian fishermen named it after the Christ child because it tends to appear around Christmas. Together with its cold counterpart La Niña, it shifts rainfall around the world, bringing floods to some regions and drought to others.

facts.title: Why home-made ice cubes are cloudy
facts.body: Ice cubes freeze from the outside in, pushing dissolved air and impurities towards the centre, where they get trapped as tiny bubbles. That is why the cloudiness gathers in the middle.

facts.title: Things Fall Apart
facts.body: Chinua Achebe's novel of 1958 tells of Okonkwo, a proud Igbo leader in Nigeria whose world collapses with the arrival of British missionaries and colonial rule. Written in an English rich in Igbo proverbs, it showed African society from within, against colonial stereotypes. It is among the most widely read African novels.

facts.title: Pansori
facts.body: Pansori is Korean musical storytelling for one singer and one drummer, who keeps rhythm on a barrel drum and calls out encouragement. Emerging in south-western Korea in the 17th century, it can be performed in full over several hours. The singer moves between song, speech and gesture, with a rough, powerful voice trained through years of practice.

facts.title: Zen Buddhism
facts.body: Zen, known in China as Chan, is a school of Mahayana Buddhism that stresses meditation and direct insight over the study of scriptures. It took shape in China in the 6th to 8th centuries and spread to Korea, Vietnam and Japan, where it flourished from the late 12th century. Its teachers used paradoxical riddles called koans to break habitual thinking, and it deeply influenced East Asian painting, poetry and gardens.

facts.title: A Bristol clock has two minute hands
facts.body: Before railways forced a national time, Bristol kept local time about ten minutes behind London. The Corn Exchange clock got a second minute hand to show both times.

facts.title: The Gold Standard
facts.body: Under the gold standard, a country's currency was convertible into a fixed amount of gold. Britain formalised it after the Napoleonic Wars, and in the 1870s many other major economies followed, creating fixed exchange rates that supported trade and investment. It tied governments' hands in recessions, however, and most countries abandoned it during the Great Depression of the 1930s.

facts.title: The Mabo Decision
facts.body: In 1992 the High Court of Australia ruled in favour of Eddie Mabo and other Meriam people of the Torres Strait, rejecting the doctrine that Australia had been terra nullius, land belonging to no one, when the British arrived. It recognised that native title to land could survive colonisation. Parliament responded with the Native Title Act of 1993.

facts.title: Yiddish
facts.body: Yiddish developed among Ashkenazi Jews, probably in the Rhineland, roughly a thousand years ago, combining a German base with Hebrew and Aramaic words and, after migration eastwards, Slavic elements. It is written in the Hebrew alphabet. Before the Holocaust it was spoken by millions across Central and Eastern Europe and had a rich modern literature, recognised when Isaac Bashevis Singer won the Nobel Prize in 1978.

facts.title: The dot on an i has a name
facts.body: The small dot above a lower-case i or j is called a tittle. The word is also thought to lie behind the phrase "to a T", meaning down to the smallest detail.

facts.title: The Integrated Circuit
facts.body: In 1958 Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments built the first integrated circuit, combining several components on one piece of semiconductor. In 1959 Robert Noyce at Fairchild devised a planar silicon version suited to mass production. Integrated circuits let ever more transistors be packed onto a single chip, making modern electronics possible, and Kilby received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000.

facts.title: The Battle of Adwa
facts.body: On 1 March 1896 the army of Emperor Menelik II of Ethiopia decisively defeated an Italian invasion force at Adwa. Italy was forced to recognise Ethiopian independence, and the victory became a lasting symbol of African resistance to colonialism.

facts.title: Neutrino Oscillation
facts.body: Neutrinos, ghostly particles proposed by Wolfgang Pauli in 1930, pass through matter almost without trace. In 1998 the Super-Kamiokande detector in Japan showed that neutrinos change from one type to another as they travel, which is possible only if they have mass. The Standard Model of particle physics had treated them as massless, and Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald shared the 2015 Nobel Prize.

facts.title: Tardigrades have survived open space
facts.body: Tardigrades, or water bears, are tiny animals that can dry out and enter a state called cryptobiosis. In 2007 some were exposed to the vacuum and radiation of space on a satellite, and a number revived and reproduced afterwards.

facts.title: Victoria Falls
facts.body: Victoria Falls is where the Zambezi River drops into a narrow gorge on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its local name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, means 'the smoke that thunders', after the column of spray visible from far away. The Scottish missionary David Livingstone named it after Queen Victoria in 1855, and it is one of the widest curtains of falling water in the world.

facts.title: Goethe's Faust
facts.body: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe worked on Faust for most of his life; Part One appeared in 1808 and Part Two after his death in 1832. The scholar Faust makes a pact with the devil Mephistopheles, staking his soul on the search for knowledge and experience. It is the central work of German literature and has inspired operas, novels and countless retellings.

facts.title: The Rite of Spring
facts.body: Igor Stravinsky's ballet, depicting a pagan sacrifice, was first performed by the Ballets Russes in Paris in 1913. Its pounding irregular rhythms, dissonance and Nijinsky's choreography caused an uproar in the theatre. It became one of the defining works of musical modernism.

facts.title: Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side
facts.body: Uranus is tilted by about 98 degrees, so each pole points almost straight at the Sun for part of its 84-year orbit. That gives each pole roughly 42 years of continuous daylight followed by 42 years of night.

facts.title: Historical Materialism
facts.body: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels argued that history is driven by material and economic conditions rather than by ideas. Each society's forces and relations of production, its economic 'base', shape its laws, politics and beliefs, the 'superstructure'. Conflict between classes, they held, moves history through stages from slavery and feudalism to capitalism and, they predicted, communism.

facts.title: Mercantilism
facts.body: Mercantilism was the dominant economic outlook of European states from the 16th to the 18th centuries. It held that national wealth and power depended on accumulating gold and silver, so governments sought trade surpluses through tariffs, colonies and monopolies. Adam Smith attacked it in The Wealth of Nations, arguing that a nation's wealth lies in what it produces, not in its stock of precious metals.

facts.title: The Manden Charter
facts.body: According to oral tradition, the Manden Charter was proclaimed at Kurukan Fuga when the Mali Empire was founded under Sundiata Keita in the 13th century. Passed down by griots, it sets out principles such as respect for human life, social harmony and the rejection of enslavement by raiding. Its date and original content cannot be verified, but UNESCO recognised it as intangible cultural heritage in 2009.

facts.title: A pirate who retired in peace
facts.body: Ching Shih commanded a vast pirate confederation off southern China in the early 1800s. Instead of being defeated, she negotiated a surrender in 1810 that let her keep her fortune and live out her life.

facts.title: Indonesian as a National Language
facts.body: At the Youth Pledge of 28 October 1928, nationalists in the Dutch East Indies vowed to uphold 'the language of unity, Indonesian'. They chose a form of Malay, long a trading lingua franca of the archipelago, rather than Javanese, the language of the largest ethnic group. As the official language of independent Indonesia, it became a shared language across hundreds of ethnic groups and is often cited as a model of successful language planning.

facts.title: Printing in East Asia
facts.body: Woodblock printing was used in China by the 8th century, and the Diamond Sutra of 868, found at Dunhuang, is the oldest known dated printed book. Around the 1040s the commoner Bi Sheng made movable type from baked clay. In Korea, the Jikji, printed with movable metal type in 1377, is the oldest surviving book of its kind and predates Gutenberg.

facts.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
facts.body: In October 1962 American spy planes found Soviet nuclear missile sites under construction in Cuba. For thirteen days the world stood close to nuclear war. Khrushchev withdrew the missiles in exchange for a US pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret promise to remove American missiles from Turkey.

facts.title: Worcestershire sauce contains fish
facts.body: The famous sauce gets part of its deep savoury taste from fermented anchovies. Other ingredients include vinegar, tamarind, molasses and onion.

facts.title: The Discovery of the Electron
facts.body: In 1897 Joseph John Thomson showed that cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles with a mass far smaller than that of the lightest atom. The electron was the first subatomic particle to be discovered, proving that atoms are not indivisible. Thomson pictured the atom as a positive sphere studded with electrons, a model soon replaced by Rutherford's.

facts.title: The Gobi Desert
facts.body: The Gobi covers much of southern Mongolia and northern China. It is a cold desert, with harsh winters, and much of it is bare rock and gravel rather than sand dunes. It lies in the rain shadow of the Tibetan Plateau and the Himalayas, and expeditions there in the 1920s made famous finds of dinosaur fossils and eggs.

facts.title: Akira Kurosawa
facts.body: The Japanese director Akira Kurosawa won the top prize at the Venice Film Festival in 1951 with Rashomon, in which witnesses give contradictory accounts of the same crime. Its success opened Western audiences to Japanese cinema. His Seven Samurai of 1954 shaped the action film and was remade in Hollywood as The Magnificent Seven.

facts.title: Welwitschia grows just two leaves for life
facts.body: Welwitschia, a desert plant of Namibia and Angola, produces only two leaves, which keep growing from the base for its whole life. Some plants are thought to be more than a thousand years old, their leaves torn by wind into ragged strips.

facts.title: The Pentatonic Scale
facts.body: A pentatonic scale has five notes per octave, like the black keys of a piano. It is found in traditional music around the world, from China and Japan to West Africa, Scotland and the Andes, and in the blues. Because it avoids semitones, its notes rarely clash, which makes it easy to sing and improvise in.

facts.title: The I Ching
facts.body: The I Ching, or Book of Changes, is one of the oldest Chinese classics. Its core is a system of 64 hexagrams, figures of six broken or unbroken lines, used for divination, to which philosophical commentaries were later added. It became one of the Confucian classics, and it later fascinated Western thinkers such as Leibniz and Carl Jung.

facts.title: The Waqf
facts.body: A waqf is an endowment under Islamic law: property is dedicated in perpetuity, and its income supports a religious or charitable purpose. Waqfs funded mosques, schools, hospitals, fountains and caravanserais across the Islamic world, and at times held a large share of urban property. Some historians argue that the model influenced the development of charitable trusts in medieval Europe, though this is debated.

facts.title: Trillions of ghostly particles pass through you
facts.body: Every second, trillions of neutrinos from the Sun pass through your body, even at night when they come up through the Earth. They barely interact with matter, so almost all of them sail straight through.

facts.title: Burke and Modern Conservatism
facts.body: In Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790), the Irish-born statesman Edmund Burke attacked the attempt to rebuild society from abstract principles. He defended tradition, gradual reform and inherited institutions as the accumulated wisdom of generations, and predicted that the Revolution would end in violence. The book is widely regarded as a founding text of modern conservatism.

facts.title: The Shuowen Jiezi
facts.body: Compiled by the scholar Xu Shen around AD 100, the Shuowen Jiezi was the first Chinese dictionary to analyse the structure of characters. It arranged about 9,000 characters under 540 radicals, or shared components, and explained each one's meaning and composition. Its radical system shaped later Chinese dictionaries, and its analyses remain important for the history of the script.

facts.title: The War of the Currents
facts.body: In the late 1880s Thomas Edison's direct current (DC) competed with the alternating current (AC) system championed by George Westinghouse, using patents of Nikola Tesla. AC can be stepped up to high voltage with transformers and sent efficiently over long distances. AC won, and it became the standard for power grids around the world.

facts.title: An island that was never there
facts.body: Sandy Island appeared on maps and even in online atlases for over a century, between Australia and New Caledonia. In 2012 scientists sailed to the spot and found only deep open ocean.

facts.title: The Unification of Egypt
facts.body: Around 3100 BC Upper and Lower Egypt were united into a single kingdom, an achievement tradition credits to a king called Menes, often identified with Narmer. It began the dynastic history of pharaonic Egypt, a state that endured, with interruptions, for nearly three thousand years.

facts.title: Leavitt's Law and Cosmic Distances
facts.body: Working at Harvard College Observatory, Henrietta Swan Leavitt found in 1912 that Cepheid variable stars that pulse more slowly are intrinsically brighter. Comparing a Cepheid's true brightness with how bright it appears gives its distance. Edwin Hubble used Cepheids in the 1920s to show that the Andromeda nebula lies far beyond the Milky Way, proving that other galaxies exist.

facts.title: The Coriolis Effect
facts.body: Because the Earth rotates, winds and ocean currents moving over its surface are deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern. Named after the French scientist Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, the effect explains why large storms spin in opposite directions in the two hemispheres. It is far too weak to decide which way water drains from a sink.

facts.title: The safety pin paid off a debt
facts.body: In 1849 the American inventor Walter Hunt twisted a piece of wire into a safety pin, reportedly in a few hours. He sold the patent for a few hundred dollars to settle a debt and never made more from it.

facts.title: The Bayeux Tapestry
facts.body: The Bayeux Tapestry, nearly 70 metres long, tells the story of the Norman conquest of England, culminating in the Battle of Hastings in 1066. Strictly speaking it is an embroidery in wool on linen, probably made in England within a few years of the events. It is a unique visual record of 11th-century dress, weapons and ships, and its permanent home is in Bayeux in Normandy.

facts.title: Kind of Blue
facts.body: Miles Davis recorded Kind of Blue in 1959 with John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley and Bill Evans. Instead of rapid chord changes, the improvisations unfold over a few scales, or modes, giving the music space and calm. It is one of the most influential jazz albums and the record that popularised modal jazz.

facts.title: The Rule of St Benedict
facts.body: In the 6th century Benedict of Nursia wrote a rule for his monastery at Monte Cassino, in Italy, organising monks' days around communal prayer, manual work and reading under the authority of an abbot. Moderate rather than extreme in its demands, it became the basis of monastic life in the Latin West. Benedictine monasteries preserved learning and copied classical texts through the early Middle Ages.

facts.title: Lichens have survived a trip to space
facts.body: A lichen is a partnership between a fungus and algae or bacteria. In 2005 two lichen species spent about two weeks exposed to space on a satellite and resumed normal activity once back on Earth.

facts.title: Bank Runs and Deposit Insurance
facts.body: A bank run happens when depositors fear a bank will fail and rush to withdraw their money, which can bring down even a sound bank, since most deposits have been lent out. Waves of runs closed thousands of US banks in the early 1930s. In 1933 the United States created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to guarantee deposits, and runs on insured banks became rare.

facts.title: Federalism
facts.body: In a federal system, power is constitutionally divided between a central government and regional units such as states or provinces, each with an area of authority protected by the constitution. Examples include the United States, Switzerland, India and Nigeria. Federalism can accommodate regional and ethnic diversity, but produces recurring disputes over which level decides what.

facts.title: Tamazight and Tifinagh
facts.body: The Berber, or Amazigh, languages have been spoken in North Africa since long before the Arab conquests but long lacked official status. Morocco made Tamazight an official language in its 2011 constitution, and Algeria did the same in 2016. Morocco adopted a modern form of the ancient Tifinagh script, which had survived among the Tuareg, for teaching the language in schools.

facts.title: Only two elements are liquid at room temperature
facts.body: Of all the elements, only mercury and bromine are liquid under everyday room conditions. Bromine is a reddish-brown liquid that gives off choking fumes, and its name comes from the Greek for stench.

facts.title: The Stirrup
facts.body: Paired stirrups appear in China by the early 4th century AD and spread across Asia and into Europe over the following centuries. By giving riders a stable footing, they made it easier to fight from horseback. Historians once linked them to the rise of feudal knighthood in Europe, but that argument is now widely disputed.

facts.title: The Kingdom of Hawaii
facts.body: Around 1810 Kamehameha I completed the unification of the Hawaiian Islands into a single kingdom. Under his successors Hawaii became a constitutional monarchy recognised by foreign powers, while American-owned sugar plantations grew in influence. In 1893 American businessmen, backed by US marines, overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani, and the United States annexed the islands in 1898.

facts.title: Galen's Medicine
facts.body: Galen, a Greek physician of the 2nd century AD who worked in Rome, built a system of anatomy and physiology largely from dissections of animals such as apes and pigs. His writings dominated medicine in Europe and the Islamic world for well over a thousand years. Some of his errors, carried over from animal anatomy, were only corrected by Vesalius and Harvey in the 16th and 17th centuries.

facts.title: In Bulgaria a nod can mean no
facts.body: Traditionally Bulgarians nod their heads to say 'no' and shake them sideways to say 'yes'. The reversed gestures can easily confuse visitors.

facts.title: The Hawaiian Islands
facts.body: The Hawaiian Islands formed as the Pacific plate moved north-west over a fixed hotspot of rising magma. Each island was built by volcanoes and then carried away from the hotspot, so the islands grow older and more eroded to the north-west. The youngest, the island of Hawai'i, still has highly active volcanoes such as Kīlauea and Mauna Loa.

facts.title: The Mahabharata
facts.body: The Mahabharata, composed in Sanskrit over many centuries, tells of the war between two branches of a royal family, the Pandavas and the Kauravas. With around 100,000 verses, it is one of the longest poems ever composed. It contains the Bhagavad Gita and a wealth of stories that have shaped art, theatre and moral thought across South and Southeast Asia.

facts.title: Al-Farabi's Great Book of Music
facts.body: The philosopher al-Farabi, who died around 950, wrote the Kitab al-Musiqa al-Kabir, a systematic treatise on music theory. Drawing on Greek theory and on the practice of his time, it analyses intervals, scales, rhythm and instruments such as the oud. It became a foundation of music theory in the Islamic world.

facts.title: A paint tube helped create Impressionism
facts.body: In 1841 the American painter John Goffe Rand invented the squeezable metal paint tube. Artists could now carry ready-mixed paint outdoors, and Renoir is reported to have said Impressionism would not exist without it.

facts.title: Mahayana Buddhism and the Bodhisattva
facts.body: Mahayana, the 'Great Vehicle', emerged in India around the beginning of the common era and became the main form of Buddhism in China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam and Tibet. Its ideal is the bodhisattva, who seeks enlightenment out of compassion and vows to help all beings reach liberation, not only themselves. Mahayana also introduced new scriptures, such as the Lotus Sutra and the Heart Sutra.

facts.title: Cowrie Shell Money
facts.body: Cowrie shells, above all from the Maldives, served as money across large parts of Asia and Africa for centuries. Durable, hard to counterfeit and easy to count, they circulated as small change in Bengal and in West Africa, where they arrived through trans-Saharan and later European trade. Huge imports by European traders in the 18th and 19th centuries, including cheaper East African cowries from the 1840s, caused cowrie inflation, and colonial authorities eventually replaced them with coins.

facts.title: Arendt and Totalitarianism
facts.body: In The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951), Hannah Arendt argued that Nazism and Stalinism were a new form of government that used ideology and terror to dominate every aspect of life and to isolate individuals. Unlike older tyrannies, it sought total control rather than mere obedience. Her later report on the trial of Adolf Eichmann coined the phrase 'the banality of evil'.

facts.title: Whale songs spread like pop hits
facts.body: Male humpback whales in a population all sing the same song, which slowly changes. Researchers have tracked new songs spreading from Australian waters eastward across the South Pacific, one population to the next, within a few years.

facts.title: The Académie Française
facts.body: Founded in 1635 under Cardinal Richelieu, the Académie française was charged with regulating the French language and producing an authoritative dictionary, the first edition of which appeared in 1694. Its forty members, known as 'the immortals', are elected for life. It became a model for language academies elsewhere, such as the Real Academia Española, founded in 1713.

facts.title: The Persian Windmill
facts.body: The earliest well-documented windmills were built in Sistan, on the border of present-day Iran and Afghanistan, by around the 9th or 10th century. Their sails turned around a vertical axis inside walls that channelled the wind, and they were used to grind grain and lift water. Windmills of a different design, with a horizontal axis, appeared in north-western Europe in the late 12th century.

facts.title: The Salt March
facts.body: In 1930 Mohandas Gandhi led a 24-day march to the coastal village of Dandi, where he made salt in defiance of the British salt tax. The civil disobedience that followed led to tens of thousands of arrests and drew worldwide attention to the Indian independence movement.

facts.title: In the Monty Hall puzzle, always switch
facts.body: With three doors, one prize and a host who opens a losing door, switching wins two times out of three. Your first pick is right only a third of the time, and the host's choice concentrates the rest on the other door.

facts.title: Smallpox Inoculation
facts.body: Long before vaccines, people in China, India, Africa and the Ottoman Empire protected themselves against smallpox by deliberately infecting healthy people with material from smallpox sores. This 'variolation' usually caused a milder illness followed by lifelong immunity, though it carried some risk. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu saw it in Constantinople and promoted it in Britain from 1721, the year it was also used in Boston on the advice of an enslaved African man, Onesimus.

facts.title: The Strait of Hormuz
facts.body: The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow channel between Iran and Oman that links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the open ocean. It is the only sea outlet for most of the Gulf's oil and gas exporters. This makes it one of the most strategically important waterways in the world.

facts.title: Vincent van Gogh
facts.body: The Dutch painter Vincent van Gogh produced almost all his work in about a decade before his death in 1890, much of it in the south of France. Paintings such as The Starry Night and Sunflowers use thick brushstrokes and intense colour to express emotion. He sold very little in his lifetime but became one of the most influential figures of Post-Impressionism.

facts.title: Ramadan travels through all the seasons
facts.body: The Islamic calendar follows the Moon and is about 11 days shorter than the solar year. So Ramadan begins earlier each year and moves through every season in roughly 33 years.

facts.title: Basso Continuo
facts.body: Basso continuo is the bass line that runs through almost all Baroque music, from about 1600 to 1750. A bass instrument plays it while a harpsichord, organ or lute improvises chords from numbers written above the notes, known as figured bass. It gave music a firm harmonic foundation from Monteverdi to Bach and Handel.

facts.title: Islam in Southeast Asia
facts.body: Islam spread to Southeast Asia mainly through trade rather than conquest, carried by Muslim merchants from Arabia, India and elsewhere along Indian Ocean routes. From the late 13th century rulers in northern Sumatra, and later the port city of Malacca, adopted Islam, and it spread across the Malay world and Java. Southeast Asian Islam was often shaped by Sufism and blended with local traditions.

facts.title: The Physiocrats
facts.body: The Physiocrats, a group of 18th-century French thinkers led by François Quesnay, are often regarded as the first school of economists. They held that only agriculture produced a net surplus, and Quesnay's Tableau économique (1758) traced how this surplus circulated between social classes. Their call for free trade in grain and a single tax on land influenced Adam Smith.

facts.title: Ravel called his Boléro music without music
facts.body: Ravel's Boléro repeats the same two melodies over a steady snare-drum rhythm, getting louder for about a quarter of an hour. Ravel himself described it as orchestral tissue without music.

facts.title: The Ottoman Millet System
facts.body: The Ottoman Empire allowed recognised religious communities, such as Greek Orthodox Christians, Armenians and Jews, to run their own family law, education and charity under their own religious leaders. Historians debate how formal this 'millet' system was before it was codified in the 19th century. It is a classic example of autonomy for minorities that is based on community rather than territory.

facts.title: The Bengali Language Movement
facts.body: When Pakistan was created in 1947, its eastern wing, today's Bangladesh, spoke mainly Bengali, but the government sought to make Urdu the sole national language. On 21 February 1952 police fired on protesting students in Dhaka, killing several. The movement won recognition for Bengali, fed the nationalism that led to Bangladesh's independence in 1971, and UNESCO later made 21 February International Mother Language Day.

facts.title: Brazil's Ethanol Programme
facts.body: After the 1973 oil shock, Brazil launched its National Alcohol Programme, Proálcool, in 1975 to replace imported petrol with ethanol made from sugar cane. By the mid-1980s most new cars sold in Brazil ran on pure ethanol. Flex-fuel cars able to run on any blend were introduced in 2003 and soon dominated sales, making Brazil a pioneer of large-scale biofuels.

facts.title: The tongue taste map is a myth
facts.body: Diagrams showing sweet at the tip and bitter at the back come from a misreading of a German study of 1901. In fact taste buds on all parts of the tongue can detect all the basic tastes.

facts.title: The Viking Age
facts.body: From the late 8th to the mid-11th century Scandinavian seafarers raided, traded and settled across Europe; the attack on the monastery of Lindisfarne in 793 is often taken as the start. They settled in England, Ireland, Normandy and Iceland, reached Greenland and North America, and travelled down Russian rivers to Constantinople.

facts.title: Java Man
facts.body: In 1891 the Dutch doctor Eugène Dubois, searching deliberately for a 'missing link', found a skullcap on the banks of the Solo River in Java, and a thigh bone the next year. They were the first known remains of the species now called Homo erectus, an early human that walked upright. It was among the first major fossil evidence for human evolution, and later finds showed that Homo erectus lived across Africa and Asia.

facts.title: The Atlas Mountains
facts.body: The Atlas Mountains stretch some 2,500 kilometres across Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, separating the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts from the Sahara. They were raised mainly by the collision of the African and Eurasian plates, and Toubkal in Morocco is their highest peak. Their rain and snow feed the farms and cities of the Maghreb, and they have long been a homeland of the Amazigh, or Berber, peoples.

facts.title: Earth's core rivals the Sun's surface
facts.body: The temperature at Earth's inner core is estimated at over 5,000 degrees Celsius, roughly the same as the Sun's surface. The heat comes from Earth's formation and from radioactive decay.

facts.title: Mughal Miniature Painting
facts.body: At the courts of the Mughal emperors Akbar and Jahangir in the late 16th and early 17th centuries, workshops of painters produced richly coloured illustrated manuscripts and albums. Blending Persian traditions with Indian styles and some European influence, they depicted court life, battles, portraits and nature. Jahangir especially prized precise studies of animals and plants.

facts.title: Gamelan
facts.body: A gamelan is an Indonesian ensemble, especially from Java and Bali, made up mainly of bronze gongs, metallophones and drums. It uses two tuning systems, the five-note slendro and the seven-note pelog, and each set of instruments is tuned as a unique whole. Interlocking parts and layered cycles marked by gongs give the music its shimmering texture.

facts.title: The Bhagavad Gita
facts.body: The Bhagavad Gita, 'Song of the Lord', is a 700-verse dialogue within the Indian epic the Mahabharata. On the eve of battle the warrior Arjuna hesitates to fight his kinsmen, and his charioteer Krishna, revealed as a form of the god Vishnu, teaches him to do his duty without attachment to its results. It presents paths to liberation through action, knowledge and devotion, and is one of Hinduism's most widely read scriptures.

facts.title: Ancient Romans grabbed street food on the go
facts.body: Pompeii had dozens of thermopolia, counters with built-in jars for serving hot food and drink. Many Romans lived in flats without kitchens, so takeaway meals were part of everyday life.

facts.title: The Washington Consensus
facts.body: The economist John Williamson coined the term in 1989 for ten policy reforms that Washington-based institutions such as the IMF, the World Bank and the US Treasury were urging on Latin American countries. They included fiscal discipline, trade liberalisation, privatisation and deregulation. The term came to stand for market-oriented reform in general, and critics blamed it for imposing austerity on developing countries as a condition of loans.

facts.title: Aristotle's Politics
facts.body: In the Politics, Aristotle classified constitutions by whether one, a few or many rule, and whether they rule for the common good (kingship, aristocracy, polity) or for themselves (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy). He called humans political animals who can flourish only in a community. His comparison of many Greek city constitutions makes him a founder of political science.

facts.title: Mandarin and Standard Chinese
facts.body: The English word mandarin came via Portuguese from Malay, ultimately from Sanskrit mantrin, 'adviser', and first meant an imperial Chinese official. The officials' common language, guanhua, was based on northern speech and served as a lingua franca across the empire. In the 20th century a standard based on Beijing pronunciation became the national language, while other Chinese varieties such as Cantonese and Hokkien are not mutually intelligible with it.

facts.title: Peter Pan helps a children's hospital
facts.body: In 1929 J. M. Barrie gave the rights to Peter Pan to Great Ormond Street Hospital in London. The hospital has received royalties from the story ever since, helped by a special act of Parliament.

facts.title: The Telescope
facts.body: The telescope appeared in the Netherlands in 1608, when the spectacle-maker Hans Lipperhey applied for a patent. In 1609 and 1610 Galileo built improved versions and discovered the moons of Jupiter, mountains on the Moon and the phases of Venus. Isaac Newton later built a reflecting telescope that used a curved mirror instead of a lens.

facts.title: The Second World War
facts.body: The war began with Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939 and became global in 1941, when Germany invaded the Soviet Union and Japan attacked Pearl Harbor. It ended with Germany's surrender in May 1945 and Japan's in August, after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. It killed an estimated 70 to 85 million people.

facts.title: Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays
facts.body: Shen Kuo, an official and scholar of China's Song dynasty, recorded a wide range of observations in his Dream Pool Essays, completed around 1088. They contain the earliest clear description of a magnetic needle compass and note that it does not point exactly south, an early recognition of magnetic declination. He also argued from fossils and silt deposits that land is formed slowly over time.

facts.title: Sloths can turn green
facts.body: Sloths move so slowly that algae grow in grooves in their fur, giving them a greenish tint that helps camouflage them in the trees. Their fur also hosts moths, beetles and fungi, a whole tiny ecosystem.

facts.title: River Deltas
facts.body: A delta forms where a river slows on entering a sea or lake and drops its load of sediment. Ancient Greeks named the Nile delta after their triangular letter delta, a usage recorded by Herodotus. Deltas such as those of the Nile, Ganges and Mekong have very fertile soils and dense populations, but they are low-lying and vulnerable to flooding and sea-level rise.

facts.title: The Dome of the Rock
facts.body: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem was completed in 691 or 692 under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik and is the oldest surviving major Islamic monument. It stands over the rock from which Muhammad is believed to have ascended to heaven, with an octagonal plan crowned by a gilded dome. Its mosaics and inscriptions are key evidence for early Islamic art.

facts.title: Ludwig van Beethoven
facts.body: Beethoven (1770–1827) bridged the Classical and Romantic eras. He wrote nine symphonies, 32 piano sonatas and string quartets that expanded the scale and expressive range of each genre. He began losing his hearing in his late twenties and composed many of his greatest works, including the late quartets, while almost completely deaf.

facts.title: A seashell does not hold the sea
facts.body: The rushing sound when you hold a shell to your ear is surrounding noise echoing inside the shell. Its shape boosts some frequencies; a cup held to your ear does something similar.

facts.title: Pascal's Wager
facts.body: Blaise Pascal, the 17th-century French mathematician, argued in his Pensées that belief in God is a rational bet. If God exists, the believer gains infinite happiness; if not, little is lost, whereas the unbeliever risks infinite loss. Critics object that one cannot simply choose to believe and that the wager ignores the many possible gods, but it was an early use of the reasoning of decision theory.

facts.title: Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices
facts.body: In 301 AD the Roman emperor Diocletian issued an edict fixing maximum prices for hundreds of goods and services, from grain to wages, on pain of death. It was meant to curb the inflation that had followed the debasement of the coinage. According to the Christian writer Lactantius, goods vanished from the markets, and the edict was soon ignored, making it a classic early example of the failure of price controls.

facts.title: Pan-Africanism
facts.body: Pan-Africanism holds that Africans and people of African descent share common interests and should unite. Shaped by figures such as W. E. B. Du Bois and Marcus Garvey and by a series of Pan-African Congresses from 1919, it inspired independence leaders including Kwame Nkrumah, who led Ghana to independence in 1957.

facts.title: A fake town that became real
facts.body: Mapmakers invented Agloe, New York, in the 1930s as a 'trap' to catch copiers. Later a shop at the spot took the name Agloe, so for a time the made-up place really existed.

facts.title: Linear B
facts.body: Linear B is a script found on clay tablets from Mycenaean Greece and Crete in the second half of the second millennium BC. In 1952 the architect Michael Ventris, later working with John Chadwick, showed that it recorded an early form of Greek, centuries older than Homer. The tablets are mostly palace administrative records, and the related Linear A script of Minoan Crete remains undeciphered.

facts.title: Bronze Metallurgy
facts.body: Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, is harder than copper alone and was used for tools, weapons and vessels. It came into use in the Near East in the late 4th millennium BC and spread widely in the 3rd. Because tin deposits are rare, bronze-making stimulated long-distance trade, and archaeologists named the Bronze Age after it.

facts.title: Sargon of Akkad
facts.body: Around 2300 BC Sargon, ruling from the city of Akkad, conquered the Sumerian city-states of Mesopotamia. The Akkadian Empire he founded is often described as the first empire, uniting different peoples under a single ruler.

facts.title: The marathon distance was set by royalty
facts.body: At the 1908 London Olympics the marathon ran from Windsor Castle to the stadium, finishing in front of the royal box. That made it 42.195 km, which later became the official distance.

facts.title: Harvey and the Circulation of the Blood
facts.body: In 1628 the English physician William Harvey showed that the heart pumps blood around the body in a continuous circuit. Through experiments and a simple calculation, he showed that the heart pumps far more blood than the body could make from food, so the same blood must circulate. The tiny capillaries linking arteries and veins, which he could not see, were observed by Marcello Malpighi in 1661.

facts.title: The Eurasian Steppe
facts.body: The Eurasian Steppe is a vast belt of grassland stretching from Hungary and Ukraine across Central Asia to Mongolia and northern China. Too dry for forest and often for farming, it was the home of horse-riding pastoral nomads. Peoples such as the Scythians, Huns and Mongols used it as a highway that linked, and repeatedly threatened, the settled civilisations around it.

facts.title: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
facts.body: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz was a nun in 17th-century Mexico City, often called the greatest poet of colonial Spanish America. Largely self-taught, she wrote lyric poems, plays and the long philosophical poem First Dream. In her Reply to Sor Filotea she defended women's right to learning.

facts.title: A tree known from fossils was found alive
facts.body: The Wollemi pine was known from a fossil record going back many millions of years, then in 1994 a park ranger found living trees in a remote gorge near Sydney. Fewer than a hundred wild trees grow there.

facts.title: Heitor Villa-Lobos
facts.body: Villa-Lobos (1887–1959) is the best-known Brazilian composer of the 20th century. He combined European forms with Brazilian folk and popular music, most famously in the Bachianas Brasileiras, which fuse Bach's style with Brazilian idioms. He also shaped music education in Brazil.

facts.title: The Hebrew Bible
facts.body: The Hebrew Bible, or Tanakh, is the scripture of Judaism and, as the Old Testament, part of the Christian Bible. Its name comes from its three parts: Torah (the five books of Moses), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings). Composed and edited over many centuries, largely in the first millennium BC, it tells of creation, God's covenant with Israel, the Exodus and the history of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.

facts.title: Bitcoin
facts.body: In 2008 a person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto published a design for Bitcoin, a digital currency that works without a central bank or other trusted intermediary. Transactions are recorded on a public ledger, the blockchain, maintained by a decentralised network of computers. Bitcoin launched in 2009 and inspired thousands of other cryptocurrencies, though economists debate whether such volatile assets can serve well as money.

facts.title: The Sun is almost the whole Solar System
facts.body: About 99.8 per cent of all the mass in the Solar System is in the Sun. All the planets, moons, asteroids and comets together make up only the tiny remainder, and Jupiter accounts for most of that.

facts.title: The Tanzimat Reforms
facts.body: Between 1839 and 1876 the Ottoman Empire carried out the Tanzimat ('reorganisation'), modernising its army, law, education and administration. Imperial edicts of 1839 and 1856 promised security of life and property and equality for all subjects regardless of religion. The era culminated in the first Ottoman constitution of 1876, which was suspended two years later.

facts.title: Rongorongo
facts.body: Rongorongo is a system of glyphs carved on a few dozen wooden objects from Easter Island (Rapa Nui), first reported by outsiders in the 1860s. It has never been deciphered, and scholars disagree on whether it is true writing and whether it arose before or after contact with Europeans in the 18th century. If it is writing invented on the island without outside influence, it would be one of the very few independent inventions of writing.

facts.title: Television
facts.body: In 1926 John Logie Baird gave the first public demonstration of television in London, using a mechanical scanning system. All-electronic television, developed by Philo Farnsworth, Vladimir Zworykin and others, soon replaced mechanical systems. Regular broadcasting began in the 1930s, and after the Second World War television became the dominant mass medium.

facts.title: The first jack-o'-lanterns were turnips
facts.body: In Ireland and Scotland people carved faces into turnips and other root vegetables for Halloween. Emigrants to North America switched to the larger, easier-to-carve pumpkin.

facts.title: The Khmer Empire
facts.body: From the 9th to the 15th century the Khmer Empire dominated much of mainland South-East Asia from its capital at Angkor, in present-day Cambodia. Its kings built vast temples, including Angkor Wat in the 12th century, and a city sustained by great reservoirs and canals. Angkor declined after the 14th century.

facts.title: Humboldt's Journey Through the Americas
facts.body: From 1799 to 1804 Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland travelled through Spanish America, measuring and collecting as they went. On the volcano Chimborazo, Humboldt observed how vegetation changes in bands with altitude, mirroring the change from the equator to the poles. His view of nature as an interconnected whole shaped biogeography and ecology and inspired Darwin.

facts.title: Waldseemüller's Map
facts.body: In 1507 the German cartographer Martin Waldseemüller published a world map that was the first to use the name 'America'. He named the new continent after the Italian navigator Amerigo Vespucci, who had argued that the lands found across the Atlantic were a new world rather than part of Asia. The name stuck, although Waldseemüller later dropped it from his own maps.

facts.title: "OK" began as a spelling joke
facts.body: OK first appeared in a Boston newspaper in 1839 as short for "oll korrect", a deliberate misspelling of all correct. Comic abbreviations were a fad at the time, and this was the one that survived.

facts.title: Chola Bronzes
facts.body: Under the Chola dynasty of southern India, from around the 10th to the 12th century, sculptors cast Hindu deities in bronze using the lost-wax method. The best known is Shiva as Nataraja, Lord of the Dance, dancing within a ring of fire that represents the cosmic cycle of creation and destruction. Made to be carried in temple processions, they are masterpieces of Indian sculpture.

facts.title: The Guqin
facts.body: The guqin is a seven-string plucked zither that has been played in China for more than two thousand years. Associated with Confucius and the ideal of the cultivated scholar, it was valued as a means of self-cultivation rather than entertainment. Its subtle sliding tones are recorded in a special tablature that records strings, finger positions and techniques but not rhythm.

facts.title: The Aboriginal Dreaming
facts.body: For Aboriginal Australians, the Dreaming (an English term; each language has its own word) is the creative era when ancestral beings shaped the land, created life and laid down law, and also their continuing presence. Dreaming stories, songs and ceremonies bind people to particular places and govern kinship, conduct and responsibilities for land. The ancestral tracks across the country, often called songlines, also serve as maps.

facts.title: The hat thrower fungus fires its spores
facts.body: Pilobolus, which grows on dung, blasts its spore capsule more than two metres. The launch is among the fastest accelerations in nature, around 20,000 times gravity, so spores land on fresh grass where animals will eat them.

facts.title: Limited Liability
facts.body: Under limited liability, shareholders can lose only what they invested in a company, not their personal assets. Britain made it widely available to ordinary companies through laws passed in 1855 and 1856, and other industrial countries adopted similar rules. By making it safer for many small investors to buy shares, it allowed the large-scale raising of capital that built railways and industrial corporations.

facts.title: The League of Nations
facts.body: Created by the peace settlement after the First World War and founded in 1920 with its seat in Geneva, the League was the first worldwide organisation of states dedicated to keeping the peace through collective security. The United States never joined, and the League failed to stop aggression by Japan, Italy and Germany in the 1930s. It was dissolved in 1946 and succeeded by the United Nations.

facts.title: The Graeco-Arabic Translation Movement
facts.body: From the late 8th to the 10th century, scholars in Abbasid Baghdad translated a large part of Greek philosophy, medicine and science into Arabic, often via Syriac. Patrons included the caliph al-Ma'mun, and the Nestorian Christian Hunayn ibn Ishaq was among the most prolific translators. The movement preserved and extended the works of Aristotle, Galen and Euclid, many of which later reached medieval Europe through Arabic.

facts.title: Mirrors swap front and back, not sides
facts.body: A mirror does not truly swap left and right: your raised right hand appears on the same side. What it reverses is front to back. We just imagine walking round to stand where the reflection is.

facts.title: The Control of Fire
facts.body: Early humans learned to control fire long before modern humans appeared, though how early is debated, with claims ranging from over a million years ago to a few hundred thousand. Fire gave warmth, light and protection from predators, and cooking made food easier to digest. Some researchers argue that cooking helped shape human evolution.

facts.title: The Haitian Revolution
facts.body: In 1791 enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose in revolt. Led by Toussaint Louverture and later Jean-Jacques Dessalines, they abolished slavery and defeated French, Spanish and British forces. In 1804 Haiti became independent: the first state founded by a successful revolt of enslaved people.

facts.title: The Discovery of HIV
facts.body: AIDS was first recognised in 1981, when doctors in the United States reported rare infections in previously healthy young men. In 1983 Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier at the Pasteur Institute in Paris isolated the virus responsible, later named HIV.
