The discovery made blood tests and antiviral drugs possible, and the two shared the 2008 Nobel Prize.

facts.title: In Thailand the year is 543 ahead
facts.body: Thailand officially counts years in the Buddhist Era, which starts 543 years before the Western calendar. So AD 2000 was 2543 in Thailand.

facts.title: The Valley of Mexico
facts.body: The Valley of Mexico is a high basin in central Mexico, more than 2,000 metres above sea level, that once held a system of lakes. The Aztecs built their capital, Tenochtitlan, on an island in Lake Texcoco, and Mexico City grew on its ruins. Draining the lakes left the city on soft clay, which amplifies earthquakes and makes the ground sink as groundwater is pumped out.

facts.title: Waiting for Godot
facts.body: Samuel Beckett's play, first staged in Paris in French in 1953, shows two tramps waiting by a road for someone called Godot who never comes. Almost nothing happens, yet the play is both comic and bleak. It is the best-known work of what the critic Martin Esslin called the Theatre of the Absurd.

facts.title: Gospel Music
facts.body: Gospel music developed in African American churches in the early 20th century, combining hymns, spirituals and blues. Thomas A. Dorsey in Chicago shaped the genre from the 1930s, and Mahalia Jackson became its best-known voice. Its vocal style was the direct source of soul music, through singers such as Aretha Franklin and Sam Cooke.

facts.title: "Pineapple" first meant pine cone
facts.body: In English, pineapple originally meant the cone of a pine tree. When Europeans met the tropical fruit, its scaly skin reminded them of a pine cone, so the name moved across. Most languages call it ananas instead.

facts.title: Democritus and Atomism
facts.body: In the 5th century BC Leucippus and his pupil Democritus proposed that everything consists of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms, from the Greek for 'uncuttable', moving in empty space. Differences between things arise from the shapes, sizes and arrangements of their atoms. Taken up by Epicurus and the Roman poet Lucretius, the theory was speculative rather than experimental, but it anticipated modern atomic theory.

facts.title: Economies of Scale
facts.body: Economies of scale arise when the average cost of each unit falls as output grows, for example because fixed costs are spread over more units or larger plants allow more specialisation. They help explain why industries such as car manufacturing and power generation tend to be dominated by large firms. Where they are very strong, a single firm can supply a market most cheaply, creating a 'natural monopoly' that governments often regulate.

facts.title: Mill's Harm Principle
facts.body: In On Liberty (1859), John Stuart Mill argued that the only legitimate reason for exercising power over anyone against their will is to prevent harm to others; a person's own good is not enough. He defended free speech on the grounds that suppressed opinions may be true, and warned against society's pressure to conform as well as against state power.

facts.title: Sperm whales sleep standing upright
facts.body: Sperm whales take short naps hanging vertically near the surface, heads up or down, completely still. Researchers discovered this in 2008 when they drifted into a group of sleeping whales that did not react to their boat.

facts.title: The Afroasiatic Languages
facts.body: The Afroasiatic family includes Arabic, Hebrew and Aramaic, the Berber languages, Hausa, Somali and Amharic, as well as ancient Egyptian and Akkadian. It probably originated in north-eastern Africa, though its homeland is debated. Its Semitic branch builds words from roots of usually three consonants: in Arabic, k-t-b gives kataba (he wrote), kitab (book) and maktab (office).

facts.title: Public-Key Cryptography
facts.body: In 1976 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published a way for two parties to agree a secret key over an open channel, and in 1977 Rivest, Shamir and Adleman created the RSA system. Public-key cryptography uses a public key to encrypt and a private one to decrypt, so strangers can communicate securely. It underpins secure websites and online payments. British intelligence had made similar discoveries earlier but kept them secret.

facts.title: The Hundred Years' War
facts.body: From 1337 to 1453 the kings of England and France fought intermittently over English claims to the French throne. England won famous victories at Crécy and Agincourt, but France recovered, inspired in part by Joan of Arc, and drove the English out of all of France except Calais.

facts.title: Most ordinary matter is hydrogen
facts.body: About three-quarters of the ordinary matter in the universe, by mass, is hydrogen, and most of the rest is helium. Nearly all heavier elements were made later inside stars.

facts.title: Franklin and the Electricity of Lightning
facts.body: In the 1740s and 1750s Benjamin Franklin experimented with electricity in Philadelphia and proposed that lightning is an electrical discharge. In 1752 experimenters in France confirmed this with a tall iron rod as he had suggested, and later that year Franklin published an account of a kite experiment, which he is said to have carried out himself. The work led to the lightning rod, and Franklin introduced the terms positive and negative charge.

facts.title: The Wallace Line
facts.body: The Wallace Line is a boundary running between Bali and Lombok and between Borneo and Sulawesi. The naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace noticed that animals to the west of it are mainly Asian, while those to the east include Australian types such as marsupials. Deep water there was never bridged by land, even when ice-age sea levels were low.

facts.title: The Taj Mahal
facts.body: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in Agra as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. Its white marble domed mausoleum, set at the end of a formal garden and flanked by four minarets, is inlaid with semi-precious stones. It is the most celebrated work of Mughal architecture, blending Persian, Islamic and Indian traditions.

facts.title: A mighty warship that sank almost immediately
facts.body: Sweden's warship Vasa capsized in 1628 on its maiden voyage, little more than a kilometre from where it set sail in Stockholm. It was top-heavy, and the cold brackish water preserved it so well that it was raised in 1961.

facts.title: The Oud
facts.body: The oud is a short-necked, fretless lute with a pear-shaped body, central to Arabic, Turkish and Persian music. Being fretless, it can produce the microtonal intervals of the maqam system. Its Arabic name, al-ʿud, passed through Spain into European languages as 'lute', and the European lute descends from it.

facts.title: The Bahá'í Faith
facts.body: The Bahá'í Faith arose in 19th-century Iran. Its founder, Bahá'u'lláh (1817–1892), proclaimed himself the messenger foretold by an earlier prophet, the Báb, and spent decades in exile, dying near Acre in Ottoman Palestine. Bahá'ís teach the unity of God, of religion and of humanity, seeing figures such as Abraham, Moses, the Buddha, Jesus and Muhammad as successive messengers of one God.

facts.title: Sen on Famines
facts.body: In Poverty and Famines (1981), the Indian economist Amartya Sen argued that famines are often caused not by a lack of food but by the collapse of people's ability to obtain it. In his analysis of the Bengal famine of 1943, food supply was not unusually low, but rising prices and lost earnings left millions unable to buy enough. Sen also argued that famines do not occur in functioning democracies with a free press, and he received the 1998 Nobel memorial prize in economics.

facts.title: The first barcode scanned was on chewing gum
facts.body: On 26 June 1974, in a supermarket in Troy, Ohio, a packet of Wrigley's chewing gum became the first product sold using a barcode scanner. The packet is now kept at the Smithsonian.

facts.title: The Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist
facts.body: In lectures given in 1970, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini argued that in the absence of the hidden Imam a qualified Shia jurist should hold political authority. After the 1979 revolution this doctrine of velayat-e faqih was written into the constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran, which places a Supreme Leader above elected institutions. Many senior Shia clerics have rejected the doctrine.

facts.title: Quechua
facts.body: Quechua served as the administrative language of the Inca Empire, which spread it along the Andes. After the Spanish conquest, missionaries adopted it as a 'general language' for evangelisation, extending it further, and a catechism printed in Lima in 1584 in Spanish, Quechua and Aymara was the first book printed in South America. Quechua is in fact a family of related varieties spoken across several Andean countries.

facts.title: Glassblowing
facts.body: Glass had been made for thousands of years, but blowing it through a tube was invented in the 1st century BC on the eastern Mediterranean coast, in the region of Syria and Palestine. Blowing made thin, transparent vessels quick and cheap to produce. The technique spread through the Roman Empire and remains the basis of handmade glassware.

facts.title: Bright light makes some people sneeze
facts.body: Many people, estimated at between a fifth and a third, sneeze when they step into bright sunlight. This 'photic sneeze reflex' runs in families and may come from signals in nerves of the eye and nose getting crossed.

facts.title: Suleiman the Magnificent
facts.body: Suleiman I ruled the Ottoman Empire from 1520 to 1566, at the height of its power. He took Belgrade, Rhodes, much of Hungary and Baghdad, and besieged Vienna in 1529. Known to Ottomans as 'the Lawgiver', he also presided over a flowering of architecture led by Sinan.

facts.title: Faraday and Electromagnetic Induction
facts.body: In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted found that an electric current deflects a compass needle. In 1831 Michael Faraday discovered the reverse effect: a changing magnetic field produces an electric current in a wire. Electromagnetic induction is the principle behind electric generators and transformers, and Faraday's idea of fields of force became central to physics.

facts.title: Drainage Basins and Watersheds
facts.body: A drainage basin is all the land whose rainfall drains into a particular river and its tributaries. Basins are separated by high ground called divides or watersheds; in North America 'watershed' often means the basin itself. Because whatever happens upstream affects everyone downstream, river basins are a natural unit for managing water.

facts.title: Somewhere on Earth the wind is always still
facts.body: The hairy ball theorem says you cannot comb a hairy sphere flat without a tuft or bald spot. Applied to wind, it means that at any moment there must be at least one point on Earth with no horizontal wind.

facts.title: The Bauhaus
facts.body: The Bauhaus was a German school of art, design and architecture founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919. It aimed to unite fine art, craft and industry, producing simple, functional designs suited to mass production. Closed under Nazi pressure in 1933, its teachers carried its ideas abroad, shaping modern architecture and design worldwide.

facts.title: Metre and Time Signatures
facts.body: Metre is the regular grouping of beats into strong and weak, which listeners feel as the pulse of the music. In Western notation a time signature such as 3/4 (a waltz) or 4/4 states how many beats are in a bar. Many traditions use more complex patterns, such as the additive metres of Balkan dances or the rhythmic cycles of Indian music.

facts.title: Jainism and Ahimsa
facts.body: Jainism is an ancient Indian religion whose last great teacher, Mahavira, was a contemporary of the Buddha. Its central principle is ahimsa, non-violence towards all living beings, which leads devout Jains to strict vegetarianism and great care not to harm even insects. Jains also teach anekantavada, the view that truth has many sides that no single viewpoint fully grasps, and their ideal of non-violence influenced Gandhi.

facts.title: A country in all four hemispheres
facts.body: Kiribati's islands straddle both the equator and the 180th meridian. That puts parts of it in the northern, southern, eastern and western hemispheres at once.

facts.title: The Bank of England
facts.body: The Bank of England was founded in 1694 as a private company to lend money to the government of William III for its war with France. It gradually took on the roles of a central bank: managing the national debt, issuing banknotes and acting as banker to other banks. Its creation, alongside a reliable system of public borrowing, helped Britain finance its wars more cheaply than its rivals.

facts.title: Rome's Mixed Constitution
facts.body: From about 509 BC the Roman Republic was governed by two annually elected consuls, a Senate of former magistrates and popular assemblies, while tribunes could veto acts against the plebeians. The Greek historian Polybius praised it as a mixed constitution combining monarchy, aristocracy and democracy. The model inspired the American founders and the idea of checks and balances.

facts.title: Basic Word Order
facts.body: Languages differ in the usual order of subject, verb and object. English, Chinese and Swahili are mainly subject-verb-object; Japanese, Korean, Turkish and Hindi put the verb last; Classical Arabic, Welsh and Irish usually put it first. Joseph Greenberg showed in the 1960s that word order correlates with other features: verb-final languages, for example, tend to use postpositions rather than prepositions.

facts.title: There is more than one Scream
facts.body: Edvard Munch made several versions of The Scream, including two paintings and two pastels, plus many prints. He often returned to his favourite images and reworked them.

facts.title: Yuri Gagarin's Spaceflight
facts.body: On 12 April 1961 the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, orbiting the Earth once in Vostok 1. The flight lasted about 108 minutes, and he ejected and landed by parachute as planned. Launched from Baikonur, the mission proved that humans could survive and work in spaceflight.

facts.title: The Taiping Rebellion
facts.body: From 1850 to 1864 a rebellion led by Hong Xiuquan, who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus, tore through southern and central China. The Taiping made Nanjing their capital before Qing forces crushed them. It was one of the deadliest conflicts in history, with deaths estimated in the tens of millions.

facts.title: Helicobacter pylori and Stomach Ulcers
facts.body: In the early 1980s the Australian doctors Robin Warren and Barry Marshall, working in Perth, found that a bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, is a major cause of stomach ulcers. Ulcers had been blamed on stress and acid, and the idea met strong scepticism until Marshall drank a culture of the bacterium and developed gastritis. Ulcers became curable with antibiotics, and the two shared the 2005 Nobel Prize.

facts.title: Arctic terns chase an endless summer
facts.body: Arctic terns breed in the far north and spend the northern winter near Antarctica, flying between them every year. Because they follow summer at both ends of the planet, they probably see more daylight than any other animal.

facts.title: Ptolemy's Geography
facts.body: Around 150 AD, Claudius Ptolemy of Alexandria compiled the Geography, a guide to mapping the known world that listed thousands of places by latitude and longitude. It set out how to project the curved Earth onto a flat map. Rediscovered in western Europe around 1400, it shaped Renaissance mapmaking, including its underestimate of the Earth's size.

facts.title: Fresco
facts.body: Fresco is the technique of painting with pigments mixed in water on freshly laid wet lime plaster; as it dries, the colour becomes part of the wall. Used since antiquity, as at Pompeii, it reached its height in Renaissance Italy, from Giotto to Michelangelo. Because work must be finished before the plaster sets, artists paint in daily sections called giornate.

facts.title: Motown
facts.body: Berry Gordy founded Motown in Detroit in 1959. With artists such as the Supremes, Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder and the Temptations, and a house band known as the Funk Brothers, it produced a polished soul sound that topped charts across racial lines. It became one of the most successful Black-owned businesses in America in its era.

facts.title: Earth's magnetic poles have swapped places
facts.body: Rocks show that Earth's magnetic field has reversed many times, with north and south switching. The last full reversal happened about 780,000 years ago, recorded in magnetised volcanic rock.

facts.title: Pragmatism
facts.body: Pragmatism, often seen as America's most distinctive philosophical movement, was developed from the 1870s by Charles Sanders Peirce, William James and John Dewey. It holds that the meaning and truth of an idea lie in its practical consequences: an idea is true insofar as it works in experience. Dewey applied it to education and democracy, influencing progressive schooling.

facts.title: Nash Equilibrium
facts.body: A Nash equilibrium is a situation in a game where no player can do better by changing strategy alone, given the strategies of the others. The American mathematician John Nash proved in 1950 that such an equilibrium exists in a wide class of games. The concept became central to game theory, which economists use to analyse competition, bargaining, auctions and arms races.

facts.title: Self-Determination of Peoples
facts.body: The principle that peoples have the right freely to choose their political status gained force after the First World War, championed in different ways by Woodrow Wilson and Lenin. It was written into the UN Charter and the 1966 human rights covenants. Its tension with the territorial integrity of existing states is one of the hardest problems of international law.

facts.title: German children start school with sweet cones
facts.body: On their first day of school, German children receive a Schultüte, a large paper cone filled with sweets and small gifts. It is meant to sweeten a big step in life.

facts.title: Sequoyah's Cherokee Syllabary
facts.body: Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith who could not read any language, devised a writing system for Cherokee and completed it around 1821. Each of its characters stands for a syllable. The Cherokee Nation adopted it, literacy spread rapidly, and the newspaper Cherokee Phoenix began printing in it in 1828. It is a rare case of an individual creating a successful script without being literate beforehand.

facts.title: Gutta-Percha and Undersea Cables
facts.body: Gutta-percha is a natural latex from trees of the Malay Peninsula and nearby islands. Introduced to Europe in the 1840s, it proved an excellent insulator that stays stable under seawater. It made the first submarine telegraph cables possible, including the cross-Channel cable of 1851 and the transatlantic cables, and the trade in it boomed.

facts.title: Great Zimbabwe
facts.body: Great Zimbabwe was the capital of a powerful southern African kingdom from about the 11th to the 15th century. Its massive dry-stone walls, built without mortar, enclosed a royal city whose wealth came from cattle and gold traded to the Swahili coast. Colonial-era writers wrongly denied it was built by Africans; modern Zimbabwe is named after it.

facts.title: An organ concert will last 639 years
facts.body: In a church in Halberstadt, Germany, an organ is playing John Cage's piece As Slow As Possible. It began in 2001 and is planned to end in 2640, so the chord changes are years apart.

facts.title: The Human Genome Project
facts.body: Launched in 1990 as an international effort, the Human Genome Project set out to read the roughly three billion DNA letters of the human genome. A draft was announced in 2000 and the project was declared complete in 2003, though the last gaps were filled only in 2022 and 2023. It showed that humans have far fewer protein-coding genes than expected, now estimated at about 20,000, and transformed medical research.

facts.title: Mount Fuji
facts.body: Mount Fuji, at about 3,776 metres, is the highest mountain in Japan and a nearly symmetrical active volcano that last erupted in 1707. It has long been a sacred site for pilgrims and a central symbol of Japan in art, notably in Hokusai's prints. It was listed as a World Heritage Site in 2013 as a cultural landscape.

facts.title: Leaves of Grass
facts.body: Walt Whitman self-published Leaves of Grass in 1855 and kept expanding it through many editions until his death in 1892. Its long, unrhymed lines of free verse celebrate democracy, the body and ordinary Americans, as in 'Song of Myself'. Breaking with traditional metre, it made Whitman a founding voice of American poetry.

facts.title: The sensitive plant folds when touched
facts.body: Mimosa pudica folds its leaflets within seconds of being touched. Cells at the base of each leaflet suddenly lose water, so the leaf collapses, which may startle grazing animals or knock off insects.

facts.title: The Shakuhachi
facts.body: The shakuhachi is an end-blown Japanese bamboo flute derived from Chinese models. In the Edo period it was played by monks of the Fuke sect of Zen as a form of meditation through breathing, known as suizen. Its breathy tone and bending pitches make it one of the most recognisable sounds of Japanese music.

facts.title: The Problem of Evil
facts.body: If God is all-powerful, all-knowing and wholly good, why does evil exist? This question, often attributed to Epicurus, is a central challenge to belief in God, and the biblical Book of Job wrestles with it. Responses, called theodicies, include the argument that free will requires the possibility of evil and that suffering can build character.

facts.title: The Euro
facts.body: The euro was launched as an electronic currency in 1999 and as notes and coins in 2002, replacing national currencies such as the Deutschmark, the French franc and the Italian lira. Monetary policy for the member states passed to the European Central Bank in Frankfurt. Countries joining were meant to meet convergence criteria on inflation, deficits and debt laid down in the Maastricht Treaty of 1992.

facts.title: The sky is blue, not violet
facts.body: Air scatters short-wavelength light most, so violet is scattered even more than blue. The sky looks blue because sunlight has less violet and our eyes are more sensitive to blue.

facts.title: The Declaration of Independence
facts.body: Adopted by the Continental Congress on 4 July 1776 and drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson, it announced the separation of thirteen American colonies from Britain. Its preamble holds that all men are created equal, with unalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed.

facts.title: Nicaraguan Sign Language
facts.body: When Nicaragua opened schools for deaf children in the late 1970s and 1980s, pupils who had used only home signs began to create a shared signing system, and younger children who joined later turned it into a fuller language with consistent grammar. Linguists studied it as a rare chance to watch a language being born. It confirmed what research since William Stokoe's 1960 work on American Sign Language had shown: sign languages are complete natural languages.

facts.title: The Spinning Jenny
facts.body: Around 1764 James Hargreaves, a Lancashire weaver, invented the spinning jenny, which let one worker spin several threads at once. Together with Richard Arkwright's water frame and Samuel Crompton's mule, it mechanised cotton spinning. These machines moved textile production into factories and helped launch Britain's Industrial Revolution.

facts.title: Easter can fall on 35 different dates
facts.body: Western Easter is the first Sunday after the church's spring full moon. It can land anywhere from 22 March to 25 April, depending on the lunar cycle.

facts.title: The September 11 Attacks
facts.body: On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four airliners, crashing two into the World Trade Center in New York and one into the Pentagon; the fourth came down in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back. Nearly 3,000 people were killed. The United States responded with the invasion of Afghanistan and a 'war on terror'.

facts.title: Vesalius and Human Anatomy
facts.body: In 1543, the same year Copernicus published his account of heliocentrism, Andreas Vesalius published On the Fabric of the Human Body. Based on his own dissections of human corpses at Padua, it corrected many of Galen's errors and was illustrated with detailed woodcuts. It grounded anatomy in direct observation and is a founding work of modern medicine.

facts.title: The Alps
facts.body: The Alps form an arc of about 1,200 kilometres across France, Switzerland, Italy, Germany, Austria and Slovenia. They were raised by the collision of the African and Eurasian plates, and Mont Blanc is their highest peak. Rivers such as the Rhine, the Rhône and the Po rise in them, which is why they are often called the water tower of Europe.

facts.title: The first Oscars ceremony was very short
facts.body: The first Academy Awards in 1929 lasted only about 15 minutes. The winners had been announced three months earlier, so there was no suspense.

facts.title: Lu Xun
facts.body: Lu Xun is regarded as the founder of modern Chinese literature. His story A Madman's Diary of 1918, one of the first major works in vernacular Chinese, portrayed traditional society as 'cannibalistic'. The True Story of Ah Q satirised national weaknesses through a self-deluding village labourer.

facts.title: The Lyres of Ur
facts.body: In the 1920s Leonard Woolley excavated the Royal Cemetery of Ur in southern Iraq and found several lyres from around 2500 BC. Decorated with bulls' heads of gold and lapis lazuli, they are among the oldest surviving stringed instruments and show that music had a central place in Sumerian court and ritual life.

facts.title: Our Lady of Guadalupe
facts.body: According to Catholic tradition, in 1531 the Virgin Mary appeared to Juan Diego, an Indigenous convert, on the hill of Tepeyac near Mexico City, leaving her image on his cloak. The dark-skinned Virgin of Guadalupe became a powerful symbol uniting Indigenous and Spanish identities and later of Mexican nationhood, carried on banners in the war of independence. Juan Diego was canonised in 2002.

facts.title: A slime mould redrew Tokyo's railways
facts.body: In 2010 Japanese researchers placed oat flakes in the pattern of cities around Tokyo for a brainless slime mould. It linked them with a network strikingly similar to the region's rail lines. Slime moulds were once classed as fungi but are not.

facts.title: The Harvester Judgment
facts.body: In 1907 Justice Henry Bournes Higgins of Australia's Commonwealth Court of Conciliation and Arbitration ruled on whether the Sunshine Harvester works paid 'fair and reasonable' wages. He defined such a wage as one enough for an unskilled labourer to support a wife and three children in frugal comfort. The judgment established the principle of a basic wage based on need, which shaped Australian wage-setting for decades.

facts.title: The Althing
facts.body: Founded in 930, Iceland's Althing was an open-air assembly at Thingvellir where chieftains met each summer to make laws and settle disputes, while a lawspeaker recited the law from memory. Though abolished in 1800 and restored in 1845, it is often called one of the oldest parliaments in the world, and its name lives on in Iceland's national parliament.

facts.title: Writing the Hawaiian Language
facts.body: American Protestant missionaries who arrived in Hawaii in 1820 worked with Hawaiian speakers to put the language into writing, settling by the late 1820s on an alphabet of only twelve letters: five vowels and seven consonants. Schools and printing spread literacy remarkably quickly, and Hawaiian-language newspapers flourished from the 1830s onwards. After an 1896 law made English the medium of schooling, the language declined sharply, and much of this printed record later became a key resource for its revival.

facts.title: Mark Twain arrived and left with Halley's Comet
facts.body: Mark Twain was born in 1835, shortly after Halley's Comet passed close to the Sun, and predicted he would go out with it. He died in April 1910, the day after the comet's next closest approach to the Sun.

facts.title: The Hejaz Railway
facts.body: Built by the Ottoman Empire between 1900 and 1908, the Hejaz Railway linked Damascus with Medina, mainly to carry Muslim pilgrims towards Mecca. It cut a journey of weeks by camel to a few days. During the First World War Arab forces, aided by the British officer known as Lawrence of Arabia, repeatedly attacked it, and its southern section was never restored.

facts.title: The Achaemenid Persian Empire
facts.body: Founded by Cyrus the Great in the mid-6th century BC, the Achaemenid Empire stretched from Egypt and the Aegean to the Indus. It was governed through provinces called satrapies, linked by royal roads. Cyrus was remembered for letting conquered peoples, such as the Jews exiled in Babylon, return home. Alexander the Great ended the empire.

facts.title: Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells
facts.body: In 2006 Shinya Yamanaka in Kyoto showed that adult mouse cells could be turned back into stem cells able to become any cell type by switching on just four genes; human cells followed in 2007. The discovery showed that cell specialisation is reversible and offered stem cells without using embryos. Yamanaka shared the 2012 Nobel Prize with John Gurdon, who had cloned frogs from specialised cells.

facts.title: Einstein was offered a presidency
facts.body: In 1952 Albert Einstein was invited to become President of Israel. He politely declined, saying he lacked the aptitude and experience to deal with people and official functions.

facts.title: The Canadian Shield
facts.body: The Canadian Shield is a vast area of ancient bedrock curving around Hudson Bay and covering much of Canada. It contains some of the oldest rocks on Earth. Scraped bare by ice-age glaciers, it has thin soils and countless lakes, and it is rich in minerals such as nickel, gold and iron.

facts.title: Beowulf
facts.body: Beowulf is the longest surviving epic poem in Old English, preserved in a single manuscript from around the year 1000. Its hero, a Geatish warrior, kills the monster Grendel and Grendel's mother, and dies many years later fighting a dragon. The date of its composition is debated, but it is a founding text of English literature.

facts.title: Rock and Roll
facts.body: Rock and roll emerged in the United States in the mid-1950s from rhythm and blues, country and gospel. Chuck Berry, Little Richard and Elvis Presley made the electric guitar and a strong backbeat central to popular music. It became the soundtrack of a new youth culture and the basis of rock music.

facts.title: Every Rubik's Cube is solvable in 20 moves
facts.body: A Rubik's Cube has about 43 quintillion possible positions, yet in 2010 researchers proved that every one can be solved in 20 moves or fewer. Ernő Rubik first made the cube as a teaching tool.

facts.title: Francis of Assisi
facts.body: Francis of Assisi (around 1181–1226) gave up his wealth as a merchant's son to live in radical poverty, preaching and caring for the poor and sick. The Franciscan order he founded, along with the Dominicans, created a new kind of religious life: friars who lived and preached among people in towns rather than in secluded monasteries. His love of creation, expressed in his Canticle of the Sun, made him a patron saint of ecology.

facts.title: The Ever-Normal Granary
facts.body: Chinese states kept public granaries that bought grain when harvests were good and prices low, and sold it when harvests failed and prices rose. The 'ever-normal granary' was established under the Han dynasty and revived by many later dynasties. The idea of using buffer stocks to stabilise prices influenced US farm policy in the 1930s.

facts.title: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation
facts.body: Founded in Shanghai in 2001 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, the organisation grew out of earlier border agreements between China and its post-Soviet neighbours. It focuses on regional security, against what its members call terrorism, separatism and extremism, as well as economic cooperation. India and Pakistan joined in 2017.

facts.title: Corals spawn together by moonlight
facts.body: On the Great Barrier Reef, many coral species release their eggs and sperm on the same few nights after a full moon. Cued by water temperature, the Moon and sunset, the reef fills with drifting pink bundles like an underwater snowstorm.

facts.title: Swahili
facts.body: Swahili developed on the East African coast as the Bantu language of trading towns in contact with Arabia, Persia and India, and it absorbed many Arabic words; its name comes from Arabic sawahil, 'coasts'. It was long written in Arabic script before the Latin alphabet took over in the colonial era. It spread inland as a lingua franca of East Africa and became a symbol of national unity in Tanzania after independence.

facts.title: The Transformer in Artificial Intelligence
facts.body: In 2017 researchers at Google described the Transformer, a neural-network design built around a mechanism called attention, in a paper titled Attention Is All You Need. It processes whole sequences in parallel and learns which parts relate to each other. The Transformer became the basis of the large language models that brought generative AI to the public in the 2020s.

facts.title: The Kamakura Shogunate
facts.body: In 1192 Minamoto no Yoritomo took the title of shogun, and his military government at Kamakura held real power in Japan while the emperor's court remained in Kyoto. This began nearly seven centuries of rule by warriors under a shogun. The Kamakura regime repelled Mongol invasions in 1274 and 1281 before falling in 1333.

facts.title: Time runs faster at your head
facts.body: Gravity slows time slightly, so clocks closer to the ground tick more slowly. In 2010 American scientists used atomic clocks to detect the difference over a height change of just 33 centimetres.

facts.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
facts.body: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all the same phenomenon, electromagnetic radiation, differing only in wavelength. Visible light is a narrow band in the middle. William Herschel discovered infrared in 1800 when a thermometer warmed beyond the red end of a spectrum, and Johann Ritter found ultraviolet the following year.

facts.title: The Pacific Ocean
facts.body: The Pacific is the largest and deepest of the oceans, covering about a third of the Earth's surface, more than all the land put together. Ferdinand Magellan named it 'peaceful' after the calm waters he met on entering it in 1520. Its rim is lined by the volcanoes and earthquake zones of the Ring of Fire.

facts.title: Parasite
facts.body: Bong Joon-ho's South Korean film of 2019 follows a poor family who scheme their way into working for a wealthy household, with violent results. A dark comedy about class inequality, it won the Palme d'Or at Cannes. In 2020 it became the first film not in English to win the Academy Award for Best Picture.

facts.title: Venice stands on a forest of wooden posts
facts.body: Much of Venice rests on millions of timber piles driven into the lagoon mud down to firmer clay. Kept waterlogged and away from oxygen, the wood has decayed only very slowly over centuries.

facts.title: The Tango
facts.body: The tango arose in the late 19th century in Buenos Aires and Montevideo, among immigrants and the urban working class of the Río de la Plata. The bandoneón, a German-made concertina, gave it its sound. Carlos Gardel made the sung tango famous, and Astor Piazzolla later brought jazz and classical elements into his nuevo tango.

facts.title: Anatta, the Doctrine of No-Self
facts.body: One of Buddhism's most distinctive teachings is anatta, or 'no-self': there is no permanent, unchanging soul. A person is instead a shifting combination of five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness. This sets Buddhism apart from Hindu teachings of an eternal atman, and clinging to the illusion of a fixed self is seen as a root of suffering.

facts.title: Dead Capital
facts.body: In The Mystery of Capital (2000), the Peruvian economist Hernando de Soto argued that the poor in developing countries hold large assets, such as houses and land, that they cannot use as collateral because they lack formal legal title. He called these assets 'dead capital'. His work inspired land-titling programmes in many countries, though later research found that formal titles alone often did less than expected to unlock credit.

facts.title: Most words for tea come from two sources
facts.body: Languages that got tea overland, such as Hindi, Russian and Turkish, use a word like chai, from Mandarin cha. Those that got it by sea through Dutch traders, such as English and French, use tea, from the Min Chinese te.

facts.title: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission
facts.body: Set up in 1995 and chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, the commission heard testimony from victims and perpetrators of human rights violations under apartheid. Perpetrators who fully disclosed politically motivated crimes could be granted amnesty. It became an influential, and much debated, model of transitional justice for other countries emerging from conflict or dictatorship.

facts.title: The Uralic Languages
facts.body: Finnish, Estonian and Hungarian are not Indo-European but belong to the Uralic family, named after the Ural Mountains, near which it probably originated. The family also includes the Sámi languages of northern Scandinavia and many smaller languages of Russia. Uralic languages typically add chains of suffixes to words, and many have large case systems and vowel harmony.

facts.title: The Water Wheel
facts.body: Water wheels harnessing flowing water to turn millstones appeared in the Greek world around the 3rd century BC. The Romans used them widely, and at Barbegal in southern France a series of sixteen wheels drove a large flour mill. Through the Middle Ages water power drove mills for grain, cloth and iron, and it powered the first factories of the Industrial Revolution.

facts.title: Your brain is an energy guzzler
facts.body: The brain makes up about 2 per cent of an adult's body weight but uses around a fifth of its energy at rest. Most of it goes on keeping neurons ready to fire by pumping charged particles across their membranes.

facts.title: The Gupta Empire
facts.body: The Gupta Empire ruled much of northern India from the early 4th to the 6th century AD. Its era is often called a classical age of Indian culture, with achievements in Sanskrit literature, art and mathematics, including the work of the astronomer Aryabhata. Hunnic invasions weakened it from the late 5th century.

facts.title: Blood Groups
facts.body: In 1901 the Austrian scientist Karl Landsteiner showed that human blood falls into distinct groups, the basis of the ABO system, and that mixing incompatible groups makes red cells clump. This explained why many early blood transfusions had been fatal. Blood typing made transfusion safe, and Landsteiner received the Nobel Prize in 1930.

facts.title: The Caspian Sea
facts.body: The Caspian is the largest enclosed inland body of water on Earth, bordered by Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan. Its surface lies below sea level, and its water is mildly salty. Whether it counts legally as a sea or a lake has long been disputed, because the answer affects how its oil, gas and fisheries are divided.

facts.title: Why chopping onions makes you cry
facts.body: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and starts reactions that release a sulfur compound gas. When the gas reaches your eyes it irritates them, and tear glands respond to wash it away.

facts.title: Olmec Colossal Heads
facts.body: The Olmec, the earliest major civilisation of Mesoamerica, carved massive stone heads on the Gulf Coast of Mexico from around 1200 BC. Some are about three metres tall and weigh many tonnes. Each has individual features and headgear, and they are widely thought to portray rulers. They are among the earliest monumental sculptures of the Americas.

facts.title: Indian Film Song
facts.body: Since the arrival of sound film in India in 1931, songs have been central to Indian cinema. Playback singers such as Lata Mangeshkar, Mohammed Rafi and Kishore Kumar recorded songs mimed by actors on screen. Film song became the main popular music of South Asia, blending Indian classical and folk elements with Western instruments.

facts.title: The Quran
facts.body: Muslims believe the Quran is the word of God, revealed to Muhammad through the angel Gabriel over about 23 years. It consists of 114 chapters, or suras, in Arabic, and its standard written text was compiled under the third caliph, Uthman. Recited in prayer and memorised by many believers, it is the supreme source of Islamic law and theology and the model of classical Arabic.

facts.title: Japanese families throw beans to chase away demons
facts.body: At Setsubun in early February, people throw roasted soya beans while shouting 'Demons out, luck in!'. Many also eat one bean for each year of their age for good health.

facts.title: Conspicuous Consumption
facts.body: In The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899), the American economist Thorstein Veblen argued that the wealthy buy expensive goods largely to display their status. For such goods a higher price can make them more desirable, not less. The phrase 'conspicuous consumption' and the idea of 'Veblen goods' entered both economics and everyday language.

facts.title: The Communist Manifesto
facts.body: Written by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels and published in London in February 1848, it opens its argument with the claim that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. It predicted that the proletariat would overthrow the bourgeoisie and abolish private property, and ended with the call for workers of all countries to unite.

facts.title: The Armenian Alphabet
facts.body: Around AD 405 the monk Mesrop Mashtots created an alphabet for Armenian, which had previously been written, if at all, in foreign scripts. Its first major use was a translation of the Bible, and a rich literature followed, including translations of Greek works that are now lost in the original. The alphabet has been used for Armenian ever since, and Mashtots is venerated as a saint by the Armenian Church.

facts.title: Cashews are never sold in their shells
facts.body: The cashew shell contains a caustic oil related to the irritant in poison ivy. The nuts are roasted or steamed and shelled before sale, which is why you never see them in their shells in shops.

facts.title: Medical Drone Delivery in Rwanda
facts.body: In 2016 Rwanda began delivering blood for transfusions to rural hospitals by drone, in partnership with the American company Zipline. Small fixed-wing aircraft launched from a central base drop packages by parachute, cutting delivery times from hours by road to minutes. It was widely hailed as the world's first national drone delivery service, and the model was later extended to other medical supplies and countries.

facts.title: The Safavid Empire
facts.body: In 1501 Ismail I founded the Safavid dynasty in Iran and made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, a lasting choice that made Iran the heartland of Shia Islam. The Safavids were long-time rivals of the Sunni Ottomans. Shah Abbas I made Isfahan his capital and one of the finest cities of the Islamic world.

facts.title: Al-Razi on Smallpox and Measles
facts.body: The Persian physician Abu Bakr al-Razi, known in Europe as Rhazes, worked in Rayy and Baghdad around 900. His treatise on smallpox and measles was the first to distinguish clearly between the two diseases by their symptoms. He also compiled a vast medical encyclopaedia and valued clinical observation over reliance on authority.

facts.title: Owls cannot move their eyes
facts.body: An owl's eyes are tube-shaped and fixed in their sockets, so it cannot roll them. Instead it can turn its head about 270 degrees, helped by extra neck vertebrae and blood vessels arranged so that circulation is not cut off.

facts.title: The Sahel
facts.body: The Sahel is a semi-arid belt of grassland and scrub stretching across Africa from the Atlantic to the Red Sea, between the Sahara to the north and the wetter savanna to the south. Its name comes from the Arabic for 'shore', as in the edge of the desert. Its rainfall varies greatly from year to year, and severe droughts in the 1970s and 1980s caused devastating famines.

facts.title: One Thousand and One Nights
facts.body: This collection of tales in Arabic grew over centuries from Persian, Indian and Arab sources. In its frame story, Scheherazade saves her life by telling the king a new story each night and breaking off at the most exciting point. Famous tales such as Aladdin and Ali Baba were added only in the early 18th century by the French translator Antoine Galland.

facts.title: The Angklung
facts.body: The angklung is a bamboo instrument from West Java made of tubes in a frame that sound a single pitch when shaken. Since each player usually holds one or two notes, a melody can only be played by a group working together. In the 20th century it was adapted to Western scales and widely used in Indonesian schools.

facts.title: A nine-year-old named the googol
facts.body: The word googol, meaning 1 followed by 100 zeros, was coined by Milton Sirotta, the young nephew of American mathematician Edward Kasner. Kasner popularised it in a 1940 book.

facts.title: The Desert Fathers
facts.body: Christian monasticism began in the deserts of Egypt in the late 3rd and 4th centuries. Anthony the Great withdrew into solitude and became a model for hermits, while Pachomius organised the first communities of monks living together under a common rule. The sayings and ascetic practices of these Desert Fathers spread across the Christian world and inspired monastic life in both East and West.

facts.title: The Indian Ocean Trade
facts.body: Long before European ships arrived, the Indian Ocean hosted one of the world's great maritime trading systems. Using the seasonal reversal of the monsoon winds, Arab, Persian, Indian, Malay, Chinese and Swahili merchants exchanged textiles, spices, gold, ivory, porcelain and horses between East Africa, Arabia, India and China. Ports such as Calicut, Malacca, Kilwa and Aden thrived on this largely decentralised commerce.

facts.title: The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty
facts.body: Opened for signature in 1968 and in force from 1970, the treaty recognises as nuclear-weapon states the five that had tested a weapon before 1967, and commits other parties not to acquire them. In return, the nuclear states undertake to pursue disarmament, and all parties may use nuclear energy peacefully under safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency.

facts.title: English weekdays honour Norse and Germanic gods
facts.body: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday are named after Tiw, Woden, Thor and Frigg. They replaced Roman gods: French still has mardi for Mars and mercredi for Mercury.

facts.title: A Language Is a Dialect with an Army
facts.body: The line between a language and a dialect is often political rather than linguistic. The Yiddish scholar Max Weinreich popularised the quip that 'a language is a dialect with an army and navy' in the 1940s. Danish, Norwegian and Swedish are largely mutually intelligible yet count as separate languages, while some Chinese varieties called dialects are not mutually intelligible at all.

facts.title: The Iron Pillar of Delhi
facts.body: The Iron Pillar, now in the Qutb complex in Delhi, was made around AD 400 under the Gupta dynasty and is about 7 metres long, with over a metre of it below ground. Forged from wrought iron, it has resisted rusting for some 1,600 years. Studies attribute this to a thin protective layer encouraged by the iron's high phosphorus content. It shows the advanced skill of ancient Indian metalworkers.

facts.title: The Vietnam War
facts.body: After the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, Vietnam was divided into a communist north and a non-communist south. From the 1960s the United States sent large numbers of troops to support the South, but withdrew after the 1973 Paris accords. Northern forces took Saigon in 1975, reunifying the country under communist rule.

facts.title: Pen caps have a hole for safety
facts.body: The small hole in the top of many pen caps lets air through if a child accidentally swallows one. It was added to reduce the risk of choking.

facts.title: Malaria and the Mosquito
facts.body: In 1880 the French army doctor Alphonse Laveran, working in Algeria, saw the malaria parasite in a patient's blood. In 1897 Ronald Ross, a British doctor in India, found the parasite in Anopheles mosquitoes that had fed on a malaria patient, and went on to show that mosquitoes transmit the disease. Ross received the Nobel Prize in 1902 and Laveran in 1907, and mosquito control became central to fighting malaria.

facts.title: The Indus River
facts.body: The Indus rises in Tibet and flows through Ladakh and the length of Pakistan to the Arabian Sea. Its valley was home to the Bronze Age Indus Valley Civilisation, with planned cities such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro. The river gave its name, through Persian and Greek, to India and to Hinduism.

facts.title: The Ajanta Caves
facts.body: The Ajanta Caves in western India are about 30 Buddhist monasteries and halls cut into a cliff, made in two phases from around the 2nd century BC to the 5th century AD. Their wall paintings of the Buddha's past lives and of court life are the finest surviving examples of ancient Indian painting. Abandoned for centuries, they were rediscovered by a British officer in 1819.

facts.title: Butterflies taste with their feet
facts.body: Butterflies have taste sensors on their feet that work on contact. A female lands on a leaf and 'tastes' it to check whether it will feed her caterpillars before she lays her eggs.

facts.title: Romanticism in Music
facts.body: Romantic music, roughly spanning the 19th century, put emotion, individual expression, nature and national identity at its centre. Orchestras grew, harmony became more chromatic and programme music told stories, as in Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique of 1830. Composers came to be seen as inspired artists rather than craftsmen in service.

facts.title: Wittgenstein's Language Games
facts.body: Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889–1951), an Austrian-born philosopher who worked at Cambridge, wrote two influential and opposing works. The Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921) held that language pictures facts and ends: 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.' The posthumous Philosophical Investigations (1953) argued instead that the meaning of a word lies in its use within 'language games'.

facts.title: Purchasing Power Parity
facts.body: Purchasing power parity holds that, over the long run, exchange rates should adjust so that the same basket of goods costs the same in different countries. The Swedish economist Gustav Cassel developed the modern version around the time of the First World War. Economists use PPP exchange rates to compare living standards across countries, since market exchange rates tend to understate incomes in poorer countries.

facts.title: Mauna Kea beats Everest from base to top
facts.body: Measured from its base on the ocean floor, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is about 10,000 metres tall, more than Everest's height above sea level. Most of it lies hidden beneath the Pacific.

facts.title: The Gana-Sanghas of Ancient India
facts.body: Around the time of the Buddha, northern India contained not only kingdoms but also gana-sanghas, states governed by assemblies of a ruling clan, such as the Vajji confederacy centred on Vaishali and the Shakyas. Buddhist texts describe their assemblies meeting to debate and decide matters. They are sometimes called early republics, though power lay with a warrior aristocracy, and most were absorbed by expanding kingdoms such as Magadha.

facts.title: Sanskrit
facts.body: Sanskrit, the classical language of ancient India, is an Indo-European language whose oldest form appears in the Rigveda, composed perhaps around 1500–1200 BC and long transmitted orally. Its classical form became the language of Hindu scripture, philosophy, science and court poetry, and was also used by Buddhists and Jains. For over a thousand years it served as a prestige language of learning and kingship across South and Southeast Asia.

facts.title: The Jet Engine
facts.body: The jet engine was developed independently in the 1930s by Frank Whittle in Britain and Hans von Ohain in Germany. In 1939 the German Heinkel He 178 made the first jet-powered flight. Jet engines allowed aircraft to fly much faster and higher, and from the 1950s jet airliners made long-distance air travel routine.

facts.title: Isaac Newton chased forgers for the Royal Mint
facts.body: Later in life Isaac Newton became Warden, then Master, of the Royal Mint. He threw himself into the job, gathering evidence against counterfeiters and helping prosecute them.

facts.title: The First Fleet
facts.body: In January 1788 eleven British ships carrying convicts, marines and officials arrived in Australia under Captain Arthur Phillip, founding a penal colony at Sydney Cove. The colony began British settlement of the continent, with devastating consequences for Aboriginal peoples through disease, violence and loss of land.

facts.title: The Maya Venus Table
facts.body: The Dresden Codex, one of the few Maya books to survive the Spanish conquest, contains tables tracking the planet Venus. The Maya knew that Venus returns to the same position relative to the Sun about every 584 days, and that five such cycles equal almost exactly eight years. The tables show the precision of Maya astronomy and its close link to their calendar and ritual.

facts.title: The Prime Meridian
facts.body: The Prime Meridian is the line of 0 degrees longitude from which east and west are measured. At the International Meridian Conference in Washington in 1884, most nations agreed to place it through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich in London. It also became the basis of Greenwich Mean Time, the reference for the world's time zones.

facts.title: Vermeer's pearl-earring girl is not a portrait
facts.body: Vermeer's famous painting is a tronie, a Dutch study of a face, expression or costume rather than a picture of a particular person. Nobody knows who modelled for it.

facts.title: Behzad and Persian Miniature Painting
facts.body: Kamal ud-Din Behzad, active in Herat in the late 15th century, was the most celebrated master of Persian miniature painting. His manuscript illustrations for the court of the Timurid ruler Sultan Husayn Bayqara brought new liveliness and naturalism to crowded scenes. He later worked for the Safavid shahs, and his style shaped both Persian and Mughal painting.

facts.title: Congolese Rumba
facts.body: Congolese rumba developed in Léopoldville (Kinshasa) and Brazzaville from the 1940s, inspired by Cuban son records heard on radio. Built on interlocking electric guitars, it was led by figures such as Franco and Grand Kallé, whose 'Indépendance Cha Cha' greeted Congolese independence in 1960. It became hugely popular across much of Africa.

facts.title: The Bhakti Movement
facts.body: Bhakti, loving devotion to a personal god, grew into a powerful movement in Hinduism, beginning with Tamil poet-saints in southern India between roughly the 6th and 9th centuries and later spreading north. Its poets, such as Kabir and Mirabai, often wrote in local languages rather than Sanskrit and challenged caste barriers and priestly ritual. Bhakti remains central to popular Hindu worship.

facts.title: Mushrooms make vitamin D in sunlight
facts.body: Like our skin, mushrooms produce vitamin D when exposed to ultraviolet light. They contain ergosterol, which sunlight converts into vitamin D2, so mushrooms left gills up in the sun gain much more of it.

facts.title: The Price Revolution
facts.body: Between the late 15th and the early 17th centuries, prices in Western Europe rose several-fold after a long period of relative stability. Contemporaries such as Jean Bodin blamed the influx of American silver and gold; later historians have added population growth and coin debasement as causes. The episode is a key test case for the quantity theory of money.

facts.title: Nationalism
facts.body: Nationalism holds that the nation, a people bound by shared culture, language or history, should govern itself in its own state. It spread with the American and French Revolutions, reshaped 19th-century Europe and later powered anti-colonial movements in Asia and Africa. Scholars such as Benedict Anderson, who called nations 'imagined communities', see them as largely modern, though others stress older roots.

facts.title: Basque, a Language Isolate
facts.body: Basque, spoken in the western Pyrenees of Spain and France, is a language isolate: it has no demonstrated relationship with any other living language. It was spoken in the region before the Indo-European languages arrived and survived Roman rule and centuries of pressure from Latin, Spanish and French. Its grammar is ergative, marking the subject of a transitive verb differently from the subject of an intransitive one.

facts.title: Why cut apples turn brown
facts.body: When an apple is cut, an enzyme in its cells meets oxygen in the air and turns natural compounds into brown pigments. Lemon juice slows this because its acid hinders the enzyme.

facts.title: The Earliest Pottery
facts.body: The oldest known pottery vessels, from Xianrendong Cave in southern China, are roughly 20,000 years old. They were made by hunter-gatherers, long before farming, overturning the idea that pottery began with agriculture. Fired clay pots allowed food to be boiled and stored, and pottery later became one of archaeology's main tools for dating sites.

facts.title: The Dissolution of the Soviet Union
facts.body: Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms of the late 1980s, glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring), loosened control over the Soviet system. A failed hardline coup in August 1991 accelerated the republics' moves to independence. On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned, and the Soviet Union was replaced by fifteen independent states.

facts.title: Radioactivity and the Curies
facts.body: In 1896 Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts give off penetrating radiation without any outside source of energy. Marie and Pierre Curie then discovered two new radioactive elements, polonium and radium, and Marie Curie coined the word radioactivity. She was the first person to receive two Nobel Prizes, in physics in 1903 and in chemistry in 1911.

facts.title: Earth's farthest-out peak is not Everest
facts.body: The summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is the point on Earth farthest from its centre. The planet bulges at the equator, so this Andean volcano sticks out further than Everest.

facts.title: The Grand Canal of China
facts.body: The Grand Canal links the Yangtze and Yellow rivers and runs north as far as Beijing. Earlier sections were joined into a single system under the Sui dynasty around 600 AD and extended under later dynasties. For more than a thousand years it carried grain from the fertile south to feed the northern capitals.

facts.title: Las Meninas
facts.body: Diego Velázquez, court painter to Philip IV of Spain, painted Las Meninas in 1656. The young Infanta Margarita stands among her attendants, while the painter himself appears at his easel and the king and queen are glimpsed in a mirror. Its puzzling play of gazes and viewpoints has made it one of the most analysed paintings in Western art.

facts.title: Schubert and the Lied
facts.body: Franz Schubert (1797–1828) wrote more than 600 songs for voice and piano before dying at 31. In works such as Erlkönig and the cycle Winterreise, the piano is an equal partner that depicts scenes and moods. He made the German art song, the Lied, a major genre of the Romantic era.

facts.title: You play the theremin without touching it
facts.body: The theremin, invented by the Russian Léon Theremin around 1920, has two antennas. Moving one hand near each changes the pitch and volume, so the player never touches the instrument.

facts.title: Aristotle's Logic and the Syllogism
facts.body: Aristotle created the first formal system of logic. Its core is the syllogism, an argument in which a conclusion follows necessarily from two premises: all humans are mortal; Socrates is a human; therefore Socrates is mortal. His logical works, later grouped as the Organon, or 'instrument', dominated logic until new systems were developed in the 19th century.

facts.title: The CFA Franc
facts.body: The CFA franc was created in 1945 for France's colonies in Africa. After independence most former French colonies in West and Central Africa kept it, in two regional versions pegged first to the French franc and then to the euro, with convertibility guaranteed by the French Treasury. Supporters credited it with low inflation, while critics saw it as a lasting form of French control over African monetary policy.

facts.title: Grotius and the Law of Nations
facts.body: The Dutch jurist Hugo Grotius argued in Mare Liberum (1609) that the seas are open to all nations, and in On the Law of War and Peace (1625) that natural law binds states even in wartime. Writing during the Thirty Years' War, he set out rules on just causes for war and on conduct within it. He is often called a father of international law.

facts.title: Parrotfish help make white sand beaches
facts.body: Parrotfish bite off algae-covered coral with beak-like teeth and grind it up with a second set of teeth in their throats. The coral passes out as fine white sand, and on many tropical reefs they produce a large share of the beach.

facts.title: Cuneiform
facts.body: Cuneiform, meaning 'wedge-shaped', was developed in Sumer around 3200 BC, first for keeping accounts, and was written by pressing a reed stylus into clay. Over three millennia it was adapted for many languages, including Akkadian, Hittite and Old Persian, before dying out around the 1st century AD. Its decipherment in the 19th century relied heavily on Henry Rawlinson's copies of the trilingual Behistun inscription in Iran.

facts.title: Radio
facts.body: In the mid-1890s Guglielmo Marconi developed wireless telegraphy, using the electromagnetic waves predicted by James Clerk Maxwell and demonstrated by Heinrich Hertz. In 1901 he reported receiving a signal across the Atlantic. Others, including Alexander Popov, Oliver Lodge and Nikola Tesla, made important contributions, and priority is still debated. Radio made communication with ships possible and later became a mass medium.

facts.title: The Shang Dynasty
facts.body: Ruling in the Yellow River valley from around 1600 BC to the mid-11th century BC, the Shang is the earliest Chinese dynasty confirmed by both archaeology and written records. Its kings consulted their ancestors by divination on turtle shells and bones, and its craftsmen were masters of bronze casting. The Shang were overthrown by the Zhou.

facts.title: One Mercury day lasts two Mercury years
facts.body: From sunrise to sunrise takes about 176 Earth days on Mercury, while a trip round the Sun takes only 88. Its slow spin and fast orbit combine so the Sun crawls across its sky extremely slowly.

facts.title: The First Heart Transplant
facts.body: On 3 December 1967 the surgeon Christiaan Barnard performed the first human-to-human heart transplant at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town. The patient, Louis Washkansky, died 18 days later of pneumonia, his immune system weakened by drugs given to prevent rejection. Survival improved greatly after immunosuppressant drugs such as ciclosporin came into use in the early 1980s.

facts.title: Iceland
facts.body: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, and also above a volcanic hotspot. As a result it has frequent eruptions, hot springs and geysers, and the word 'geyser' comes from Icelandic. Geothermal energy heats most of its homes, and large ice caps cover its highlands.

facts.title: The Sydney Opera House
facts.body: Designed by the Danish architect Jørn Utzon, who won an international competition in 1957, the Sydney Opera House opened in 1973. Its white roof shells, rising like sails over the harbour, posed engineering problems that took years to solve. Utzon resigned during construction, but the building became a symbol of Australia and a World Heritage Site in 2007.

facts.title: Scots welcome the first visitor of the year
facts.body: At Hogmanay the first person to cross the threshold after midnight, the 'first-foot', sets the year's luck. A tall dark stranger carrying coal, shortbread or salt is traditionally the luckiest.

facts.title: Reggae and Bob Marley
facts.body: Reggae developed in Jamaica in the late 1960s from ska and rocksteady, with accents on the offbeat and a prominent bass line. Its lyrics often carry the spirituality and social criticism of the Rastafari movement. Bob Marley and the Wailers made it a global music in the 1970s.

facts.title: Zhu Xi and Neo-Confucianism
facts.body: Neo-Confucianism revived Confucian thought in Song-dynasty China, partly in answer to Buddhism and Daoism, by adding a metaphysics of li (principle) and qi (vital energy). Its great synthesiser, Zhu Xi (1130–1200), made the Four Books the core of the Confucian canon. His commentaries became the basis of the imperial civil-service examinations from the 14th century until 1905, and his school shaped thought in Korea and Japan.

facts.title: Quantitative Easing
facts.body: Quantitative easing is a policy in which a central bank creates money to buy large quantities of financial assets, usually government bonds, to lower long-term interest rates when short-term rates are already near zero. The Bank of Japan pioneered it in 2001. After the 2008 crisis it was adopted on a large scale by the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of England and later the European Central Bank.

facts.title: The Jaws shark was nicknamed Bruce
facts.body: The film crew named the mechanical shark Bruce after Steven Spielberg's lawyer. It kept breaking down in salt water, so the shark appears less than planned, which made the film more suspenseful.

facts.title: The Mongol Kurultai
facts.body: Among the Mongols and other steppe peoples, a kurultai was a great assembly of princes and chiefs that chose the khan and decided on war. A kurultai proclaimed Temüjin as Genghis Khan in 1206, and after his death new great khans had to be confirmed in the same way. Succession disputes that kurultais failed to settle helped split the Mongol Empire.

facts.title: The Mongolian Script
facts.body: The traditional Mongolian script, written in vertical columns, was adopted under Genghis Khan in the early 13th century from the Old Uyghur alphabet. That alphabet came from the script of the Sogdians, Iranian merchants who were key middlemen of the Silk Road, and ultimately from Aramaic. Mongolia switched to Cyrillic in the 1940s, while the vertical script continued in use in Inner Mongolia in China.

facts.title: The Astrolabe
facts.body: The astrolabe is a hand-held model of the sky used to tell the time, measure the altitude of stars and solve astronomical problems. Developed by the ancient Greeks, it was greatly refined by astronomers in the medieval Islamic world, who also used it to find prayer times and the direction of Mecca. It reached Europe through Islamic Spain and remained widely used until the 17th century.

facts.title: You have about as many microbes as cells
facts.body: The old claim that bacteria outnumber our own cells ten to one was revised in 2016. A careful count found the numbers are roughly equal, at a few tens of trillions each.

facts.title: The Mexican Revolution
facts.body: Beginning in 1910 as a revolt against the long rule of Porfirio Díaz, the Mexican Revolution became a decade of civil war with leaders such as Francisco Madero, Pancho Villa and Emiliano Zapata. Its Constitution of 1917 promised land reform and workers' rights, and the revolution shaped Mexico for the rest of the century.

facts.title: The Discovery of Ice Ages
facts.body: In 1837 the Swiss-born naturalist Louis Agassiz argued that great ice sheets had once covered much of northern Europe, and later North America. Scratched bedrock, U-shaped valleys and boulders far from their source were evidence of former glaciers. In the 20th century Milutin Milanković linked the repeated advance and retreat of the ice to cyclical changes in the Earth's orbit and tilt.

facts.title: Latitude and Longitude
facts.body: Latitude measures how far a place is north or south of the equator, from 0 to 90 degrees; longitude measures how far it is east or west of the Prime Meridian, from 0 to 180 degrees. Together they give every point on Earth a unique address. Latitude could be found from the Sun or stars, but longitude at sea required accurate timekeeping, a problem solved only by marine chronometers in the 18th century.

facts.title: A custard that turns solid when punched
facts.body: A mix of cornflour and water flows like a liquid when stirred gently but becomes hard when hit or squeezed suddenly. The starch grains cannot slide past each other fast enough and jam together.

facts.title: Angkor Wat
facts.body: Angkor Wat was built in the early 12th century under the Khmer king Suryavarman II as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu, and later became a Buddhist site. Its five towers represent Mount Meru, the home of the gods, and its galleries hold long reliefs of Hindu epics. The masterpiece of Khmer architecture, it appears on the national flag of Cambodia.

facts.title: Ars Nova and Machaut
facts.body: Ars nova, 'new art', names the French music of the 14th century, after a treatise associated with Philippe de Vitry that introduced more flexible rhythmic notation. Its leading figure, the poet-composer Guillaume de Machaut, wrote the Messe de Nostre Dame, the earliest complete polyphonic setting of the Mass Ordinary by a single known composer.

facts.title: Zoroastrianism
facts.body: Zoroastrianism, founded by the Iranian prophet Zarathustra (Zoroaster), whose dates are much debated, teaches a cosmic struggle between Ahura Mazda, the wise creator, and the destructive spirit Angra Mainyu. Humans must choose the good through good thoughts, good words and good deeds. It was the state religion of Sasanian Persia until the Islamic conquest, and many scholars think its ideas of final judgement, heaven and hell influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

facts.title: There was no year zero
facts.body: In the usual Western count, 1 BC is followed directly by AD 1. The system was devised in the 6th century, before the idea of zero had reached Europe.

facts.title: Oikonomia and Chrematistics
facts.body: The word 'economics' comes from the Greek oikonomia, the management of a household. Aristotle distinguished this natural art of providing for needs from chrematistics, the pursuit of money-making for its own sake, which he regarded as limitless and suspect. He also condemned lending at interest as making money breed money, an argument that shaped medieval Christian thinking on usury.

facts.title: The Responsibility to Protect
facts.body: Endorsed by world leaders at the UN World Summit in 2005, the Responsibility to Protect holds that every state must protect its population from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity. If a state manifestly fails to do so, the international community should act, using force only through the Security Council. It was a response to the failures in Rwanda and Srebrenica.

facts.title: Grice's Maxims of Conversation
facts.body: The philosopher Paul Grice argued, in lectures from the late 1960s, that conversation rests on a cooperative principle: speakers are expected to be informative, truthful, relevant and clear. When a speaker seems to break one of these maxims, listeners infer an unstated meaning, which Grice called an implicature. A reference letter praising only a candidate's handwriting, for example, implies a weak candidate.

facts.title: Monopoly began as a warning against monopolies
facts.body: Monopoly grew out of The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 by Lizzie Magie. She designed it to show how landlords grow rich while tenants grow poor.

facts.title: The Voltaic Pile
facts.body: In 1800 the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by brine-soaked cloth and produced a steady electric current. This first battery made continuous electricity available for experiments for the first time. It quickly led to electrolysis and the discovery of new elements, and the volt, the unit of electric potential, is named after him.

facts.title: Alexander the Great
facts.body: Alexander became king of Macedon in 336 BC and within about a decade conquered the Persian Empire, campaigning from Egypt to the Indus. He died in Babylon in 323 BC, aged 32, and his generals divided his empire. His conquests spread Greek culture across the Near East, opening the Hellenistic period.

facts.title: Endosymbiotic Theory
facts.body: In 1967 the American biologist Lynn Margulis argued that mitochondria and chloroplasts, the energy-producing structures in complex cells, descend from free-living bacteria engulfed by other cells long ago. Both have their own DNA and double membranes, like bacteria. At first widely rejected, the theory came to be accepted as a key step in the evolution of complex life.

facts.title: Naked mole-rats live remarkably long lives
facts.body: Naked mole-rats, from the dry lands of East Africa, are about the size of a mouse yet can live for more than 30 years and rarely develop cancer. They live underground in colonies with a single breeding queen, like bees.

facts.title: The Megalopolis
facts.body: In 1961 the French geographer Jean Gottmann used the term megalopolis for the almost continuous chain of cities on the north-east coast of the United States, from Boston to Washington. He argued that this urban region worked as a single interconnected system. The idea has since been applied to other city regions, such as the Tokyo–Osaka corridor in Japan.

facts.title: Migrant Mother
facts.body: Dorothea Lange took this photograph in California in 1936 while documenting rural poverty during the Great Depression for a US government agency. It shows a careworn mother, later identified as Florence Owens Thompson, with her children leaning on her. It became the defining image of the Depression and a landmark of documentary photography.

facts.title: The Didgeridoo
facts.body: The didgeridoo is a wind instrument of Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia, made from a branch hollowed out by termites. Players use circular breathing to sustain a continuous drone, shaping it with the voice, lips and tongue. Known among the Yolŋu as the yidaki, it accompanies song and ceremony.

facts.title: Tin can crumble in the cold
facts.body: Below about 13 degrees Celsius, shiny metallic tin can slowly turn into a crumbly grey powder called tin pest. The atoms rearrange into a different, less dense crystal structure that falls apart.

facts.title: Spinoza's God or Nature
facts.body: Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a Dutch philosopher of Portuguese-Jewish descent, was expelled from Amsterdam's Jewish community in 1656 for his views. In his Ethics, set out like a geometry textbook, he argued that there is only one substance, 'God or Nature', of which mind and matter are two aspects. His denial of a personal God and his defence of freedom of thought made him a key figure of the radical Enlightenment.

facts.title: The Maghribi Traders
facts.body: The Maghribi traders were Jewish merchants based in North Africa, notably in Tunisia and Fustat (Old Cairo), who traded across the Mediterranean in the 11th century. Their letters and accounts survive in the Cairo Geniza, a synagogue storeroom where documents were kept rather than destroyed. The economist Avner Greif argued that they kept overseas agents honest through a coalition in which cheats were collectively shunned, a classic study of how trade can work without courts, though other historians have challenged his interpretation.

facts.title: Weber's Three Types of Authority
facts.body: The German sociologist Max Weber distinguished three sources of legitimate rule: traditional authority based on custom, charismatic authority based on a leader's extraordinary qualities, and legal-rational authority based on impersonal rules and bureaucracy. In 'Politics as a Vocation' (1919) he defined the state as a community that claims a monopoly on the legitimate use of physical force within a territory.

facts.title: Australia once fought a war against emus
facts.body: In 1932 soldiers with machine guns were sent to Western Australia to cull emus damaging wheat crops. The fast, scattering birds proved so hard to hit that the 'Great Emu War' is remembered as a failure.

facts.title: Hangul
facts.body: Hangul, the Korean alphabet, was created at the court of King Sejong and promulgated in 1446 in a text called Hunminjeongeum, 'the correct sounds for instructing the people'. Until then Koreans wrote in Classical Chinese, which few could master. Its consonant shapes were designed to depict the speech organs, and its letters are grouped into syllable blocks; South Korea celebrates its creation each October on Hangul Day.

facts.title: Optical Fibre Communication
facts.body: In 1966 Charles Kao, working in England, showed that glass fibres could carry light signals over long distances if impurities were removed. Low-loss fibres were produced a few years later. Optical cables became the backbone of long-distance telecommunications and the internet, and Kao shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics.

facts.title: The Inca Empire
facts.body: In the 15th century the Inca expanded from Cusco to build the largest state of the pre-Columbian Americas, stretching along the Andes from present-day Ecuador to Chile. They ruled through a great road network and kept records on knotted cords called quipu. Weakened by civil war and disease, the empire fell to Francisco Pizarro's Spaniards from 1532.

facts.title: A lady was once a bread-kneader
facts.body: "Lady" comes from Old English hlǣfdīge, probably meaning "loaf-kneader", and "lord" from hlāfweard, "loaf-guardian". Both words seem to tie the heads of an Anglo-Saxon household to its bread.

facts.title: The Sushruta Samhita
facts.body: This Sanskrit treatise on medicine and surgery is attributed to Sushruta; its date is uncertain, but its core is usually placed in the first millennium BC.
