It describes a wide range of surgical instruments and operations, including cataract surgery and the rebuilding of a nose with the patient's own skin. It is a founding text of Indian medicine and of plastic surgery.

facts.title: Uluru
facts.body: Uluru is a great sandstone monolith in the desert of central Australia, famous for glowing red at sunrise and sunset. It is sacred to the Anangu, its Aboriginal traditional owners, to whom ownership was formally returned in 1985. Long known to outsiders as Ayers Rock, it is now generally called by its Aboriginal name, and climbing it was banned in 2019.

facts.title: Matsuo Bashō
facts.body: Matsuo Bashō, a 17th-century Japanese poet, raised the short verse form later called haiku to great art. His famous poem about a frog jumping into an old pond captures a single moment with striking simplicity. His travel journal The Narrow Road to the Deep North, which mixes prose and verse, is a classic of Japanese literature.

facts.title: Coffee flowers give bees a caffeine buzz
facts.body: Coffee and citrus flowers lace their nectar with small amounts of caffeine. A 2013 study found bees that drank it remembered the flower's scent much better, so they were more likely to return and pollinate it.

facts.title: Cristofori's Piano
facts.body: Around 1700, Bartolomeo Cristofori, instrument keeper to the Medici in Florence, built a keyboard whose strings were struck by hammers instead of plucked. It could play soft or loud according to touch, hence its name, gravicembalo col piano e forte. The piano went on to become the central instrument of Western music from the late 18th century.

facts.title: Zhuangzi's Butterfly Dream
facts.body: The Daoist book Zhuangzi, named after a thinker of the 4th century BC, is famous for its playful stories. In one, Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly and on waking cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamt of being a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming of being a man. The tale expresses Daoist doubt about fixed distinctions and celebrates the constant transformation of things.

facts.title: Externalities
facts.body: An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on people outside a transaction, such as pollution from a factory or the wider protection given by vaccination. Because buyers and sellers do not take it into account, markets produce too much of goods with harmful externalities and too little of those with beneficial ones. The British economist Arthur Pigou proposed in 1920 taxing harmful activities to correct this, the idea behind modern carbon taxes.

facts.title: Some infinities are bigger than others
facts.body: Georg Cantor showed in the 1870s and 1890s that there are more real numbers than whole numbers, even though both are infinite. No list, however long, can include every decimal number.

facts.title: Marbury v. Madison
facts.body: In this 1803 case the US Supreme Court, under Chief Justice John Marshall, held for the first time that it could strike down an Act of Congress that conflicted with the Constitution. The principle of judicial review became central to American government and has been adopted, in various forms, by constitutional courts around the world.

facts.title: Brahmi and Its Descendant Scripts
facts.body: The Brahmi script is first securely attested in the edicts of the emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BC, and James Prinsep deciphered it in the 1830s. It is an abugida: each consonant carries an inherent vowel, which is changed by added marks. Brahmi is the ancestor of Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil and other Indian scripts, and also of the Tibetan, Thai, Burmese, Khmer and Javanese scripts.

facts.title: Su Song's Astronomical Clock Tower
facts.body: In the late 11th century the Chinese official Su Song built a water-driven astronomical clock tower at Kaifeng, more than 10 metres tall. A waterwheel, advanced in controlled steps by an escapement-like mechanism, drove an armillary sphere, a celestial globe and figures that announced the time. Su Song's detailed illustrated description survives, making it one of the best-documented machines of the medieval world.

facts.title: An island that switches country every six months
facts.body: Pheasant Island in the river Bidasoa is ruled by Spain for half the year and France for the other half. The shared arrangement dates from the 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees, signed on the island.

facts.title: Shaka and the Zulu Kingdom
facts.body: In the 1810s and 1820s Shaka built the Zulu kingdom in south-eastern Africa into a powerful military state, reorganising its army and tactics. In 1879 a Zulu army inflicted a heavy defeat on the British at Isandlwana, before Britain conquered the kingdom later that year.

facts.title: Galileo and Falling Bodies
facts.body: Using balls rolled down inclined planes, Galileo Galilei showed that falling objects accelerate at a steady rate and that, without air resistance, heavy and light bodies fall equally fast. This contradicted Aristotle, whose physics had been taught for some two thousand years. Galileo published his results in Two New Sciences in 1638; the story that he dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa may be a legend.

facts.title: Patagonia
facts.body: Patagonia is the southern end of South America, shared by Argentina and Chile. Its Andean side has great ice fields, glaciers and wet forests, while the plains to the east are dry, windswept steppe in the rain shadow of the mountains. The name dates from Magellan's voyage in 1520, whose crew called the local people Patagones.

facts.title: Fortune cookies are probably Japanese, not Chinese
facts.body: Fortune cookies are almost unknown in China. Researchers have traced them to Japanese crackers made near Kyoto, which Japanese immigrants brought to California in the early 20th century.

facts.title: The Arnolfini Portrait
facts.body: Jan van Eyck painted this double portrait of an Italian merchant and his wife in Bruges in 1434. Its astonishing detail and glowing colour show the possibilities of oil paint, which the early Netherlandish painters perfected. A convex mirror on the back wall reflects two further figures, and the painting's meaning is still debated. It hangs in the National Gallery in London.

facts.title: Prehistoric Bone Flutes
facts.body: Flutes carved from bird bone and mammoth ivory, found in caves in southern Germany, are more than 35,000 years old and are among the oldest known musical instruments. At Jiahu in China, bone flutes about 9,000 years old have been excavated, some still playable. Such finds show that music is one of the oldest human activities.

facts.title: Rawls's Veil of Ignorance
facts.body: In A Theory of Justice (1971), John Rawls asked what principles people would choose for society if they stood behind a 'veil of ignorance', not knowing their own class, talents or position. He argued they would choose equal basic liberties for all and allow inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged. The book revived political philosophy in the English-speaking world.

facts.title: Fairy rings are fungi growing outwards
facts.body: Rings of mushrooms in grass, once blamed on dancing fairies, mark the edge of a fungus spreading out from a central point. As it uses up nutrients in the middle, only the outer edge keeps fruiting, so the ring widens each year.

facts.title: Creative Destruction
facts.body: The Austrian-born economist Joseph Schumpeter popularised the term creative destruction in Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942). He argued that capitalism advances through waves of innovation by entrepreneurs, in which new products, technologies and firms destroy old ones. For Schumpeter this process, rather than price competition, was the essential fact about capitalism.

facts.title: Gandhi's Satyagraha
facts.body: Developed by Mohandas Gandhi in South Africa from 1906 and later in India, satyagraha ('holding firmly to truth') is a method of nonviolent resistance that seeks to convert opponents through self-suffering rather than to coerce them. Its best-known campaign was the Salt March of 1930. It inspired later movements worldwide, including the American civil rights movement.

facts.title: Vietnamese Quốc Ngữ
facts.body: Quốc ngữ, the Latin-based alphabet of Vietnamese, was developed in the 17th century by Portuguese and other Catholic missionaries, and Alexandre de Rhodes's dictionary of 1651 helped fix it. Diacritics mark Vietnamese tones and vowel qualities. Promoted under French rule and then by Vietnamese nationalists as a route to mass literacy, it replaced Classical Chinese and the character-based chữ Nôm in the early 20th century.

facts.title: Hailstones are layered like onions
facts.body: Cut a big hailstone in half and you often see rings. As it is swept through a storm cloud it passes through regions with more or less supercooled water, adding layers of clear and cloudy ice. Repeated up-and-down trips were once thought necessary, but are not.

facts.title: The First Nuclear Reactor
facts.body: On 2 December 1942 a team led by Enrico Fermi achieved the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction, in Chicago Pile-1. Built of graphite blocks and uranium beneath the stands of a university sports field, it was part of the Manhattan Project. Controlled chain reactions later made nuclear power stations possible, starting in the 1950s.

facts.title: The Maratha Empire
facts.body: In the 17th century Shivaji carved out a Maratha kingdom in western India in defiance of the Mughals and was crowned in 1674. After the death of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb in 1707, the Marathas expanded across much of India. Defeat at Panipat in 1761 checked them, and the British overcame them by 1818.

facts.title: Human Origins in Africa
facts.body: Fossil and genetic evidence shows that modern humans, Homo sapiens, evolved in Africa; fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, about 300,000 years old, are among the earliest. Africa was also home to earlier human relatives, such as the 3.2-million-year-old skeleton known as Lucy, found in Ethiopia in 1974. Modern humans later spread from Africa to the rest of the world.

facts.title: Ukrainian Christmas trees wear spider webs
facts.body: Some Ukrainians decorate trees with spider-web ornaments. A folk tale tells of a poor widow's bare tree that spiders covered in webs which turned to silver and gold in the morning light.

facts.title: The Red Sea
facts.body: The Red Sea separates Africa from the Arabian Peninsula. It is a young ocean in the making, formed as the Arabian plate pulls away from Africa, and it is one of the saltiest and warmest seas, with rich coral reefs. Linked to the Mediterranean by the Suez Canal and to the Indian Ocean through the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, it is a vital shipping route.

facts.title: Naguib Mahfouz
facts.body: The Egyptian novelist Naguib Mahfouz was the first writer in Arabic to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1988. His Cairo Trilogy follows a Cairo family through three generations from the First World War to the 1940s. He did much to shape the modern Arabic novel, and his allegorical Children of the Alley led to an attempt on his life in 1994.

facts.title: Polyrhythm
facts.body: Polyrhythm is the simultaneous use of contrasting rhythms, such as three beats against two. It is central to West and Central African drumming, where interlocking parts are often anchored by a repeating bell pattern. Carried to the Americas through the slave trade, it shaped Afro-Cuban music, jazz and much modern popular music.

facts.title: Superglue was rejected for being too sticky
facts.body: Chemist Harry Coover first made the glue in 1942 while trying to make clear plastic gun sights. It stuck to everything, so it was set aside, until he rediscovered it years later and saw its value.

facts.title: Yin and Yang
facts.body: In Chinese thought, yin and yang are complementary forces whose interplay produces all change: yin is associated with darkness, cold, rest and the feminine, yang with light, heat, activity and the masculine. Neither is good or bad, and each contains the seed of the other, as the familiar taijitu symbol shows. The idea underlies traditional Chinese medicine and cosmology and runs through both Daoism and Confucianism.

facts.title: The Dojima Rice Exchange
facts.body: In Osaka, merchants traded rice and rice receipts at the Dojima exchange, which the Tokugawa shogunate officially recognised in 1730. Traders there dealt in standardised contracts for future delivery, settled in cash, so Dojima is often described as the first organised futures market. Rice was central to Japan's economy, since samurai stipends and land taxes were measured in it.

facts.title: The Treaty of Waitangi
facts.body: Signed in 1840 by representatives of the British Crown and many Māori chiefs, the treaty is regarded as New Zealand's founding document. Its English and Māori versions differ significantly, notably on whether the chiefs ceded sovereignty or only a right of governance. Since 1975 the Waitangi Tribunal has investigated breaches of the treaty, leading to settlements with many iwi.

facts.title: Deep-sea vents host life without sunlight
facts.body: In 1977 scientists exploring off the Galápagos found giant tubeworms, clams and crabs around hot springs on the dark sea floor. Their food chain starts with bacteria that draw energy from chemicals in the vent water, not from sunlight.

facts.title: Classical Chinese Across East Asia
facts.body: For many centuries Classical Chinese was the shared written language of East Asia, used by scholars and officials in Korea, Japan and Vietnam much as Latin was used in Europe. Each country read the texts with its own pronunciation, and huge numbers of Chinese-derived words entered Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese. As a result, a large part of the vocabulary of these unrelated languages is of Chinese origin.

facts.title: The First Stone Tools
facts.body: The oldest widely accepted stone tools, known as the Oldowan industry, date from about 2.6 million years ago in East Africa. Early humans struck flakes off stones to make sharp edges for cutting meat and plants, and later Acheulean hand axes were shaped to a deliberate pattern. Toolmaking began more than two million years before our own species appeared.

facts.title: The Emancipation of the Russian Serfs
facts.body: In 1861 Tsar Alexander II abolished serfdom in Russia, freeing over 20 million peasants who had been bound to landowners. Freed serfs had to make redemption payments for their land over decades, and many remained poor. The reform followed Russia's defeat in the Crimean War.

facts.title: Mint feels cold without being cold
facts.body: Menthol in mint triggers the same nerve sensors in your mouth that respond to cold. The brain gets a cold signal even though the temperature has not changed.

facts.title: Rutherford's Nuclear Atom
facts.body: In experiments at Manchester, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at thin gold foil and found that a few bounced almost straight back. In 1911 Ernest Rutherford explained this by proposing that an atom's positive charge and nearly all its mass are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus, with electrons around it. The nuclear model is the basis of all later atomic physics.

facts.title: The Taiga
facts.body: The taiga, or boreal forest, is a belt of mainly coniferous forest across northern Russia, Scandinavia, Canada and Alaska, between the tundra and the temperate zones. It is one of the largest land biomes on Earth, dominated by spruce, pine, fir and larch adapted to long, cold winters. Its trees and soils store vast amounts of carbon.

facts.title: Crime and Punishment
facts.body: Fyodor Dostoevsky's novel of 1866 follows Raskolnikov, a poor former student in St Petersburg who murders an old pawnbroker to prove he stands above ordinary morality. Most of the book traces his psychological torment and his path towards confession. Its moral and psychological depth made it a landmark of the modern novel.

facts.title: The year 1900 was not a leap year
facts.body: Century years are leap years only if divisible by 400, so 2000 was a leap year but 1900 was not. This rule keeps the calendar close to the true solar year of about 365.2422 days.

facts.title: Béla Bartók
facts.body: The Hungarian composer Bartók (1881–1945) collected thousands of folk songs in Hungary, Romania, Slovakia and beyond, often with Zoltán Kodály and a phonograph. He absorbed their rhythms and modes into a modern style in works such as his six string quartets and the Concerto for Orchestra. He was also a pioneer of ethnomusicology.

facts.title: Zeno's Paradoxes
facts.body: Zeno of Elea, a follower of Parmenides in the 5th century BC, devised paradoxes, traditionally read as defending his teacher's view that motion is an illusion. In the most famous, swift Achilles can never overtake a tortoise with a head start, because whenever he reaches where it was, it has moved further on. The paradoxes puzzled thinkers for two millennia; the standard modern answer, though not accepted by everyone, is that an infinite series can have a finite sum.

facts.title: Say's Law
facts.body: Say's law, associated with the French economist Jean-Baptiste Say, is often summarised as 'supply creates its own demand'. The idea is that producing goods generates the income to buy other goods, so a general glut of everything is impossible. Keynes rejected it in the 1930s, arguing that savings can go unspent and leave an economy stuck with too little demand.

facts.title: Leonardo's Last Supper began fading quickly
facts.body: Instead of painting on wet plaster, as in true fresco, Leonardo painted The Last Supper on a dry wall so he could work slowly. The paint did not bond well and started flaking within his lifetime.

facts.title: Fascism
facts.body: Benito Mussolini founded the Fascist movement in Italy in 1919 and came to power after the March on Rome in 1922. Fascism glorified the nation and the leader, rejected both liberal democracy and Marxism, and used violence and mass mobilisation to build a one-party state; Nazi Germany drew on the same model. Scholars still debate how precisely to define it.

facts.title: The Oxford English Dictionary
facts.body: The Oxford English Dictionary began in 1857 when the Philological Society called for a new dictionary recording the history of English words. Under its chief editor James Murray it appeared in instalments from 1884 and was completed in 1928. Built on millions of quotation slips sent in by volunteer readers, it traces each word's meanings in the order of their first recorded use.

facts.title: The Shipping Container
facts.body: In 1956 the American trucking entrepreneur Malcom McLean shipped containers aboard the Ideal X from New Jersey to Texas. Standard steel boxes that move unopened between ships, trains and lorries cut loading times and costs dramatically. Containerisation reshaped ports and greatly accelerated global trade.

facts.title: A single gene decides your earwax type
facts.body: Earwax comes in a wet, sticky type and a dry, flaky type, decided by a single gene. The dry type is most common in East Asia, while the wet type predominates in Europe and Africa.

facts.title: The Armenian Genocide
facts.body: From 1915, during the First World War, the Ottoman government organised the deportation and mass killing of its Armenian population. Around a million or more Armenians died in massacres and death marches into the Syrian desert. Most historians call it genocide, a term Turkey rejects.

facts.title: The Four Fundamental Forces
facts.body: Physics recognises four fundamental forces: gravity, electromagnetism, and the strong and weak nuclear forces. The strong force binds atomic nuclei, the weak force drives some radioactive decay, and electromagnetism governs light and chemistry. Gravity is by far the weakest yet dominates on cosmic scales, while electromagnetism and the weak force were unified in theory in the 1960s and 1970s.

facts.title: The Khyber Pass
facts.body: The Khyber Pass crosses the mountains between Afghanistan and Pakistan. For thousands of years it has been one of the main gateways between Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent, used by traders, pilgrims and invading armies. Its strategic value made it a focus of rivalry in the 19th century.

facts.title: The Moon drifts away at fingernail speed
facts.body: Lasers bounced off mirrors left by Apollo crews show the Moon moving away by about 3.8 centimetres a year. Tides on Earth steal a little of our planet's spin and pass that energy to the Moon, pushing it outwards.

facts.title: Chinese Landscape Painting
facts.body: Landscape painting, called shan shui or 'mountains and water', became the most prestigious genre of Chinese painting from around the 10th century. Song dynasty painters such as Fan Kuan depicted towering mountains in ink, with tiny human figures showing the smallness of people in nature. Rather than recording a single view, such works aimed to capture the spirit of the landscape.

facts.title: The Hurrian Hymn
facts.body: Clay tablets from Ugarit on the Syrian coast, dating from around 1400 BC, record Hurrian hymns together with cuneiform instructions for a lyre player. The best-preserved, a hymn to the goddess Nikkal, is often called the oldest substantially surviving notated melody. Scholars still disagree on how the notation should be read, so modern performances differ widely.

facts.title: The Mind–Body Problem
facts.body: The mind–body problem asks how mental states, such as thoughts and sensations, relate to the physical body and brain. René Descartes's dualism held that mind and matter are different substances, raising the puzzle of how they interact. Materialists hold that the mind is ultimately physical, yet how brain processes give rise to conscious experience, sometimes called the 'hard problem', remains unexplained.

facts.title: A medieval traveller who outdid Marco Polo
facts.body: Ibn Battuta, from Morocco, spent nearly 30 years travelling in the 1300s, reaching West Africa, India and China. His journeys covered far more ground than Marco Polo's, and he dictated them in a famous book, the Rihla.

facts.title: Import Substitution Industrialisation
facts.body: After the Second World War many Latin American countries, influenced by the Argentine economist Raúl Prebisch and the UN Economic Commission for Latin America, tried to industrialise by replacing imports with domestic production behind high tariffs. Prebisch argued that countries exporting raw materials faced worsening terms of trade against manufactured goods. The strategy built industries but often left them inefficient, and it was largely abandoned in the 1980s.

facts.title: South Korea's Candlelight Protests
facts.body: From late 2016 weekly candlelit demonstrations, drawing huge crowds over several months, demanded the removal of President Park Geun-hye over a corruption and influence-peddling scandal. The National Assembly impeached her in December 2016 and the Constitutional Court upheld the decision in March 2017, making her the first South Korean president removed from office through impeachment.

facts.title: The Invention of Writing
facts.body: Writing was invented independently at least three times: in Mesopotamia around 3200 BC, in China by about 1200 BC and in Mesoamerica in the first millennium BC. Egyptian hieroglyphs appeared at about the same time as Mesopotamian cuneiform, and scholars debate whether they arose independently. A key step was the rebus principle, using a sign for its sound rather than its meaning, which let scribes write names and grammatical words.

facts.title: The tuning fork was invented by a trumpeter
facts.body: John Shore, a trumpeter who played for Handel, invented the tuning fork in 1711. He reportedly joked that it was his "pitch-fork".

facts.title: Al-Jazari's Ingenious Devices
facts.body: In 1206 the engineer al-Jazari, working for the Artuqid rulers in south-eastern Anatolia, completed his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices. It describes and illustrates water clocks, automata, water-raising machines and a double-acting pump, with instructions for building them. It is one of the most important engineering texts of the medieval period.

facts.title: The Opium Wars
facts.body: Britain fought two wars against Qing China, in 1839–1842 and 1856–1860, after China tried to stop the opium trade. Defeat forced China to open ports to foreign trade, pay indemnities and cede Hong Kong Island to Britain. In China the wars are seen as the start of a 'century of humiliation'.

facts.title: The Photoelectric Effect
facts.body: When light strikes a metal it can knock out electrons, but whether it does depends on the light's colour, not its brightness. In 1905 Albert Einstein explained this by proposing that light consists of packets of energy, later called photons. The idea helped found quantum theory, and it was for this, not relativity, that Einstein received the Nobel Prize.

facts.title: Crows remember human faces
facts.body: In experiments in Seattle, researchers in masks trapped and released crows. Years later the birds still scolded anyone wearing those masks, and crows that had never been trapped joined in, showing they learn who is dangerous from each other.

facts.title: Al-Idrisi's World Map
facts.body: In 1154 the Arab geographer al-Idrisi completed a great description of the known world for King Roger II of Sicily, with an accompanying world map. It drew on Greek, Arab and travellers' knowledge and, as was common in Islamic maps, placed south at the top. It was one of the most accurate world maps of the Middle Ages.

facts.title: Moby-Dick
facts.body: Herman Melville's novel of 1851 follows Captain Ahab's obsessive hunt for the white whale that took his leg, narrated by a sailor who begins 'Call me Ishmael'. It mixes adventure with detailed whaling lore and philosophical reflection. Poorly received at first, it was rediscovered in the 20th century and is now counted among the great American novels.

facts.title: Frédéric Chopin
facts.body: Chopin (1810–1849) was a Polish composer and pianist who lived in Paris from 1831. He wrote almost exclusively for the piano, in forms such as nocturnes, études, ballades, mazurkas and polonaises, the last two drawing on Polish dances. His lyrical style and use of rubato transformed piano writing.

facts.title: A glass drop that resists a hammer
facts.body: Prince Rupert's drops form when molten glass falls into cold water. Their round head can survive a hammer blow, yet snapping the thin tail makes the whole drop burst into powder, as locked-in stresses are released.

facts.title: Leibniz and the Best of All Possible Worlds
facts.body: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716), who developed calculus independently of Newton, argued that the world is made of simple, mind-like substances he called monads. To reconcile God's goodness with the existence of evil, he claimed that this is the best of all possible worlds, a view Voltaire ridiculed in Candide. He also formulated the principle of sufficient reason: nothing happens without a reason why it is so rather than otherwise.

facts.title: Rent-Seeking
facts.body: Rent-seeking is the pursuit of wealth by capturing a share of existing income, for example by lobbying for subsidies, tariffs or exclusive licences, rather than by creating new value. Gordon Tullock analysed it in 1967 and Anne Krueger gave it its name in 1974. Because the resources spent on rent-seeking produce nothing, economists see it as a hidden cost of monopoly and of some government intervention.

facts.title: The Monroe Doctrine
facts.body: In 1823 US President James Monroe declared that the Americas were closed to further European colonisation and that the United States would regard European intervention in the hemisphere as an unfriendly act. Little enforceable at first, it was later used to justify repeated US intervention in Latin America, notably through the Roosevelt Corollary of 1904.

facts.title: Nepal's flag is not a rectangle
facts.body: Nepal's national flag is made of two stacked pennants, giving it a double-pointed shape. Every other national flag is a rectangle or a square.

facts.title: The Inca Khipu
facts.body: Without a conventional script, the Incas kept records on khipus, cords of cotton or camelid fibre with knots tied in a decimal system. Specialists called khipukamayuq used them for censuses, tribute and accounts, and Spanish officials sometimes accepted their readings as evidence. Whether some khipus also recorded narratives or language, and not only numbers, is still debated.

facts.title: The Steam Locomotive
facts.body: Richard Trevithick ran the first steam locomotive on rails in Wales in 1804. In 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, using locomotives such as George and Robert Stephenson's Rocket, became the first intercity line worked entirely by steam. Railways spread across the world within decades, shrinking travel times and transforming trade.

facts.title: The 1948 Arab–Israeli War
facts.body: On 14 May 1948, as the British Mandate in Palestine ended, Jewish leaders proclaimed the State of Israel, and neighbouring Arab states invaded. Israel survived and ended the war with more territory than the 1947 UN partition plan had allotted. About 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled, an event Palestinians call the Nakba, or 'catastrophe'.

facts.title: India's first talking film started a tradition
facts.body: Alam Ara, released in 1931, was India's first sound film. It included several songs, beginning the tradition of music being central to Indian cinema.

facts.title: The Greenhouse Effect
facts.body: In the 1820s Joseph Fourier suggested that the atmosphere keeps the Earth warmer than it would otherwise be. In 1859 John Tyndall measured how gases such as water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb heat radiation, and in 1896 Svante Arrhenius calculated that adding carbon dioxide would warm the planet. Without the natural greenhouse effect the Earth would be far colder, but its strengthening by human emissions drives climate change.

facts.title: The Rain Shadow
facts.body: When moist wind meets a mountain range, the air rises, cools and drops its rain on the windward side. Having lost its moisture, it descends the far side as dry air, creating a rain shadow. This is why lush forests and deserts can lie only a short distance apart on opposite sides of the same mountains.

facts.title: Spirited Away
facts.body: Hayao Miyazaki's animated film of 2001, made by Studio Ghibli, follows ten-year-old Chihiro, who must work in a bathhouse for spirits to free her parents. It won the Golden Bear at the Berlin Film Festival and the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature. It is widely seen as a masterpiece of hand-drawn animation.

facts.title: A 2,000-year-old seed grew into a tree
facts.body: In 2005 scientists planted a date palm seed found at Masada, the ancient fortress in Israel, and radiocarbon dated to about 2,000 years old. It sprouted, and the palm, nicknamed Methuselah, has grown into a healthy tree.

facts.title: The Hornbostel–Sachs Classification
facts.body: In 1914 Erich von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs proposed classifying instruments by how they produce sound: idiophones (the body itself vibrates), membranophones (a stretched skin), chordophones (strings) and aerophones (air). Electrophones were added later. Because it does not depend on any one culture's categories, it is the standard system used in museums and ethnomusicology.

facts.title: Sunni and Shia Islam
facts.body: Islam's main division began in disputes over who should lead the community after Muhammad's death in 632. Sunnis accepted the caliphs chosen by the community, beginning with Abu Bakr, while the Shia held that leadership belonged to Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law Ali and his descendants, the imams. The killing of Ali's son Husayn at Karbala in 680, mourned by Shia Muslims at Ashura, deepened the split.

facts.title: Hayek and the Knowledge Problem
facts.body: In his 1945 essay 'The Use of Knowledge in Society', Friedrich Hayek argued that the knowledge needed to run an economy is dispersed among millions of people and cannot be gathered by any central planner. Prices act as signals that coordinate their actions without anyone needing to see the whole picture. The argument became central to the case against central planning.

facts.title: Table salt comes from two dangerous elements
facts.body: Sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water, and chlorine is a poisonous gas. Combined, they form sodium chloride, a stable compound we sprinkle on chips.

facts.title: Japan's Pacifist Constitution
facts.body: Drafted under American occupation and taking effect in 1947, Japan's postwar constitution made the emperor a symbol of the state without governing powers. Its Article 9 renounces war as a sovereign right of the nation and the threat or use of force to settle international disputes. How this fits with Japan's Self-Defense Forces has been debated ever since.

facts.title: Dara Shikoh's Persian Upanishads
facts.body: In 1657 the Mughal prince Dara Shikoh, eldest son of Shah Jahan, had some fifty Upanishads translated from Sanskrit into Persian, believing they shared truths with the Quran. The French scholar Anquetil-Duperron translated this Persian version into Latin in the early 1800s. Through it the Upanishads reached European readers such as Schopenhauer, who called them the consolation of his life.

facts.title: AlphaGo
facts.body: In 2016 AlphaGo, a program from the Google-owned company DeepMind, defeated Lee Sedol, one of the world's strongest Go players, by four games to one in Seoul. Go had long been considered far harder for computers than chess because of its enormous number of possible positions. The program combined deep neural networks with search and learned partly by playing against itself.

facts.title: Swedes watch Donald Duck every Christmas Eve
facts.body: Since 1959 Swedish television has shown a Disney cartoon special at 3 pm on Christmas Eve. Watching 'Kalle Anka' with the family has become a beloved ritual.

facts.title: The Indus Valley Civilisation
facts.body: Flourishing from around 2600 to 1900 BC in present-day Pakistan and north-western India, the Indus or Harappan civilisation was one of the earliest urban societies. Cities such as Mohenjo-daro had planned streets and advanced drainage. Its script has never been deciphered.

facts.title: Linnaean Classification
facts.body: The Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus created a system for naming and classifying living things, first set out in Systema Naturae in 1735. He gave every species a two-part Latin name, genus followed by species, as in Homo sapiens. His binomial names, applied systematically to plants in 1753 and to animals in 1758, became the international basis for naming species.

facts.title: The San Andreas Fault
facts.body: The San Andreas Fault runs for more than 1,000 kilometres through California, where the Pacific plate slides north-west past the North American plate. Movement along it caused the earthquake that devastated San Francisco in 1906. It is one of the most closely studied faults in the world because of the risk it poses to major cities.

facts.title: Scrabble scores come from counting newspaper letters
facts.body: Alfred Butts, who invented Scrabble, decided how many tiles each letter should have, and their points, by counting how often letters appeared in newspapers such as The New York Times.

facts.title: The Epic of Gilgamesh
facts.body: The Epic of Gilgamesh, from ancient Mesopotamia, is among the oldest surviving works of literature; its best-known version was written in Akkadian on clay tablets. It follows Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, his friendship with Enkidu and his failed quest for immortality after Enkidu's death. Its flood story closely parallels the account of Noah in the Bible.

facts.title: Saint Yared
facts.body: Yared was a 6th-century Ethiopian musician whom tradition credits with creating the sacred chant, zema, of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. The chant is organised in three modes, ge'ez, ezel and araray, and is written with a system of notation signs. He is venerated as a saint and remains a national cultural figure in Ethiopia.

facts.title: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church
facts.body: Christianity became the religion of the kingdom of Aksum, in present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea, under King Ezana in the 4th century, making it one of the earliest Christian states. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church developed largely apart from the rest of Christendom, keeping its liturgy in the ancient Ge'ez language and a broader biblical canon that includes the Book of Enoch.

facts.title: Some fungi seem to feed on radiation
facts.body: Black fungi rich in melanin grow on the walls of the ruined Chernobyl reactor. Laboratory studies found some such fungi grew faster when exposed to radiation, suggesting they may harvest its energy, though how is still studied.

facts.title: Paper Money in Song China
facts.body: Merchants in Sichuan began issuing paper notes called jiaozi as receipts for heavy iron coins, and in the early 1020s the Song government took over their issue. These were the first government-issued paper money in the world. Later governments, especially under the Yuan and early Ming, printed notes to excess, and the resulting inflation discredited paper currency in China for centuries.

facts.title: The Indian National Congress
facts.body: Founded in Bombay in 1885 as a forum for educated Indians seeking a greater share in government, the Congress became the main vehicle of the independence movement under leaders such as Gandhi and Nehru. It mobilised millions in non-cooperation and civil disobedience campaigns, and after independence in 1947 it governed India for most of its first decades.

facts.title: Turkey's 1928 Alphabet Reform
facts.body: In 1928 Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's government replaced the Arabic script, used for Ottoman Turkish for centuries, with a Latin-based alphabet adapted to Turkish sounds. The change was enforced within months, and Atatürk himself toured the country teaching the new letters. A language reform followed that replaced many Arabic and Persian loanwords with Turkish ones, making Ottoman texts hard for later generations to read.

facts.title: 1729 is not as dull as it looks
facts.body: When G. H. Hardy called his taxi number 1729 dull, Srinivasa Ramanujan replied that it is the smallest number expressible as the sum of two cubes in two ways: 1 cubed plus 12 cubed, and 9 cubed plus 10 cubed.

facts.title: The Lighthouse of Alexandria
facts.body: The Pharos of Alexandria, completed in the 3rd century BC under the Ptolemies, was one of the tallest structures of the ancient world, probably over 100 metres high. A fire at its top guided ships into Egypt's great harbour. Counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, it was ruined by earthquakes in the Middle Ages, and its name became the word for lighthouse in several languages.

facts.title: Kievan Rus'
facts.body: From the late 9th century a state centred on Kyiv, whose early rulers are generally thought to have been of Scandinavian origin, united East Slavic lands along the trade route from the Baltic to the Black Sea. In 988 Prince Vladimir adopted Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium, shaping the religion and culture of the region. Weakened by division into rival principalities, it was destroyed by the Mongol invasion, which took Kyiv in 1240. Russia, Ukraine and Belarus all trace their origins to it.

facts.title: The Plague Bacterium
facts.body: During an outbreak of plague in Hong Kong in 1894, Alexandre Yersin and Kitasato Shibasaburō independently searched for its cause, and the bacterium is now named Yersinia pestis after Yersin. In 1898 Paul-Louis Simond showed that fleas carried by rats transmit the disease. Ancient DNA has since confirmed the same bacterium as the cause of the Black Death.

facts.title: Japan's era name came from ancient poetry
facts.body: Japan names years after imperial eras. 'Reiwa', which began in 2019, was the first era name taken from a Japanese classic, the poetry collection Man'yōshū, rather than from Chinese texts.

facts.title: The Köppen Climate Classification
facts.body: Developed by the climatologist Wladimir Köppen between the 1880s and the 1930s, this is the most widely used system for classifying the world's climates. It divides them into five main groups, labelled A to E, from tropical to polar, using temperature, rainfall and their seasons. Köppen drew his boundaries largely from the distribution of natural vegetation.

facts.title: Wayang Kulit
facts.body: Wayang kulit is the shadow puppet theatre of Java and Bali, in which a single puppeteer, the dalang, moves flat, intricately carved leather puppets behind a lit screen. Accompanied by a gamelan orchestra, performances often last all night and draw on the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. UNESCO recognised wayang as a masterpiece of intangible heritage in 2003.

facts.title: Tōru Takemitsu
facts.body: Takemitsu (1930–1996) was one of Japan's most internationally renowned composers. Largely self-taught, he combined Western modernism with Japanese aesthetics, as in November Steps (1967) for biwa, shakuhachi and orchestra. He also wrote many film scores, including for Akira Kurosawa's Ran.

facts.title: Quarantine means forty days
facts.body: "Quarantine" comes from Venetian quaranta giorni, forty days. During medieval plague outbreaks, ships arriving at Venice had to wait that long before passengers and crew could come ashore.

facts.title: Arendt and the Banality of Evil
facts.body: Reporting on the 1961 trial of the Nazi official Adolf Eichmann in Jerusalem, the philosopher Hannah Arendt was struck that he seemed not a monster but an ordinary, thoughtless bureaucrat. She called this 'the banality of evil': great crimes can be committed by people who simply fail to think about what they are doing. The idea, set out in Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963), was controversial but has remained influential.

facts.title: The Coase Theorem
facts.body: Ronald Coase argued in 1960 that if property rights are clearly defined and bargaining is costless, the parties will negotiate an efficient outcome whoever holds the rights. Since bargaining is rarely costless, his deeper point was that transaction costs and legal rules matter. In 1937 Coase had also explained why firms exist: organising some activities inside a firm is cheaper than using the market for everything.

facts.title: The Twelve Tables
facts.body: Around 450 BC the Roman Republic set down its laws on twelve tablets displayed in the Forum, partly in response to plebeians who complained that unwritten law favoured the patricians. The tablets themselves are lost and survive only in quotations by later authors. They stand at the start of Roman law, which later shaped the legal systems of much of Europe.

facts.title: Starfish have an eye on each arm
facts.body: At the tip of each arm, many sea stars have a small red eye made of dozens of light-sensing units. It cannot see detail or colour, but lets the animal make out large shapes, such as the reef where it lives.

facts.title: Meiji Japan's New Vocabulary
facts.body: As Meiji Japan absorbed Western learning in the late 19th century, scholars coined many words from Chinese characters for new concepts. Nishi Amane is credited with tetsugaku (philosophy), and terms such as keizai (economy) and shakai (society) took on their modern meanings in this period. Many of these coinages were then borrowed into Chinese and Korean, so much modern East Asian intellectual vocabulary was shaped in Japan.

facts.title: The Solar Cell
facts.body: In 1954 researchers at Bell Labs demonstrated the first practical silicon solar cell, which converted about 6 per cent of sunlight into electricity. Solar cells exploit the photovoltaic effect, in which light frees electrons in a semiconductor. They powered satellites from the late 1950s, and falling costs later made solar power a major source of electricity.

facts.title: The Mughal Empire
facts.body: Founded by Babur in 1526, the Mughal Empire came to rule most of the Indian subcontinent. Akbar, who reigned in the late 16th century, built an efficient administration and practised tolerance towards his Hindu subjects. Mughal power peaked in the 17th century, the age of the Taj Mahal, and declined in the 18th.

facts.title: Saharan dust feeds the Amazon
facts.body: Satellite studies show winds carry millions of tonnes of dust from the Sahara across the Atlantic every year. It contains phosphorus, a nutrient that helps replace what heavy rains wash out of Amazon soils.

facts.title: Ptolemy's Almagest
facts.body: Claudius Ptolemy, working in Alexandria in the 2nd century AD, set out in the Almagest a mathematical model of the heavens with the Earth at the centre. By combining circles upon circles, called epicycles, it predicted the positions of the planets with useful accuracy. Preserved and refined by Arabic-language astronomers, it remained the standard work of astronomy until Copernicus.

facts.title: The Australian Outback
facts.body: The Outback is the vast, dry and thinly populated interior of Australia. Most of the continent is arid or semi-arid, so most Australians live near the coasts, especially in the south-east. Much of the interior relies on water drawn from the Great Artesian Basin, one of the largest underground water reserves in the world.

facts.title: Surrealism
facts.body: Surrealism was launched in Paris by the poet André Breton with his manifesto of 1924. Drawing on Freud's ideas about the unconscious, its writers and artists sought to free the imagination through dreams, chance and automatic writing. Salvador Dalí's melting clocks and René Magritte's paradoxical images are among its best-known works.

facts.title: A Roman emperor who preferred cabbages
facts.body: Diocletian became one of the few Roman emperors to retire, stepping down in 305. When later urged to return to power, he reportedly said that anyone who saw the cabbages he grew would not ask him to.

facts.title: The Violin Makers of Cremona
facts.body: In the 16th century Andrea Amati of Cremona, in northern Italy, gave the violin family its classic form. In the following generations Antonio Stradivari and Giuseppe Guarneri 'del Gesù' raised violin making to a level that later makers still try to match. Their instruments remain the most prized among concert soloists.

facts.title: Haitian Vodou
facts.body: Haitian Vodou took shape in the 18th century among enslaved Africans in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, blending religions of West and Central Africa, including those of the Fon and Kongo peoples, with elements of Catholicism. Believers serve a distant creator, Bondye, through many spirits called lwa, who are honoured with drumming, dance and offerings and may possess worshippers during ceremonies. Long suppressed and caricatured abroad as 'voodoo', it is central to Haitian culture.

facts.title: The Division of Labour
facts.body: Adam Smith opened The Wealth of Nations (1776) with a pin factory, where splitting the work into about eighteen operations let ten workers make tens of thousands of pins a day. Specialisation raises productivity through greater skill, time saved and the invention of machinery. Smith added that the division of labour is limited by the extent of the market, linking growth to trade.

facts.title: Nutmeg and mace grow on the same fruit
facts.body: Nutmeg is the seed of the nutmeg tree's fruit, and mace is the lacy red covering wrapped around that seed. They are dried separately and taste similar, but mace is more delicate.

facts.title: China's Imperial Examinations
facts.body: Introduced under the Sui dynasty around 600 and expanded under the Tang and Song, the examinations selected state officials by testing their knowledge of the Confucian classics. In principle open to most men regardless of birth, they created a scholar-official class and lasted until 1905. The system was copied in Korea and Vietnam and is often said to have influenced European civil service exams.

facts.title: Nahuatl
facts.body: Nahuatl was the language of the Aztecs and a lingua franca of central Mexico before the Spanish conquest. Spanish friars wrote grammars of it in Latin letters, and works such as Bernardino de Sahagún's Florentine Codex recorded Aztec culture in Nahuatl and Spanish. Through Spanish it gave English words such as chocolate, tomato, avocado and chilli, and it is spoken in Mexico to this day.

facts.title: The International Space Station
facts.body: The International Space Station was built in low Earth orbit by the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada. Assembly began in 1998 from modules launched separately, and from November 2000 crews lived aboard without a break for decades. It hosted thousands of experiments on how materials, plants and the human body behave in weightlessness.

facts.title: Each eye has a blind spot
facts.body: Where the optic nerve leaves the back of each eye there are no light-sensing cells, so there is a gap in your vision. You never notice it because the other eye covers it and the brain fills in the hole.

facts.title: The Reconquista
facts.body: After the Muslim conquest of most of Iberia from 711, Christian kingdoms in the north gradually pushed south over nearly eight centuries. The Reconquista ended in 1492, when Ferdinand and Isabella took Granada, the last Muslim state in the peninsula. The same year Spain expelled its Jews.

facts.title: Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics
facts.body: Ibn al-Haytham, born in Basra around 965 and active in Cairo, wrote the Book of Optics in the early 11th century. He argued that we see because light travels from objects into the eye, not from the eye outwards, and tested his ideas with systematic experiments. Translated into Latin, the book shaped European optics up to Kepler.

facts.title: The Arctic Ocean
facts.body: The Arctic Ocean, around the North Pole, is the smallest and shallowest of the world's oceans. Much of it is covered by floating sea ice, so the North Pole itself lies on drifting ice rather than land. The ice cover has been shrinking markedly since satellite records began in the late 1970s, a clear sign of a warming climate.

facts.title: Water can be ice, liquid and vapour together
facts.body: At 0.01 degrees Celsius and a pressure under 1 per cent of normal air pressure, water reaches its triple point. There ice, liquid water and water vapour can all exist together in stable balance, melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing at equal rates.

facts.title: Journey to the West
facts.body: Journey to the West, a 16th-century Chinese novel usually attributed to Wu Cheng'en, retells the pilgrimage of the monk Xuanzang to India to bring back Buddhist scriptures. He is protected by fantastic companions, above all the rebellious Monkey King, Sun Wukong. One of the four classic novels of Chinese literature, it has inspired countless plays, films and comics.

facts.title: The Mevlevi Sema
facts.body: The Mevlevi order, founded in Konya by followers of the poet Rumi after his death in 1273, developed the sema, a ceremony in which dervishes turn in a whirling prayer. It is accompanied by the ney reed flute, drums and voices in long compositions. The ceremony became one of the high forms of Ottoman classical music.

facts.title: Averroes
facts.body: Ibn Rushd, known in Latin as Averroes (1126–1198), was a judge, physician and philosopher in Córdoba in Muslim Spain. He wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle and in The Incoherence of the Incoherence defended philosophy against al-Ghazali. Translated into Latin, his commentaries earned him the title 'the Commentator' among medieval scholars and inspired the controversial Latin Averroist movement in Paris.

facts.title: A Roman road map nearly seven metres long
facts.body: The Tabula Peutingeriana, a medieval copy of a Roman road map, is a scroll about 6.7 metres long but only about a third of a metre tall. It squashes the empire into a strip to show routes and distances, not true shapes.

facts.title: From GATT to the WTO
facts.body: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, signed in 1947, set rules for trade and organised successive rounds of negotiations that sharply reduced tariffs on manufactured goods. Its Uruguay Round created the World Trade Organization in 1995, with a stronger system for settling disputes between countries. The core principle is non-discrimination: a tariff cut granted to one member should apply to all.

facts.title: Participatory Budgeting
facts.body: In 1989 the Brazilian city of Porto Alegre began letting residents decide, through neighbourhood assemblies, how part of the municipal investment budget would be spent. The experiment was credited with shifting spending towards poorer districts and reducing clientelism. Participatory budgeting has since been adopted in various forms by many cities around the world.

facts.title: Sibawayh and the Founding of Arabic Grammar
facts.body: Sibawayh, a Persian scholar working in Basra in the late 8th century, wrote the first comprehensive grammar of Arabic, known simply as al-Kitab, 'the Book'. His teacher al-Khalil ibn Ahmad compiled the first Arabic dictionary, Kitab al-Ayn, and systematised the metres of Arabic poetry. Their work, driven partly by concern for the correct reading of the Quran, founded the Arabic linguistic tradition.

facts.title: "Escalator" was once a brand name
facts.body: Escalator was a trademark of the Otis Elevator Company. People used it so widely for any moving staircase that in 1950 it was ruled a generic word, and Otis lost the exclusive right to it.

facts.title: The First Electronic Computers
facts.body: Britain's Colossus, built in 1943 and 1944 to break German teleprinter codes, was the first programmable electronic digital computer, though it was kept secret for decades. In the United States ENIAC, completed in 1945, was a general-purpose machine with about 18,000 vacuum tubes. These machines marked the start of electronic computing.

facts.title: The First Emperor of China
facts.body: In 221 BC the king of Qin completed the conquest of the rival Warring States and took the title Shi Huangdi, 'First Emperor'. He standardised weights, measures, coinage and script. His dynasty fell soon after his death, but the unified empire he created lasted for over two thousand years. His tomb is guarded by the Terracotta Army.

facts.title: Lind's Scurvy Trial
facts.body: In 1747 the Scottish naval surgeon James Lind divided twelve sailors with scurvy into pairs and gave each pair a different remedy. The two given oranges and lemons recovered quickly, while the others did not. It is one of the earliest controlled clinical trials, although the Royal Navy only issued lemon juice to its sailors decades later.

facts.title: Japanese monkeys enjoy hot baths
facts.body: At Jigokudani in Japan, macaques soak in hot springs during the snowy winter. A 2018 study found that bathing lowered levels of stress hormones in the monkeys, suggesting it helps them conserve energy and stay calm in the cold.

facts.title: The Okavango Delta
facts.body: The Okavango River flows from the highlands of Angola into Botswana and never reaches the sea. Instead it spreads into a vast inland delta of channels, lagoons and islands at the edge of the Kalahari Desert. The seasonal flood arrives during the dry season, drawing huge numbers of animals to one of Africa's richest wildlife areas.

facts.title: Frida Kahlo
facts.body: The Mexican painter Frida Kahlo, badly injured in a bus accident as a teenager, made her body and her pain central subjects of her art. Her many self-portraits combine Mexican folk traditions with dreamlike imagery. Long overshadowed by her husband Diego Rivera, she became an international icon in the late 20th century.

facts.title: Pythagoras and Musical Ratios
facts.body: Greek tradition credits Pythagoras, in the 6th century BC, with discovering that consonant intervals match simple ratios of string length: 2:1 for the octave, 3:2 for the fifth and 4:3 for the fourth. Pythagorean tuning, built from pure fifths, followed from this. The idea that harmony is governed by number shaped Western music theory and the ancient notion of the music of the spheres.

facts.title: Pluto has not orbited once since its discovery
facts.body: Pluto was discovered in 1930, but it takes about 248 Earth years to circle the Sun. It will not complete its first full orbit since being spotted until the 2170s.

facts.title: Jesus of Nazareth
facts.body: Jesus was a Jewish preacher from Galilee who was crucified on the orders of the Roman governor Pontius Pilate in Jerusalem, probably around AD 30. The Gospels describe his healings and his teaching of the Kingdom of God, love of neighbour and forgiveness, often through parables. Christians believe he rose from the dead and is the Son of God; in Islam he is honoured as the prophet Isa. Almost all historians accept that he existed.

facts.title: The Corn Laws
facts.body: Britain's Corn Laws, tightened in 1815, imposed tariffs on imported grain to protect landowners' incomes. Manufacturers and the Anti-Corn Law League, led by Richard Cobden and John Bright, argued that they raised the price of bread. Their repeal in 1846 under Robert Peel split the Conservative Party and marked Britain's turn to free trade.

facts.title: The Sustainable Development Goals
facts.body: Adopted by all UN member states in 2015, the 17 Sustainable Development Goals set targets for 2030, including ending extreme poverty and hunger, achieving gender equality and tackling climate change. They succeeded the eight Millennium Development Goals of 2000 and, unlike them, apply to rich as well as poor countries.

facts.title: A Tibetan greeting with the tongue
facts.body: Traditionally some Tibetans greet others by showing their tongue. A popular story links it to a cruel 9th-century king, Langdarma, said to have had a black tongue, so a pink one proved good intentions.

facts.title: Jerome's Vulgate
facts.body: In the late 4th century Pope Damasus commissioned Jerome to revise the Latin Bible. Working largely in Bethlehem, Jerome translated most of the Old Testament directly from Hebrew rather than from the Greek Septuagint. His version, later called the Vulgate (the 'common' edition), became the standard Bible of the Western Church for over a thousand years, and the Council of Trent declared it authoritative in 1546.

facts.title: Iron Smelting
facts.body: Iron was smelted in Anatolia and the Near East during the 2nd millennium BC, and its use spread widely after about 1200 BC. Unlike copper and tin, iron ore is common, so iron tools and weapons could be made in large numbers. Early smiths produced a spongy mass of iron, called a bloom, that had to be hammered to drive out impurities.

facts.title: The Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific
facts.body: Using double-hulled canoes and detailed knowledge of stars, winds and swells, Polynesian navigators settled the islands of the remote Pacific. The furthest corners of the Polynesian triangle, Hawaii, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) and New Zealand, were probably reached between about 1000 and 1300.

facts.title: A painting shredded itself after being sold
facts.body: In 2018 Banksy's Girl with Balloon passed through a shredder hidden in its frame moments after it was sold at auction in London. The half-shredded work was renamed Love is in the Bin.

facts.title: Chagas Disease
facts.body: In 1909 the Brazilian physician Carlos Chagas described a new disease, identified the parasite that causes it, Trypanosoma cruzi, and showed that it is carried by blood-sucking insects. It is a rare case of one researcher working out the pathogen, the carrier and the illness. Chagas disease, which can damage the heart decades after infection, has long been a major health burden in Latin America.

facts.title: The Fertile Crescent
facts.body: The Fertile Crescent is the arc of land running from the Persian Gulf through Mesopotamia to the eastern Mediterranean coast. Around 11,000 years ago people there were among the first to farm, domesticating wheat, barley, sheep and goats. The name was coined by the American archaeologist James Henry Breasted in the early 20th century.

facts.title: Michelangelo's David
facts.body: Michelangelo carved the marble David in Florence between 1501 and 1504, from a block other sculptors had abandoned. More than five metres tall, it shows the biblical hero before his fight with Goliath, tense and alert. It became a symbol of the Florentine Republic and is a defining work of Renaissance sculpture.

facts.title: A frog that survives being frozen
facts.body: In winter the North American wood frog can let about two-thirds of its body water freeze, with no heartbeat or breathing. Sugar flooding its cells limits the damage, and in spring it thaws and hops away.

facts.title: The Mbira
facts.body: The mbira is a lamellophone of the Shona people of Zimbabwe: metal keys fixed to a wooden board, plucked with the thumbs and often placed in a gourd resonator. It is played at all-night bira ceremonies to communicate with ancestral spirits. Two players typically interlock complementary parts to create a dense, cyclical texture.

facts.title: Shankara and Advaita Vedanta
facts.body: Advaita, or 'non-dual', Vedanta is the school of Hindu philosophy most closely associated with Adi Shankara, traditionally dated to the 8th century AD. It holds that only Brahman is ultimately real and that the world of separate things is maya, an appearance rather than final reality. Liberation comes through the knowledge that one's own self is identical with Brahman, and the school became one of the most influential in Hindu thought.

facts.title: The Single Whip Tax Reform
facts.body: In the late 16th century the Ming government of China, under the grand secretary Zhang Juzheng, extended the 'single whip' reform, which consolidated many land taxes and labour obligations into a single payment in silver. The reform simplified taxation and accelerated the use of money throughout the Chinese economy. China's resulting demand for silver drew in vast quantities of the metal from Japan and the Americas.

facts.title: Dry spaghetti rarely snaps in two
facts.body: Bend a dry spaghetti strand from both ends and it usually breaks into three or more pieces. The first break sends a vibration back along each half, causing extra breaks. Twisting it first can make it snap in two.

facts.title: Al-Farabi's Virtuous City
facts.body: The 10th-century philosopher al-Farabi, active in Baghdad and Damascus, wrote The Opinions of the People of the Virtuous City, adapting Plato's Republic to an Islamic setting. He argued that the best city is ruled by a philosopher-prophet who leads citizens to happiness, and analysed the ignorant and corrupt cities that fall short. He was known as the 'Second Teacher' after Aristotle.

facts.title: Australian Aboriginal Languages
facts.body: At the time of British colonisation Australia had around 250 languages, most belonging to the Pama-Nyungan family, and many have since died out or have few speakers. Some show striking features: Guugu Yimithirr describes positions using compass directions rather than left and right. The same language gave English the word kangaroo, recorded by James Cook's expedition in 1770.

facts.title: The Black Box Flight Recorder
facts.body: In the 1950s the Australian scientist David Warren, at a government aeronautical laboratory in Melbourne, developed one of the first devices to record cockpit voices and instrument data. Investigating air crashes was hard because there were often no survivors or witnesses. After initial scepticism, flight recorders, popularly called black boxes, became compulsory on airliners and have greatly helped improve air safety.

facts.title: Sixty minutes comes from ancient Babylon
facts.body: Our 60 minutes and 60 seconds come from the base-60 counting used in ancient Mesopotamia. Sixty divides neatly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30.

facts.title: The Spanish Philippines
facts.body: In 1565 a Spanish expedition under Miguel López de Legazpi began the colonisation of the Philippines, named after Philip II. Manila, founded as the capital in 1571, became the hub of the galleon trade that carried Chinese silks to Mexico in exchange for American silver. Spanish rule lasted until 1898 and made the islands largely Catholic.

facts.title: Jenner's Smallpox Vaccine
facts.body: In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner inoculated a boy with material from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid's hand, and then showed that the boy did not catch smallpox. Cowpox is mild and gave protection against the deadly disease. The word vaccine comes from the Latin vacca, cow, and Jenner's method became the model for immunisation against many diseases.

facts.title: How Many Continents There Are
facts.body: There is no single agreed number of continents. English-speaking countries usually count seven, while many Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries treat the Americas as one continent, and some count Europe and Asia as one landmass, Eurasia. The division between Europe and Asia in particular is a cultural convention rather than a clear physical boundary.

facts.title: West African drums can talk
facts.body: Hourglass-shaped talking drums have cords that the player squeezes to change the pitch. Because Yoruba and other West African languages are tonal, the drums can copy the melody of speech and send messages.

facts.title: Borobudur
facts.body: Borobudur in central Java is a vast Buddhist monument built in the 8th and 9th centuries under the Shailendra dynasty. Shaped like a stepped pyramid crowned by stupas, it leads pilgrims upwards past galleries of relief carvings, symbolising the path from the world of desire to enlightenment. Abandoned for centuries, it was brought to wider attention under British rule in 1814.

facts.title: The Ukulele
facts.body: The ukulele was developed in Hawaii in the 1880s from a small guitar-like instrument, the machete, brought by immigrants from Madeira. King Kalākaua encouraged its use in Hawaiian music. It spread to mainland America in the early 20th century and became a symbol of Hawaii worldwide.

facts.title: Han Feizi and Legalism
facts.body: Legalism was a school of Chinese political thought that rejected Confucian moral persuasion in favour of strict laws, harsh punishments and generous rewards. Its leading theorist, Han Feizi, died in 233 BC; Legalist ideas guided the state of Qin, which unified China in 221 BC. Later dynasties officially honoured Confucianism but kept many Legalist methods of government.

facts.title: Japan has a national fungus
facts.body: Koji mould, Aspergillus oryzae, is used to make soy sauce, miso and sake. It is so important to Japanese cooking that the Brewing Society of Japan named it the country's 'national fungus' in 2006.

facts.title: The Stone Money of Yap
facts.body: On the Pacific island of Yap, in Micronesia, large stone discs called rai, quarried on Palau and carried back by canoe, served as a store of value and a means of payment. Many were too heavy to move, so ownership passed by common agreement while the stones stayed in place. Economists including Milton Friedman have used Yap to show that money rests on shared belief rather than physical possession.

facts.title: The Genocide Convention
facts.body: The word 'genocide' was coined in 1944 by the Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin. The UN General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide on 9 December 1948, the day before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It defines genocide as acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

facts.title: Baybayin
facts.body: Baybayin is a pre-colonial script of the Philippines, an abugida related to the Brahmi-derived scripts of Indonesia. Spanish observers in the 16th century noted its wide use for Tagalog, and the Doctrina Christiana of 1593, among the first books printed in the Philippines, used it alongside Latin letters. It gave way to the Latin alphabet under Spanish rule but has become a symbol of Filipino heritage.

facts.title: Firework colours come from metals
facts.body: Strontium gives fireworks red, barium green, copper blue and sodium yellow. Heat excites the metals' electrons, and each element gives off light at its own characteristic colours as they settle back.

facts.title: The Grand Anicut
facts.body: The Grand Anicut, or Kallanai, is a stone dam across the Kaveri river in Tamil Nadu, traditionally attributed to the Chola king Karikala around the 2nd century AD. It diverts water into the fertile Kaveri delta for irrigation. Remodelled by British engineers in the 19th century, it is among the oldest water-diversion works in the world still in use.

facts.title: Bolívar and Spanish American Independence
facts.body: Between 1810 and the mid-1820s most of Spain's American colonies won independence. Simón Bolívar, 'the Liberator', led campaigns that freed present-day Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia, named after him, while José de San Martín helped free Argentina, Chile and Peru. Bolívar's dream of a united South America failed.

facts.title: Chromosomes and Heredity
facts.body: From 1910 Thomas Hunt Morgan and his students at Columbia University bred fruit flies and traced mutations such as white eyes through generations. They showed that genes lie in a line along chromosomes, and Alfred Sturtevant produced the first genetic map in 1913. Morgan received the Nobel Prize in 1933, and the fruit fly became a standard organism of genetics.

facts.title: England had a nine-day queen
facts.body: Lady Jane Grey was proclaimed Queen of England in July 1553 but was replaced by Mary I just over a week later. Her claim lacked support, and the country swung behind Henry VIII's daughter.

facts.title: Cape Horn and the Drake Passage
facts.body: Cape Horn, on a Chilean island at the southern tip of South America, was named by Dutch sailors in 1616 after the town of Hoorn. South of it, the Drake Passage separates the continent from Antarctica and carries strong winds and some of the roughest seas on Earth. Before the Panama Canal opened, ships sailing between the Atlantic and Pacific had to face it.

facts.title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
facts.body: Gabriel García Márquez's novel of 1967 follows the Buendía family over seven generations in the fictional Colombian town of Macondo. Its blend of everyday reality with the miraculous made it the best-known work of magical realism. It was central to the 'Boom' of Latin American literature, and its author won the Nobel Prize in 1982.

facts.title: Rhapsody in Blue
facts.body: George Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue for piano and jazz band was premiered in New York in 1924 at a concert by Paul Whiteman's orchestra. Opening with a famous clarinet glissando, it brought jazz into the concert hall. Gershwin later wrote the opera Porgy and Bess (1935).

facts.title: Godzilla is part gorilla, part whale
facts.body: Godzilla's Japanese name, Gojira, blends gorira (gorilla) and kujira (whale). The monster first appeared in a Japanese film in 1954.

facts.title: What Is Enlightenment?
facts.body: In a 1784 essay, Immanuel Kant defined Enlightenment as humanity's emergence from its self-imposed immaturity, the inability to use one's own understanding without another's guidance. Its motto, he wrote, is 'Sapere aude!': dare to know. The essay became a classic statement of the Enlightenment ideals of reason, free public debate and intellectual independence.

facts.title: The Trans-Saharan Gold Trade
facts.body: From around the 8th century, camel caravans linked North Africa with the West African kingdoms of Ghana, Mali and Songhai. Gold from West African fields went north, while salt mined in the Sahara and goods from the Mediterranean went south. The trade financed powerful states and trading cities such as Timbuktu, and West African gold was a major source of metal for medieval Islamic and, later, Italian gold coins.

facts.title: The Oyo Mesi
facts.body: In the Yoruba Oyo Empire, in what is now south-western Nigeria and Benin, the king or Alaafin was checked by the Oyo Mesi, a council of seven nobles. According to tradition, if the council lost confidence in the Alaafin it could signal that he must take his own life. The arrangement is often cited as an African example of institutional checks on royal power.

facts.title: The panda's thumb is not a thumb
facts.body: Giant pandas grip bamboo with what looks like a sixth finger. It is actually an enlarged wrist bone covered in a fleshy pad, which works against the other fingers to hold stems while the panda strips them.

facts.title: From Latin to the Romance Languages
facts.body: Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian and Romanian descend not from classical literary Latin but from the spoken Latin of ordinary people, often called Vulgar Latin. After the Western Roman Empire fragmented, regional speech drifted apart until it was recognised as distinct from Latin. The Strasbourg Oaths of 842 are often cited as the earliest text in an early form of French.

facts.title: Sputnik 1
facts.body: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, from Baikonur in present-day Kazakhstan. The polished metal sphere, about 58 centimetres across, transmitted radio beeps that could be picked up around the world. Its success shocked the United States and started the space race.

facts.title: The Year of Africa
facts.body: In 1960 seventeen African countries gained independence, most of them former French colonies, together with Nigeria and the Belgian Congo. The year marked the peak of the decolonisation of sub-Saharan Africa and transformed the political map of the continent.

facts.title: The magic number 6174
facts.body: Take a four-digit number with at least two different digits, arrange its digits largest-first and smallest-first, and subtract. Repeat, and you reach 6174 within seven steps, as Indian mathematician D. R. Kaprekar found.

facts.title: Ulugh Beg's Samarkand Observatory
facts.body: Ulugh Beg, a grandson of Timur and ruler of Samarkand, built a great observatory there in the 1420s, with a huge curved instrument set along the meridian. His astronomers produced a catalogue of around a thousand stars based on fresh, highly accurate observations. He was killed in 1449, and the observatory soon fell into ruin.

facts.title: The Mississippi River
facts.body: Together with its great tributary the Missouri, the Mississippi drains most of the United States between the Rocky Mountains and the Appalachians. It flows south to the Gulf of Mexico, ending in a large delta below New Orleans. For centuries it has been the main inland waterway of North America, and its name comes from an Ojibwe word meaning 'great river'.

facts.title: The Alhambra
facts.body: The Alhambra in Granada is a palace and fortress complex built mainly in the 13th and 14th centuries by the Nasrid dynasty, the last Muslim rulers in Spain. Its courtyards, such as the Court of the Lions, combine water, gardens and intricate carved stucco and tilework. It is the finest surviving example of the Islamic architecture of al-Andalus.

facts.title: 'Here be dragons' is rare on old maps
facts.body: Despite its fame, the Latin phrase 'hic sunt dracones' is known from almost no historical maps, most famously the Hunt–Lenox Globe of about 1510. Old mapmakers more often drew sea monsters than wrote warnings.

facts.title: Aboriginal Songlines
facts.body: Songlines are Aboriginal Australian song cycles that follow the tracks of ancestral beings across the land. A songline names landmarks, water sources and events in sequence, so that singing it serves as a map, a body of law and a history. They show music functioning as a store of knowledge in an oral culture.

facts.title: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha
facts.body: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha or 'Awakened One', was born at Lumbini in what is now Nepal, probably in the 6th or 5th century BC; scholars disagree on the exact dates. According to tradition he left a princely life, tried extreme asceticism, and then attained enlightenment through meditation at Bodh Gaya. He taught a 'Middle Way' between indulgence and self-denial and spent decades teaching across northern India.

facts.title: China's Reform and Opening
facts.body: From 1978, under Deng Xiaoping, China began dismantling central planning. Farmers were allowed to sell surplus output under the household responsibility system, and special economic zones such as Shenzhen were opened to foreign investment. The reforms launched decades of rapid growth that lifted hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty.

facts.title: In kabaddi you must chant without breathing
facts.body: In the South Asian sport kabaddi, a raider runs into the other team's half while chanting "kabaddi, kabaddi" without pausing. The chant proves the raider is holding a single breath.

facts.title: Germany's Basic Law
facts.body: Adopted in 1949 for West Germany and extended to the whole country at reunification in 1990, the Basic Law was designed to prevent a repeat of the Weimar Republic's collapse. It declares human dignity inviolable, shields core principles from amendment, allows parties hostile to democracy to be banned, and lets parliament remove a chancellor only by electing a successor.

facts.title: The Phoneme
facts.body: A phoneme is the smallest unit of sound that can distinguish one word from another in a particular language. In English, p and b are separate phonemes because they separate pin from bin, but sounds that are distinct in one language may count as one in another: Japanese, for instance, does not distinguish English r and l. The concept is the foundation of phonology and of alphabetic spelling.

facts.title: Spectacles
facts.body: Spectacles were invented in northern Italy around 1286. Early pairs had convex lenses to correct long sight and were perched on the nose or held in front of the eyes. They extended the working lives of scholars and craftsmen, and concave lenses for short sight followed in the 15th century.

facts.title: Most deep-sea animals make their own light
facts.body: Studies of animals filmed off California found roughly three-quarters of those living in the open ocean can produce light. They use it to lure prey, find mates, or hide their silhouette against the faint light from above.

facts.title: The American Revolution
facts.body: Disputes over taxation without representation led thirteen British colonies in North America to rebel in 1775, and on 4 July 1776 they adopted the Declaration of Independence. With decisive help from France they won, and Britain recognised the United States in 1783. Its ideals of popular sovereignty inspired revolutions elsewhere.

facts.title: Smoking and Lung Cancer
facts.body: In 1950 Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill in Britain, and Ernst Wynder and Evarts Graham in the United States, published studies showing that lung cancer patients were far more likely to be smokers. Doll and Hill's long-running study of British doctors, begun in 1951, confirmed the link. The findings helped found modern chronic-disease epidemiology and led to anti-smoking campaigns worldwide.

facts.title: Glaciers
