facts.body: A glacier is a mass of ice, formed from compacted snow over many years, that moves slowly downhill under its own weight. As they flow, glaciers grind out U-shaped valleys and bowl-shaped hollows called cirques, and leave ridges of debris called moraines. Most of the world's glacial ice is in Antarctica and Greenland, and mountain glaciers worldwide have been retreating as the climate warms.

facts.title: Some sand dunes sing
facts.body: Certain dunes, such as Mingsha Shan near Dunhuang in China, make a loud booming hum when sand slides down them. Avalanching grains move in step, producing a low note that can last for minutes.

facts.title: The Tale of Kieu
facts.body: Nguyễn Du wrote this long narrative poem in the early 19th century in Vietnamese, using the vernacular chữ Nôm script. It tells of Thúy Kiều, a gifted young woman who sells herself to save her family and endures years of suffering. Regarded as the masterpiece of Vietnamese literature, its lines are widely quoted in everyday speech.

facts.title: Musique Concrète
facts.body: In Paris in 1948, the radio engineer Pierre Schaeffer began composing with recorded sounds, such as trains, transformed on discs and later tape. He called this musique concrète. Together with electronic music produced in Cologne by Karlheinz Stockhausen and others, it laid the foundation of electronic music and of sampling.

facts.title: Shamanism
facts.body: Shamanism is a set of religious practices in which a specialist, the shaman, is believed to enter a trance and travel to the spirit world to heal, divine or guide the souls of the dead. The word comes, via Russian, from a Tungusic language of Siberia, probably Evenki, and such practices were central to the religions of many Siberian and Central Asian peoples, including the Mongols and Turks. Scholars debate how far the term can be applied to similar practices elsewhere.

facts.title: Māori greet by pressing noses together
facts.body: The hongi is a traditional Māori greeting in which two people press their noses and foreheads together. It symbolises sharing the breath of life.

facts.title: Henry George's Land Value Tax
facts.body: In Progress and Poverty (1879), the American writer Henry George asked why poverty persisted alongside economic progress. His answer was that landowners captured the gains of growth through rising land rents, and he proposed replacing other taxes with a single tax on the value of land. Many economists regard land value taxation as efficient, because the supply of land cannot shrink in response to the tax.

facts.title: Populism
facts.body: Populism is commonly defined as politics that divides society into a virtuous 'people' and a corrupt 'elite', and claims to speak for the people's will. It can be combined with left- or right-wing ideas, as in the American People's Party of the 1890s or Juan Perón's Argentina. Scholars disagree about whether it is best understood as an ideology, a style or a strategy.

facts.title: The Sapir–Whorf Hypothesis
facts.body: The idea that the language we speak shapes how we think is linked to the American linguist Edward Sapir and his student Benjamin Lee Whorf, writing between the 1920s and 1940s. Its strong form, that language determines thought, is now generally rejected. Experiments have, however, found weaker effects, for instance on how speakers of different languages divide up colours or describe directions.

facts.title: A window is a "wind eye"
facts.body: The English word window comes from Old Norse vindauga, literally "wind eye". Early Scandinavian houses had simple holes in the roof or wall that let out smoke and let in the wind.

facts.title: The First Oil Wells
facts.body: Drilling for oil began in the mid-19th century: wells were drilled near Baku on the Caspian Sea in the 1840s, and Edwin Drake's well of 1859 in Titusville, Pennsylvania, launched the American oil boom. Oil was at first wanted mainly for kerosene lamps, replacing whale oil. The internal combustion engine later made petroleum the central fuel of 20th-century transport.

facts.title: The Iranian Revolution
facts.body: In 1978–79 mass protests forced Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, an ally of the United States, to leave Iran. Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini returned from exile and established an Islamic republic led by Shia clergy. The revolution transformed Iran's relations with the West and gave momentum to political Islam.

facts.title: Homeostasis
facts.body: Living bodies keep internal conditions such as temperature, blood sugar and water balance within narrow limits despite changes outside. In the 19th century Claude Bernard described this stable 'internal environment', and in the 1920s Walter Cannon named it homeostasis. It works mainly through negative feedback: a change triggers responses that reverse it, as when sweating cools an overheated body.

facts.title: You cannot tickle yourself
facts.body: When you move, your brain predicts the touch that will follow and dampens your response to it. Tickling yourself is therefore never a surprise, so it does not feel ticklish.

facts.title: The Danube
facts.body: The Danube rises in Germany's Black Forest and flows east to a delta on the Black Sea in Romania and Ukraine. It passes through or along ten countries, more than any other river, and through four capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade. It is the second-longest river in Europe after the Volga and has long been a major trade route and frontier.

facts.title: The Tale of Genji
facts.body: Written in the early 11th century by Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese imperial court, The Tale of Genji follows the life and loves of the 'Shining Prince'. Its subtle portrayal of character and feeling has led some to call it the world's first novel. It is the masterpiece of classical Japanese literature.

facts.title: The Octave
facts.body: An octave is the interval between a note and one with double its frequency. The two sound so alike that nearly all musical cultures treat them as the same note at a different height. Scales divide the octave into steps: Western music uses twelve semitones, while other traditions divide it differently.

facts.title: Why metal feels colder than wood
facts.body: A metal spoon and a wooden one in the same room are equally warm, yet the metal feels colder. Metal conducts heat away from your skin much faster, and your nerves sense that heat loss.

facts.title: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali
facts.body: The Yoga Sutras, attributed to Patanjali and probably compiled in the early centuries AD (their dating is debated), are the foundational text of the Yoga school of Hindu philosophy. They define yoga as the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind and set out an eight-limbed path, from ethical restraints and postures to breath control, meditation and absorption. Physical postures, central to modern yoga, play only a small part in the text.

facts.title: The Eurozone Debt Crisis
facts.body: From late 2009, revelations that Greece's deficit was far larger than reported set off a crisis of confidence in the debt of several eurozone governments. Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Cyprus received bail-outs tied to austerity, and Spain's banks also needed help. Unable to devalue or set their own interest rates, members faced painful adjustments, and the crisis eased after the ECB's president Mario Draghi pledged in 2012 to do 'whatever it takes' to preserve the euro.

facts.title: The Iranian Constitutional Revolution
facts.body: Between 1905 and 1911 protests by merchants, clerics and intellectuals forced the Qajar shah to grant a constitution and an elected parliament, the Majlis, in 1906. It was one of the first constitutional revolutions in Asia. Though weakened by internal conflict and by Russian and British intervention, it rooted the idea of constitutional government in Iran.

facts.title: Roman hours changed length with the seasons
facts.body: Romans split daylight into 12 hours whatever the time of year. So a summer daytime hour was much longer than a winter one.

facts.title: Click Consonants
facts.body: Click consonants, made by drawing the tongue sharply away from the roof of the mouth, are ordinary speech sounds almost only in southern and eastern Africa. They are characteristic of the languages often grouped as Khoisan, spoken by San and Khoekhoe peoples, and were borrowed into neighbouring Bantu languages such as Zulu and Xhosa. In writing, the letters c, q and x often represent clicks, as at the start of the name Xhosa.

facts.title: Liquid-Fuel Rockets
facts.body: In 1926 the American physicist Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fuelled rocket, in Massachusetts; it flew for only a few seconds. Liquid propellants are more efficient than the solid gunpowder-type fuels of earlier rockets. In Germany, Wernher von Braun's team built the V-2 missile during the Second World War, and its technology led directly to the rockets of the space race.

facts.title: Augustus, the First Roman Emperor
facts.body: After defeating Mark Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC, Octavian, Julius Caesar's adopted heir, became sole master of the Roman world. In 27 BC the Senate gave him the name Augustus, and he ruled as emperor while keeping the outward forms of the Republic. His reign began the long Pax Romana.

facts.title: A 12-year-old boy saved the vanilla industry
facts.body: In 1841 on Réunion, Edmond Albius, an enslaved boy of 12, worked out how to pollinate vanilla flowers by hand. Outside Mexico the plant had no natural pollinators, and his method is still used today.

facts.title: Dalton's Atomic Theory
facts.body: In 1808 the English chemist John Dalton proposed that each element is made of identical atoms with a characteristic weight, and that compounds form when atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios. He drew up the first table of relative atomic weights. His theory turned the ancient idea of atoms into a working basis for chemistry.

facts.title: The Great Rift Valley
facts.body: The East African Rift is a long system of valleys where the African continent is slowly being pulled apart along diverging tectonic plates. It holds deep lakes such as Tanganyika and Malawi and volcanoes such as Kilimanjaro. Many of the most important early human fossils have been found along it, which makes it central to the study of human origins.

facts.title: The Harlem Renaissance
facts.body: In the 1920s the New York neighbourhood of Harlem became the centre of a flowering of African American literature, art and music. Writers such as Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston, and the critic Alain Locke, asserted a confident new Black cultural identity. The movement shaped American culture and inspired later Black writers and artists.

facts.title: Dung beetles navigate by the Milky Way
facts.body: Some South African dung beetles roll their balls in straight lines even on moonless nights. In a 2013 study in a planetarium, they only kept their course when the band of the Milky Way was visible, the first animals shown to use it.

facts.title: Flamenco
facts.body: Flamenco is the music and dance of Andalusia in southern Spain, closely associated with its Gitano (Romani) communities. It combines song (cante), guitar (toque), dance (baile) and rhythmic hand-clapping. Its precise origins are debated, but it took its recognisable form in the 19th century, partly in the cafés cantantes.

facts.title: Tibetan Buddhism
facts.body: Buddhism reached Tibet from India from the 7th and 8th centuries and developed into a distinctive form of Vajrayana, or tantric, Buddhism with elaborate ritual, meditation and a large monastic culture. Its schools include the Gelug, whose leading teachers are the Dalai Lamas, believed to be successive reincarnations of the bodhisattva of compassion. The tradition spread to Mongolia and, after 1959, to the wider world through Tibetan exiles.

facts.title: Fiat Money
facts.body: Fiat money has value because a government declares it legal tender and people accept it, not because it can be exchanged for gold or another commodity. Since the United States ended the convertibility of the dollar into gold in 1971, all major currencies have been fiat money. Its value depends on trust in the institutions that issue it, which is why the credibility of central banks matters so much.

facts.title: Total eclipses rely on a cosmic coincidence
facts.body: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and also about 400 times farther away, so both look almost the same size in our sky. That is why the Moon can just cover the Sun's disc during a total eclipse.

facts.title: The Napoleonic Code
facts.body: France's Civil Code of 1804, promoted by Napoleon, replaced a patchwork of regional customs with a single, clearly written law on persons, property and contracts. It enshrined equality before the law and secular authority, while strengthening the power of husbands and fathers. Spread by conquest and imitation, it shaped civil law in much of Europe, Latin America and the Middle East.

facts.title: Esperanto
facts.body: Esperanto was published in 1887 by Ludwik Zamenhof, an eye doctor from Białystok in the Russian Empire, under the pseudonym Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'. He designed it as an easy, neutral second language with regular grammar and vocabulary drawn mainly from European languages. Unlike most invented languages, it gained a lasting international community of speakers, including some who learned it from birth.

facts.title: Papermaking
facts.body: Paper was invented in China; fragments survive from the 2nd century BC, and the court official Cai Lun is traditionally credited with improving it around AD 105. Made from plant fibres such as bark, hemp and rags, it was far cheaper than silk or bamboo strips. Papermaking spread to the Islamic world in the 8th century and reached Europe by the 12th, preparing the way for printing.

facts.title: Athenians voted with broken pottery
facts.body: In ancient Athens citizens could banish a powerful politician for ten years by scratching his name on a pottery shard called an ostrakon. That practice gives us the word 'ostracism'.

facts.title: Muhammad Ali of Egypt
facts.body: Muhammad Ali, an Ottoman officer of Albanian origin, took power in Egypt in 1805. Nominally a vassal of the sultan, he built a modern army, state industries and schools, and his armies conquered Sudan and even challenged the Ottomans. His dynasty ruled Egypt until the revolution of 1952.

facts.title: Clonal Selection Theory
facts.body: In 1957 the Australian virologist Frank Macfarlane Burnet proposed that each immune cell carries receptors for just one specific target. When a cell meets its matching invader it multiplies into a large clone, which explains how the body fights infection and remembers past ones. The theory became a foundation of modern immunology, and Burnet shared the 1960 Nobel Prize for related work on immune tolerance.

facts.title: The Trade Winds
facts.body: The trade winds are steady easterly winds blowing towards the equator across the tropics, from the north-east in the Northern Hemisphere and the south-east in the Southern. They meet near the equator in a zone of rising air, rain and calms that sailors called the doldrums. Sailing ships relied on them to cross the Atlantic from Europe to the Americas.

facts.title: A woman on a tram invented the wiper
facts.body: On a snowy trip to New York, Mary Anderson saw a tram driver lean out of the window to clear his windscreen. She designed a hand-operated wiper, patented in 1903.

facts.title: Giotto
facts.body: The Florentine painter Giotto di Bondone, active in the early 14th century, broke with the flat, stylised manner of Byzantine painting. In his frescoes in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua, completed around 1305, figures have weight, gesture and visible emotion. Later writers from Vasari onwards saw him as the founder of the Renaissance tradition in painting.

facts.title: The Steelpan
facts.body: The steelpan was developed in Trinidad and Tobago in the 1930s and 1940s from discarded oil drums, hammered into surfaces with tuned areas that each produce a note. It grew out of Afro-Trinidadian percussion traditions that colonial authorities had tried to restrict. Steel bands became central to Carnival, and the pan is Trinidad and Tobago's national instrument.

facts.title: Plotinus and Neoplatonism
facts.body: Plotinus (around 204–270), a Greek-speaking philosopher from Egypt who taught in Rome, founded Neoplatonism. He held that all reality flows from a single, transcendent source, the One, through Intellect and Soul down to the material world, and that the soul can return to the One through contemplation. His writings, the Enneads, edited by his pupil Porphyry, influenced Christian, Jewish and Islamic thought.

facts.title: The potato is a tomato's close cousin
facts.body: Potatoes and tomatoes belong to the same genus, Solanum, and their leaves and flowers look alike. The sweet potato, despite its name, is from a different family altogether and is related to morning glory.

facts.title: Double-Entry Bookkeeping
facts.body: In double-entry bookkeeping, every transaction is recorded twice, as a debit in one account and a credit in another, so the books must always balance. The method developed among Italian merchants in the late Middle Ages and was first described in print by Luca Pacioli in 1494. It made errors easier to detect and is the foundation of modern accounting.

facts.title: The Haudenosaunee Great Law of Peace
facts.body: The Haudenosaunee or Iroquois Confederacy united five nations, later six, in what is now the north-eastern United States under an oral constitution known as the Great Law of Peace. Clan mothers chose the chiefs who sat in the common council and could remove them. The confederacy's founding date is disputed, as is the extent of its influence on the framers of the US Constitution.

facts.title: Tamil and the Dravidian Languages
facts.body: Tamil belongs to the Dravidian family, which also includes Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam and is unrelated to the Indo-European languages of northern India. Tamil has a continuous literary tradition reaching back about two thousand years to the Sangam poetry, and its early grammar, the Tolkappiyam, is of uncertain but early date. In 2004 the Indian government declared Tamil the first 'classical language' of India.

facts.title: Scientists slowed light to cycling speed
facts.body: In 1999 a team led by Danish physicist Lene Hau slowed light to about 17 metres per second by sending it through an ultra-cold cloud of sodium atoms, roughly the speed of a fast cyclist.

facts.title: The Pendulum Clock
facts.body: In 1656 the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock, using the observation, made earlier by Galileo, that a pendulum swings in a regular time. It reduced the error of the best clocks from many minutes a day to well under a minute. For nearly three centuries pendulum clocks were the most accurate timekeepers available.

facts.title: The Voyages of Zheng He
facts.body: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming admiral Zheng He led seven great expeditions across the Indian Ocean, reaching South-East Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa. His fleets of hundreds of ships displayed Chinese power and gathered tribute. The voyages were then halted, and Ming China turned away from overseas expansion.

facts.title: Gravitational Waves
facts.body: Einstein's general relativity predicted that accelerating masses send ripples through spacetime. On 14 September 2015 the two LIGO detectors in the United States recorded such waves for the first time, from two black holes merging more than a billion light-years away. The discovery opened a new way of observing the universe, and Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne received the 2017 Nobel Prize.

facts.title: California was once drawn as an island
facts.body: For much of the 1600s and 1700s many European maps showed California as a huge island. The mistake spread from copied maps until Spanish explorers confirmed it was connected to the mainland.

facts.title: The Galápagos Islands
facts.body: The Galápagos are volcanic islands in the Pacific nearly 1,000 kilometres west of Ecuador, to which they belong. Their isolation produced unique wildlife such as giant tortoises, marine iguanas and many species of finch. Charles Darwin's visit in 1835 helped shape his later theory of evolution by natural selection.

facts.title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
facts.body: Katsushika Hokusai produced this woodblock print around 1831 for his series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji. A towering wave threatens fishing boats while the mountain appears small in the distance. It is the best-known work of ukiyo-e, the Japanese art of 'pictures of the floating world', which strongly influenced European artists such as Monet and Van Gogh.

facts.title: Ziryab
facts.body: Ziryab was a 9th-century musician who left Baghdad for Córdoba, where he served the Umayyad emir Abd al-Rahman II. He is credited with adding a fifth string to the oud and founding a music school, and with bringing new fashions in dress and dining to al-Andalus. Many details of his life are legendary, but he symbolises the transfer of eastern Islamic culture to Spain.

facts.title: Prussian blue was discovered by accident
facts.body: Around 1706 a Berlin colour-maker trying to make a red got a deep blue instead, because one of his ingredients was contaminated. Prussian blue is often called the first modern synthetic pigment.

facts.title: The Kyoto School
facts.body: The Kyoto School was a group of 20th-century Japanese philosophers centred on Nishida Kitarō at Kyoto University. They sought to combine Western philosophy, especially German thought, with Zen Buddhist ideas, notably the concept of 'absolute nothingness'. It is regarded as the first major movement to bring Japanese philosophy into dialogue with the West, though the wartime nationalism of some members remains controversial.

facts.title: Debt Cancellation in Mesopotamia
facts.body: Rulers in ancient Mesopotamia periodically proclaimed edicts, known in Babylonia as misharum, that cancelled certain debts and freed people who had fallen into debt bondage. Such decrees were issued by Babylonian kings in the first half of the second millennium BC, continuing a tradition attested in Sumer centuries earlier. Historians often see them as attempts to stop debt from ruining the free peasants on whom armies and taxes depended.

facts.title: The Constitution of India
facts.body: Drafted by a Constituent Assembly whose drafting committee was chaired by B. R. Ambedkar, it came into force on 26 January 1950, which India celebrates as Republic Day. One of the longest written national constitutions, it created a federal parliamentary republic, granted universal adult suffrage from the outset and abolished untouchability.

facts.title: Mushrooms create their own breeze
facts.body: Mushrooms release water vapour that cools the air around them. A 2016 study showed this makes small air currents that lift spores out from under the cap, so they can spread even when the air is still.

facts.title: Persian, a Language of Empires
facts.body: After the Arab conquest of Iran, New Persian emerged in the 9th and 10th centuries, written in Arabic script with many Arabic loanwords, and Ferdowsi's Shahnameh helped establish it as a literary language. For centuries Persian was a language of administration, poetry and diplomacy from Anatolia to Central Asia and India, including at the Mughal court. Its influence shows in the vocabulary of Turkish, Urdu, Hindi and many other languages.

facts.title: Communications Satellites
facts.body: In 1945 the writer Arthur C. Clarke proposed relaying signals via satellites in geostationary orbit, which circle the Earth once a day and so appear fixed in the sky. In 1962 the satellite Telstar relayed the first live transatlantic television pictures. Communications satellites soon made live global broadcasts and long-distance telephone links routine.

facts.title: The Kingdom of Aksum
facts.body: Aksum, in present-day northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, was a major trading power from roughly the 1st to the 7th century AD, linking the Roman world, Arabia and India via the Red Sea. It minted its own coins and raised tall stone stelae. In the 4th century King Ezana adopted Christianity.

facts.title: An element was named after a living chemist
facts.body: In 1997 element 106 was officially named seaborgium after American chemist Glenn Seaborg while he was still alive. Only one other element, oganesson, has been named after a person living at the time.

facts.title: Hipparchus and the Precession of the Equinoxes
facts.body: In the 2nd century BC the Greek astronomer Hipparchus, working mainly on Rhodes, compiled one of the first star catalogues, recording the positions and brightness of hundreds of stars. Comparing his measurements with older observations, he found that the equinox points drift slowly against the stars, a motion now known to be caused by a slow wobble of the Earth's axis. He also developed early trigonometry, and his work underpinned Ptolemy's Almagest.

facts.title: The Yangtze River
facts.body: The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia, flowing from the Tibetan Plateau across China to the East China Sea at Shanghai. Its basin holds a large share of China's people and much of its rice farming. The river has long served as the traditional dividing line between northern and southern China.

facts.title: Kalidasa's Shakuntala
facts.body: Kalidasa, who probably lived around the 4th or 5th century AD, is regarded as the greatest poet and playwright of classical Sanskrit. His play Shakuntala tells of a king who marries a girl raised in a hermitage, forgets her under a curse and finally recognises her. Translated into English in 1789, it enchanted European readers, among them Goethe.

facts.title: A Polish Christmas table has a spare seat
facts.body: At the Christmas Eve supper, Wigilia, many Polish families set an extra place. It is kept for an unexpected guest or wanderer, so nobody is turned away.

facts.title: Ottoman Mehter Music
facts.body: The mehter was the military band of the Ottoman Janissaries, with shrill zurnas, kettledrums, cymbals and a large bass drum. Its sound fascinated Europeans and inspired a 'Turkish' style, heard in Mozart's Rondo alla Turca and the march in the finale of Beethoven's Ninth. This Turkish-style music helped bring the bass drum, cymbals and triangle into Western orchestral writing.

facts.title: Hegel's Dialectic
facts.body: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770–1831) saw history as the progressive self-realisation of Spirit (Geist) towards freedom. His dialectic describes how ideas and societies develop through contradictions that are overcome yet preserved in a higher stage. The formula 'thesis, antithesis, synthesis' is often attached to him, though he did not use it to describe his method. His thought shaped Marx and much of later European philosophy.

facts.title: Ujamaa in Tanzania
facts.body: With the Arusha Declaration of 1967, Tanzania's president Julius Nyerere launched ujamaa, a form of African socialism named after the Swahili word for 'familyhood'. Banks and major industries were nationalised, and millions of rural people were moved, often under pressure, into collective villages. The policy brought gains in literacy and national unity, but agricultural output suffered and it was gradually abandoned in the 1980s, especially after Nyerere stepped down in 1985.

facts.title: The erhu's bow is trapped between its strings
facts.body: The Chinese erhu has just two strings and no fingerboard. Its bow hair passes between the two strings, so the bow cannot be removed and the player plays by pushing it against one string or the other.

facts.title: Machiavelli's The Prince
facts.body: Written around 1513 and published in 1532, Niccolò Machiavelli's The Prince advised rulers to judge actions by their results for the state rather than by conventional morality, arguing that it is safer to be feared than loved if one cannot be both. It made 'Machiavellian' a byword for cunning, though his Discourses on Livy reveal a committed republican.

facts.title: The International Phonetic Alphabet
facts.body: The International Phonetic Alphabet was created by the International Phonetic Association, founded in Paris in 1886, to give one symbol to each distinct speech sound in any language. Based largely on Latin letters with additions such as ʃ and ŋ, it lets linguists, language teachers and dictionaries record pronunciation unambiguously. It has been revised periodically as knowledge of the world's sounds has grown.

facts.title: The Magnetic Compass
facts.body: Chinese scholars knew that a magnetised needle points north and south, and the Song dynasty writer Shen Kuo described the needle compass in the late 11th century. Within a few decades it was being used for navigation at sea. The compass appeared in Europe around 1200 and became essential for ocean voyages.

facts.title: Clownfish can change from male to female
facts.body: Clownfish live in small groups in a sea anemone, led by one large female and her male mate. All start as males, and if the female dies her mate becomes female and the next largest fish takes his place.

facts.title: The 1973 Chilean Coup
facts.body: On 11 September 1973 Chile's armed forces overthrew the elected socialist president Salvador Allende, who died during the attack on the presidential palace. General Augusto Pinochet then ruled as dictator until 1990; thousands of opponents were killed or disappeared and many more were tortured or exiled.

facts.title: Hanaoka Seishū and General Anaesthesia
facts.body: In 1804 the Japanese surgeon Hanaoka Seishū removed a breast tumour from a patient under general anaesthesia, using a herbal drink he had developed. This was decades before ether anaesthesia was publicly demonstrated in Boston in 1846. Because Japan was largely closed to the outside world, his work had little influence abroad, while ether and chloroform soon transformed surgery in the West.

facts.title: The Demographic Transition
facts.body: The demographic transition is the model, developed by social scientists in the mid-20th century, of how populations change as societies modernise. First death rates fall thanks to better food, sanitation and medicine, and the population grows rapidly; later birth rates also fall, and growth slows. It describes the experience of Europe and many other regions, though not every country follows the same path.

facts.title: A Chinese fraction nailed pi for centuries
facts.body: In the 5th century, Zu Chongzhi gave 355/113 as an approximation of pi, correct to six decimal places. For almost 900 years afterwards, no one is known to have calculated a more precise value.

facts.title: The School of Athens
facts.body: Raphael painted this fresco between about 1509 and 1511 in a room of the papal apartments in the Vatican. It gathers the great thinkers of antiquity in an imagined classical hall, with Plato and Aristotle at the centre. Its balanced composition and deep perspective make it a model of High Renaissance painting.

facts.title: Hip Hop
facts.body: Hip hop arose in the Bronx, New York, in the 1970s, at block parties where DJs such as Kool Herc looped the drum breaks of records. Its elements were DJing, rapping, breakdancing and graffiti. From 'Rapper's Delight' in 1979 onwards it grew into one of the most influential forms of popular music worldwide.

facts.title: Ambedkar and Navayana Buddhism
facts.body: Bhimrao Ambedkar, the Dalit leader and jurist born into an 'untouchable' caste, concluded that Hinduism could not be reformed to end caste discrimination. In 1956 in Nagpur he converted to Buddhism together with hundreds of thousands of his followers, weeks before his death. His rationalist, socially engaged reading of Buddhism, set out in The Buddha and His Dhamma, inspired a movement among Dalits often called Navayana or Ambedkarite Buddhism.

facts.title: Benjamin Franklin's daylight-saving idea was a joke
facts.body: Franklin's 1784 essay about Parisians wasting candles was satire. Modern daylight saving was proposed by New Zealand insect collector George Hudson in 1895, who wanted more evening light for bug hunting.

facts.title: The South Sea Bubble
facts.body: The South Sea Company, granted a monopoly of British trade with Spanish America, took over much of the national debt in 1720 in exchange for its own shares. Its share price soared in a speculative frenzy and collapsed later that year, ruining many investors. A parallel bubble in John Law's Mississippi Company burst in France the same year.

facts.title: The Refugee Convention
facts.body: The 1951 UN Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees defines a refugee as a person outside their country with a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. Its core principle, non-refoulement, forbids returning refugees to places where they face serious threats. A 1967 protocol removed its original limits in time and geography.

facts.title: The Vernacular Chinese Movement
facts.body: For two thousand years formal Chinese writing used Classical Chinese, a terse literary language far from everyday speech. Around 1917 reformers such as Hu Shi and Chen Duxiu called for writing in the vernacular, baihua, and Lu Xun's story 'A Madman's Diary' (1918) showed what modern fiction in it could do. Linked to the May Fourth Movement, the change brought written Chinese close to spoken Mandarin.
